title: Anthology of brawny Lumberjacks and the ladies with gumption who catch their heart.
text:
Synopsis:
Each story moves us further in time, from mid 19th century through the Gilded age, and from east to west US.

1. All That Glitters by Candice Sue Patterson
North Lubec ME, Summer 1851
Wini Hayes, who never learnt how to swim, has to take over supplying the Lobster for the local prison since her brothers and father left for the gold rush in Cali. She bravely ventures out alone every morning to empty the traps- which are heavy- having the wives of her brothers, their children and her mother dependent on her. Jess Lee, owner of a Lumberjack concern, jumps into the ocean when he witnesses a Lobsterman fall out of his boat, he is surprised to find it's actually a Lobsterlady. Needless to say the honor of 'Best Meet-Cute' of the anthology goes to this one.

There is a fascinating conspiracy plot that is uncovered by the protagonists, based on a true event, interesting historical details, and in my very biased opinion, the best setting. The imagery of Maine in the summer, the water, the natural beauty, was evocative throughout.

2. Winter Roses By Pegg Thomas
Michigan, Winter 1865
Wesley Fisk a Union sergeant veteran is arriving via ship from Buffalo NY to Michigan to earn some money as a lumberjack. Eliza Beth Edmonds is also on said ship and they both have the same destination. After being dismissed from her teachers position in favor of a man returned from war, Eliza Beth has no choice but to rejoin her mother as cook for a lumbering camp. She worked hard for her education and does not desire to return to the isolated camp. The profession claimed the life of her father, and she does not want to live surrounded by that life and death uncertainty. So when Wesley starts to intrigue her, she must guard her heart, she could not bear loving a lumberman, no matter how charming.

This one had a really cute development between the leads, cute romantic gestures, and incredible winter imagery.

3. Not For Love by Naomi Musch
Wisconsin, Winter/Spring 1881
Maggie Duncan at 22 years young is 2 months a widow from a love match. However if she does not find another husband to help her run her farm, she won't be able to afford it, and with a persistent buyer closing in, she can't afford to observe a full mourning. She enlists the help of a kindly traveling priest to take a letter she wrote detailing her predicament up to the lumber camps he will visit. The priest and her brother are rightly worried who may answer the ad and how honorable their intentions may be.

Jack McAllister is read the letter, and begins to entertain the idea. He always wanted his own farm, and was friends with the widow's husband, from who he heard good, domestic blissful things about Maggie, so after much deliberating he goes for it.

This one was the most poignant, featuring beautiful prose, and overall quite moving. The slow burn here was executed to perfection.

4. Undercover Logger by Jennifer Lamont Leo
Idaho, Winter 1890
Michael Tate, is the son of a wealthy Chicago banker, when he gets on the newspaper headlines for drinking, partying, and roughhousing his father exiles him to the Idaho branch of the bank as punishment to work under his uncle who runs it. Michael is far from thrilled to be sent from his cushy city life to the sticks, leaving behind the lady he thought he may one day marry.

In the train ride over, Michael meets a lady who reminds him of one back home he had been courting. Carrie Coker at 23 years of age is a widow fresh out of mourning. She is returning with some urgency to the business her husband left her, Coker Lumber, after being alerted she has 60 days to pay a bank loan she wasn't aware was outstanding. Out of depth with how one runs a business, she had been relying on the aid of her husbands cousin, Reed Coker, for the past year.

Michael's uncle assigns him some unorthodox work, having him go undercover in the Coker Lumber business to see how it is possible it is performing so poorly.

The conspiracy was creative & clever, the chemistry between the leads was palpable, and the resolution utterly satisfying.

The Brass Tacks:
I am actually not huge on short stories, but I had to pick up a story that included my dear Maine as a setting. To my immense delight this exceeded my expectations and I adored all the stories. I highly recommend this collection. I tend to read HR's that feature Heiresses and gentry, so this story full of self made heroes and heroines, who work the land, who live in challenging, humble circumstances was a breath of fresh air.

There was not a runt in this litter of yarns, I loved them all! Considering they are each around 120 pages give or take they did an excellent job fleshing out the characters, the atmosphere of the time, and each featured admirable protagonists, especially the ladies, who were strong and self sufficient. They were not looking for romance, they were realists in a tough time.

I liked how the love interests only complimented them, rather than completed them, for they were already capable all on their own. They were partners, each pulling their own weight, as it ought to be.

Most intriguing plots: Undercover Logger & All that Glitters
Best Setting & Meet Cute: All that Glitters
Favorite female protagonists:Winter Roses & Not for Love
Favorite male protagonists: Undercover Logger & Not for Love
Best Chemistry: Undercover Logger & Winter Roses
Favorite Prose: Not for Love

I received an ARC from the publisher via Netgalley in exchange for my honest opinion.

title: There is no Morgenstern
text: I have to laugh while reading some of the reviews where people are bothered that Goldman took Morgenstern’s classic book and added a bunch of random comments. In case you didn’t catch on…MORGENSTERN NEVER EXISTED. Goldman is pretending the entire time to be abridging a classic book but in reality Goldman is the original author. THIS is The Princess Bride. I find that to be the sign of a literary genius to have fooled so many. Some may get annoyed by his continual interrupting of the story. I found many of his comments to be hilarious. But I suppose if I hadn’t realized that he was the original author that I might have gotten more annoyed. I’m sure I’m in the minority but I actually prefer the book to the movie. I found myself laughing out loud while reading…a sure sign of a great book.

title: Beautiful writing and lovable characters
text:
Nina LaCour writes heartfelt and heartbreaking stories about people finding each other through all kinds of life's tragedies. Yerba Buena is a beautiful LGBGQ+ romance and, ultimately, a story of two women trying to move beyond life's painful memories. Yerba Buena is a the healing herb, and its presence in both of the women's lives is what ultimately connects them together.

I don't want to give much more of the plot away, so I will just say that if you are not yet a fan of Nina LaCour-- you should be. While some of her other books skew more young adult, this one feels meant for adults. It's beautiful writing, lovable characters, and an immersive story told in multiple perspectives.

title: Frustrating
text:
So, let me begin by saying, I read the first 6 books of the series in less than a month. I LOVED them. I loved the way they were written, how the characters began to develop and evolve, but still leaving the tension of who was going to end up on the throne just under the surface. I preordered the 7th book as soon as I finished so it would be delivered to my Kindle ASAP.

That being said, I was hugely disappointed. I had to double check and make sure the same authors had written this book. It felt rushed and the language completely changed. It became crass and more vulgar than it needed to be. I am not a prude by any stretch of the imagination, but some of the verbiage sounded like I had stepped into a frat house. It made it very difficult to connect the characters in this book with the ones I had become invested with previously. It's one thing to have a characters attitude or outlook change, but to change the very way they speak makes it difficult for the reader.

This point aside, this book did feel like a lot of filler. There was so much potential and it seems like a wasted opportunity. I will be reading the next book because I have a compulsion to finish any series (no matter how horrible) that I start. I am just holding out hope that the authors take into account mine and so many other reviews. I hate to see a series finish weak or rushed and I hope they can get it back to the Zodiac characters we love for the final book.

title: Sweet and steamy friends-to-lovers, fake relationship romance!
text:
Tease is the perfect friends-to-lovers, fake relationship story! There's so much heart and passion, steam and sweetness, and of course the best HEA!

Oh sweet Hutton and Felicity! They've both harbored feelings for each other but neither one wanted to risk their friendship. Hutton has terrible anxiety and some quirks that make him relatable and sweet. Melanie Harlow did an excellent job writing about the tough subject of anxiety. When Hutton's dominant side comes out behind closed doors, you'll likely need to fan yourself! Felicity has some quirks of her own that make her an amazing person and someone you'd want to be friends with. Like blurting out things when she's nervous! Gah! I loved it!

These two complete each other in all the best ways! I love how they have seen each other at their best and their worst. They have always been there for one another and even have their own secret code they write in. Hutton makes Felicity feel beautiful and special. She helps him to feel grounded and accepted. I can't say enough positive things about this book! Very highly recommend it!

title: Biblical Christmas with a little gingerbread spice!
text:
25 single-spread stories that are engaging to read and a joy to look at. It covers most of the Biblical aspects to the Christmas story, mixing in everyday creative license like conversations, and leaves out traditionalist elements not found in Scripture (aside from the traditional names of the Magi), quoting extensively from the KJV with an appendix of longer passages. I love the quirky humor and the imagery, and the illustrations are of the timeless variety that stand out amongst the hyperrealistic art or cartoonish characters we are seeing right now.

I’d say it’s best for reading aloud to or with school-aged kids, but could be enjoyed alone by upper elementary or older; preschoolers would enjoy the pictures and a parent-edited readaloud. I plan to purchase a few copies to send to friends and their children for next year!

title: A fantastically fun educational read !
text: Wow… the author of this book is one-of-a-kind! The biographical story of this important man’s life is told in an eloquently-worded & perfectly laid out book that I did NOT want to put down once I started (I also didn’t want it to end, but here we are). Lister’s is such an essential story that I only briefly learned about going to school to become an Animal Nurse here in America, but none the less one whose contributions are far-reaching & still implicated today. This book taught me a lot about how dangerous & archaic medicine was up until fairly recently, & those stories not only added to the entertainment aspect of the book but also my appreciation for the way things are done in the field today. I highly recommend this book to anyone with an interest in or passion for medicine & history. Thank you to the author for taking the time to write this excellent book encompassing one man’s vital contributions to science & medicine.

title: I'm Loving This Series!
text:
I found this series of books when the Hoopla app suggested book one based on my reading history. I read various genres and discovered a renewed love of children's books several years ago when I became a mother. Mostly, I read middle-grade books with my 12-year-old at night, but sometimes I find myself reading them alone.

This is the second book in the series, and I enjoyed it just as much as the first. I loved book one so much that I purchased a physical copy for my son, and I will be buying this one, also. In book one, Arcade receives a magical token that allows him to travel to different places using a magical elevator. At the end of book one, the story left us with questions about the origins of the token. Book two answers some of those questions.

The story takes place in Virginia when Arcade and his sister, Zowie, return to their former hometown to visit their cousins Derek and Celeste. Arcade's new friend from New York, Doug, goes with them. There are new adventures for the five children and lessons about humility, generosity, and forgiveness.

As a mother and a Christian, I loved how the author included references to the Bible throughout the book. He did it with a light touch that was not the least preachy and would appeal to kids. When it comes to books that entertain kids and teaches them essential life lessons, you can't get better than this series! Happy reading!

title: What a delightful read from beginning to the end.
text:
A state of perfection for this cozy crime mystery!

Molly, the Maid, is a little different than everyone else, she may not always understand but she always shows up. Brought up by her Gran, she learns to live a humble life, where doesn't feel above or below anyone and she feels incredibly blessed. She loves her job as a maid at the Regency Grand Hotel.

There is something so uniquely refreshing about Molly, you can't help but adore her. Beginning to understand her and all her quirks was a journey. I found myself sighing out "Oh Molly" several times. By the time I hit the 58% I knew where it was going and my heart didn't slow down again until the end.

Never judge a book by its cover; when people underestimate Molly and frame her for things she would never be involved in, she becomes confused and upset. Once she pieces her puzzle together, she becomes angry. Watching her fight her way out of a tough spot was empowering. I loved that she kind some kind and loving people to support her.

What a delightful read from beginning to the end.

title: Fun space adventure with great leads and a unique voice
text:
This was my first science fantasy book ever - and oh, I was not disappointed! I had so much fun reading this.

This is the story of Gideon Nav, who lives in the Dominicus star system in the Ninth House. Being an indentured servant, she constantly tries to escape, only to have her last attempt foiled by Harrowhark, the Ninth House heiress, who is about to compete to become an immortal necromancer and a right hand of the Emperor. What results is them traveling to a crumbling palace, where, with members of seven other houses, they must work together to solve the mystery and discover the secrets of the Lyctors, or immortal necromancers.

There was such a unique voice and I loved Gideon and Harrow and their dynamic so much. I found myself chuckling at some of the things they said - which doesn’t happen often!

It took me awhile to understand all the worldbuilding, but much of it is explained in further detail after the Epilogue. I didn’t connect much with the side characters - I felt like I didn’t know them that well even though they were quite present in the story, so it didn’t matter to me much when some of them met their fates.

Still, the ending took me by surprise and the climactic battle was fun to read, and it leaves several questions unanswered which I assume will be addressed in the sequel.

Looking forward to reading part 2 in this trilogy!

title: The Moral Failure of a Pope
text:
We like to think that our religious leaders are people of faith who are not afraid to speak against worldly powers of oppression and destruction. We expect a moral vision and example from them, that they will even risk their lives to do the right thing. You won’t find that leader in these pages. Pope Pius II was primarily concerned with protecting his flock of Catholics. He heard the heartbreaking stories of the rounding up and extermination of Jews. But he would take a stand. By staying neutral, insisting the church had no political voice, he fantasized being able to broker peace at the end of the war.

David I. Kertzer’s book on Pope Pius XI, The Pope and Mussolini, won the Pulitzer Prize. At his death in 1939, the outspoken Pope Pius XI was replaced by Pope Pious XII, the preferred choice of Germany, as he had lived in German and spoke the language fluently. Unlike his predecessor, Pope Pius XII determined to do nothing that would bring repercussions to Catholicism. He went out of his way to not upset Hitler or Mussolini. He silenced the Vatican press, insisted the church had no interest in politics, and even preached that heads of state were God-ordained.

Pope Pius XII’s archives have been finally opened and Kertzer’s study of thousand of pages of these documents, and other government declassified documents, brought about startling revelations.

Mussolini needed the pope and the halo of Catholicism, and the pope cooperated. H truly believed that the Nazis would win the war and rule Europe. He didn’t want Catholics to be victims of fascist wrath.

Catholic oppressions of Jews was ingrained with practices that kept them separated, impoverished, and unable to exert power. The Nazis claimed they weren’t really doing anything that the Catholics weren’t already doing. Somehow, they skipped over the death camps.

Perhaps the pope did protect some Catholics from fascist repercussion. The Polish Catholics pleaded for him to intervene. His acquiescence allowed Hitler free reign in his crusade of genocide of all Jews. The pope fought to protect baptized Jews, but remained silent even when the Nazis came for Rome’s own Jewish population.

It’s a broad history with a large cast that takes us into the complicated relations between Italy, Germany, and the Vatican.

I received a free egalley from the publisher through NetGalley. My review is fair and unbiased.

title: Compelling tales
text:
Lobodón Garra was one of the noms de plume of Liborio Justo (1902 - 2003), son of Argentine president General Agustín P. Justo (1932 to 1938). The thirties in Argentina were called the Década Infame (Infamous Decade) where reactionary conservative governments were installed on the basis of scandalously rigged elections. Liborio’s take on politics was the opposite of his father’s; during a reception given by the latter in honor of President F. D. Roosevelt Liborio shouted “Down with Yankee Imperialism!”. He was an active participant in left wing causes such as university reform, a political theorist, a supporter of of the IV International and believed the unification of South America would be a decisive step in ending US and European pillage.

Liborio was a writer of note. Some of his books were political traits like Leon Trotzky and Wall Street (1959) or Our Vassal Country (5 tomes, 1968/1993). Others were literary like his first, La Tierra Maldita (The Cursed Land, 1932), a collection of short stories based on Liborio’s own experiences in the far south of the American continent. Some of the tales are about historical happenings, such as the 1928 disappearance of the Kobenhavn, a Danish five-masted barque used as naval training vessel, or the annihilation of Admiral Von Spee’s squadron, fresh from its victory at Coronel, at the hands the British Navy in 1914. Other tales are of more personal character. The scenarios are the stormy coasts of Patagonia subject to the fury of the winds, the Magellan Straits, the solitary, treacherous channels and deserted islands of Southern Patagonia, the city of Ushuaia (southernmost in the world, fronting the Beagle Channel) and the legendary Cape Horn, a few miles south, grave of many ships. Some of these stories have echoes of Jack London and of B. Traven’s The Death Ship.

I read one of these tales, The Battle, long ago, in my early youth. The story left an indelible imprint in my memory. I read it again recently with the same awe. Unfortunately, Justo’s works seem not to have been translated into English, and are not in Kindle (even in their original Spanish). I hope this omission is remedied.

title: Strait of Magellan in Spain?
text:
Am I the only person disturbed by Settle mistakenly referring to the Strait of Gibraltar as the Strait of Magellan? Not once but twice. The former is the narrow expanse of sea between Spain and Morocco. The latter is a passage at the southern tip of South America. This seems an egregious error in a travel narrative that covers the invasion of Spain across the Strait of Gibraltar from North Africa and discusses Spanish history in the Americas during the Age of Exploration including Magellan.

Such fact-checking would normally fall to the book's editor, and I originally dismissed the mislabeled geography from one who came from West Virginia and Eastern Kentucky since I too grew up in the hollers of Appalachia. But Ms. Settle is much too worldly for the error having lived in England and Turkiye among other countries. So, I tried to remind myself how the author herself frequently mentioned getting lost in Spain as she traveled around the country. But that's not the same as sitting at your desk months later writing about the journey and calling Spain Chile.

Fortunately for me, the errors come so late in the book I finished reading it anyway. But now I'm finding it hard to take seriously.

title: A FRANK MEMOIR, WITH REVEALING INSIGHTS, BY A PROMINENT GANG MEMBER
text:
Kody Scott wrote in the Preface of this 1993 book, “I have lived in South Central Los Angeles all my life. I grew up on Florence and Normandie. That is a part of my territory. I was recruited into the Crips at the ripe old age of eleven. Today I am twenty-nine years old. I am a gang expert---period. There are no other gang experts except participants… I have come full circle in my twenty-nine years… sixteen of those with the Crips. I have pushed people violently out of this existence and have fathered three children. I have felt completely free and have sat in total solitary confinement in San Quentin state prison. I have shot numerous people and have been shot seven times myself. I have been in gunfights in South Central and knife fights in Folsom state prison. Today, I languish at the bottom of one of the strictest maximum-security state prisons in this country.

“I propose to take my reader through the life and times of my own chilling involvement as a gang member with the Crips… to allow my readers the first ever glimpse at South Central from my side of the gun, street, fence, and wall…. Although no longer aligned with gang or criminal activity, I still draw a great deal of support from this quarter… It is not for glory that I write this. It is out of desperation for the survival of the youths and civilians who are directly and indirectly involved in the fighting. I will attempt to draw serous analytical conclusions designed to bring about a better, more in-depth overstanding of this malady, so as to help reach workable solutions for all concerned.”

He recounts, “Crazy De overstood me and my thirst for a reputation---the purpose of all gang members. For I had learned early that there were three stages of reputation to go through before the title of O.G.---Original Gangster---would apply righteously. 1. You must build the reputation of your name… as a individual. 2. You must build your name in association with your particular set, so that when your name is spoken … it is synonymous; and 3. You must establish yourself as a promoter of Crip or Blood, depending, of course, on which side of the color bar you live.” (Pg. 14-15)

His mother came to visit him in Juvenile Hall: “she looked straight into my eyes … and spoke through quivering lips. ‘Kody, what has happened to you? What is wrong?’ And for the first time in a while I started to shed tears and could not speak… My life was totally consumed by all aspects of gang life. I had turned my bedroom into a virtual command post, launching attacks from my house with escalating frequency. My clothes, walk, talk, and attitude all reflected my love for and allegiance to my set. Nobody was more important than my homeboys… My transformation was subtle. I guess this is why most parents can’t nip it in the bud.” (Pg. 69)

He advises, “With each new generation of Crip and Blood bangers comes a more complex system, which is now reaching institutional proportions. It is precisely because of this type of participation in the development and expansion of these groups’ mores, customs, and philosophies that gangbanging will never be stopped from without. The notion of the ‘war on gangs’ being successful is as realistic as the People’s Republic of China telling Americans to stop being American. When gang members stop their wars and find that there is no longer a need for their set to exist, banging will cease. But until then, all attempts to law enforcement to seriously curtail its forward motion will be in vain.” (Pg. 79)

He recalls, “At sixteen I felt twenty-four. Life meant very little to me. I felt that my purpose on earth was to bang… I had little respect for life when practically all my life I had seen people assaulted, maimed, and blown away at very young ages, and no one seemed to care… the underlying factor that usually got you killed was the principle. The principle is respect, a linchpin… magnified by thirty in the ghettos and slums across America. I had no idea of peace and tranquility… The set was my clearest vision of stability.” (Pg. 102-103)

A fellow gang member\s came to visit him in the ICU: “I was Li’l Bro’s hero, the closest thing he had to total invincibility… We hugged briefly, as much as my stitches would allow, and then Bro left without looking back. It was times like this that I hated my life. Perhaps this was due to my not knowing answers to certain questions or being able to present my emotions on an intelligible level. Being ignorant is, to me, the equivalent to being dead.” (Pg. 117)

He explains, “the threat of being in prison for life was a m-thaf-cka. What we did in the juvenile tank was reflected in side the prisons where we were headed… I didn’t want to stay here all my life, but I had no way to stop the wheels of fate… If I just stopped gangbanging, perhaps I could avoid prison, an early death, and a few other occupational hazards. But to ‘just stop’ is like to ‘just say no’ to drugs… It ‘just wasn’t happening.’” (Pg. 163)

He recounts, “One particular night I rode up on a carload of Miller Gangster Bloods … I was on a ten-speed bike, and once I confirmed that they were enemy, I … emptied my clip into the faces and bodies of the occupants. Our of bounds, trespassing, free-fire zone---hell, I had a dozen reasons to fire on them. ‘Free country’ never crossed my mind. Besides, this wasn’t America---it was South Central.” (Pg. 169)

He recalls, “I had been reading Mario Puzo’s ‘The Godfather’ and was devising a grand scheme for the set based on the Corleone family structure. Never did I take into account that first and foremost the Italians had a clear sense of who they were… they understood their heritage and their relation to the world as European people. We, on the other hand, were just Crips with no sense of anything before us or where we were headed. We were trapped behind the veil of cultural ignorance without even knowing it. Yet here I was, trying to pattern our set after some established people, Europeans at that.” (Pg. 207-208)

He states, “In my cell… I reread for the hundredth time ‘Message to the Oppressed’… I felt the words seeping deeper into me, their power coursing through my body, giving me strength to push on. I was changing. I felt it. For once I didn’t challenge it or see it as being a threat to the established mores of the ‘hood,’ though, of course, it was. Muhammed’s teachings corresponded with my condition of being repressed on the Rock. Never could I have been touched by such teachings in the street.” (Pg. 223)

He observes, “In a perverted sort of way I enjoyed being Monster Kody. I lived for the power surge of playing God, having the power of life and death in my hands. Nothing I knew could compare with riding in a car with three other homeboys with guns, knowing that they were as deadly and courageous as I was. To me, at this time in life, this was power…. The thought of controlling something substantial---like land---never occurred to me. The thought of responsibility for the welfare of my daughter… never crossed my mind. I was only responsible to my ‘hood and my homeboys.” (Pg. 226)

His mother told him, “Kody, I have tried my hardest to raise you guys up right. But I had to work hard every day just to feed you by myself. You know Scott and I got a divorce in 1969 and there has not been a man in your lives since. I wonder if that’s how I lost you and Shaun to the streets. You guys have turned… into savage little animals and I lust don’t know what to do no more. I really don’t.” “But Mom, it’s not your fault, it’s not your fault,’ I said over and over.” (Pg. 332)

He later realizes, “I learned that I had to be a real father to my own children, no matter what. The pain I was experiencing because of my parents’ promiscuity and father’s lack of responsibility was not something I wanted my children to feel.” (Pg. 348)

He concludes, “What it boils down to is an overwhelming sense of inadequacy, the invisible man syndrome… it would seem that this country’s 130-year-old experiment of multiculturalism has failed. Perhaps it was never designed to work. My fear is that an atmosphere is developing here similar to that in Bosnia and Herzegovina due to the failure of positive multicultural existence My person al belief is that separation is the solution.” (Pg. 382)

This very insightful book will be of great interest to those studying inner-city gangs.

title: A good primer on how to retire via the stock market, but also totally uninspired and derivative
text:
Not really a bad book on investing and saving, but it is overly simplistic. The entire book can be summarized in what I already knew it would be about before reading: save as much money as possible and invest it in an ETF to reduce risk.

The prose is well-written, though there are some places where it is literally unfinished (Missing sentences at the ends of chapters). Problem is, his information is derivative. It's directly ripped from his footnotes, with the exception that the footnotes provide much more nuanced details about the subject matter. A Random Walk Down Wall Street, by Burton J. Malkiel, will offer much more detailed and descriptive statements about investor panic and the madness of crowds than this book ever could. The structure is also poor and needed to be edited. He shouldn't be giving this broad and generic investing advice for value investing because it's a very complicated and nuanced subject, and even reading ten books that go into great technical detail about what investors like Warren Buffett do will not scratch the surface, so the bludgeoning simplicity of his statements are not just out of place but quite frankly dangerous.

Now, truth be told, about half of Americans can put an extra 10-20k they'd spend on a new car or other luxury item into an ETF and hold it for a very long time. So that's fine advice, but the rest of this stuff just feels out of place and besides, the synopsis of this book is financial freedom, not retirement planning. I was hoping for a little bit more creative and unique information, but I suppose most of this book is passable as the cliffnotes for the far superior books he references in his footnotes, which are books that someone who is serious about making money investing in the stock market should read.

title: Interesting (full spoilers).
text:
I don't have words to describe this short story. All I can really say is interesting.

The story is about a slave girl named Sully, and her connection to a girl she birth after murdering the family that owned her. Yeah!

One night Sully slips poison into the tea of the people who are holding her captive as a slave. When the family of five pass out, Sully brutally murders them all. While she is burying the bodies, she goes into labor; her belly spontaneously swell, and she pushes out a child. The child instantly starts growing into an adult. This kid starts talking and everything.

We quickly are told why Ziza has been born. Ziza is a soul from the Etherworld made flesh through Sully's womb. The Etherworld (afterlife) must correct disturbances. When Sully murdered her slave family, she created a rift\ anomaly that had to be repaired to creates a balance. Sully's unending anger and act of murder did a number on the Etherworld.

Sulky Sully. That's what I call her because she is quite ornery. She is very resistant to Ziza's offers of friendship and companionship at first. A few months have passed and Sully gives birth to more ghost people. Five souls for the five people she murdered in cold blood.

Overtime, Sully learns to trust, except others, and love. She loves her weird ghost children so much that she hatches up a plan to overtake her town. She wants her ghost kids to live in peace.

This book was wild, and I would love to read more about the weird Etherworld, and it's inhabitants.

This is kind of a weird review. I'm trying something different. I like this story because it is like nothing that I have read before. I've never read of someone birthing themselves.

The story is a little rushed, but it left me wanting more. A scene where the Etherworld ghost fight the towns people would have been great, but that would turn this short into a novel. However, Sully progression doesn't seem too rushed.

If you want something that strange and quirky, this is definitely the story for you.

title: Insightful book
text:
I enjoyed the insight offered on each page of this book. The book also reminds researchers of the value of lived experiences of participants as part of research analysis. The people that have experienced prison, especially the young, can teach us a lot about what works and doesn’t work. They can also offer insight and solutions regarding the role PTSD play in the lives of ex-inmates. Reading the book confirmed that a lot of brilliant people end up in the penitentiary system. The system is clearly not meant to reform and at worst may be designed to keep a constant flow of cheap inmate labor. Clearly we are losing talent to the prison walls and prison industrial complex.

The author, T Lamont Baker, offers readers an opportunity to harness the wisdom and experiences of those that have been through the system. Baker is clearly smarter than many lawmakers and policymakers that developing shortsighted guidelines and policies. More research needs to come from the actual experiences of ex-inmates and their families. If we are serious about justice, reform, recidivism, and addressing mental health, this book is the best place start.

title: Good Reading of a Very Great Book
text: Herodotus is quite properly called the father of history, and his work remains among the most entertaining and enlightening books that have ever been made public.  His successor Thucydides deserves equal praise for applying profound political understanding to historical events.  As a hard-minded analyst of history, he has rarely been equalled, never surpassed.  I might, to clear up some confusion introduced by reviewers, that these are not essays but a coherent account of the origins and development of the wars between the Spartans and their allies and the Athenians and their allies.  As an Athenian political and military leader, Thucydides was exiled for a failure that was not his fault, and he thus had the opportunity to hear the various sides of the story.  He was a patriotic Athenian, but his family belonged to what we would now all the conservative party, and he treats Athens' self-glorification with considerable skepticism, though it is not always on the surface of his narrative.  His work is conventionally divided into books, but there are no real chapters, much less chapter titles.  This translation was made by Benjamin Jowett, an esteemed classical scholar of the Victorian period known best for his translation of Plato.  The earlier translation of Thomas Hobbes in the 17th century would be more difficult for readers and somewhat less accurate.  To appreciate this great work, it might help some readers to look first at a general history of ancient Greece, perhaps Bury's, for a broader context of what was at stake

title: This book sure lived up to its title, especially in the last two chapters of the book.
text:
Roger Craig wrote Strictly Business so you could get to know him as a football player and as a human being. And the book also served as a medium for Craig to air out his true feelings on his playing days as a San Franciso 49er running back from 1983 to 1990.

Craig saw his best days as a runner and pass catcher for the 49ers in the 1980s, but on the other hand it was cruel and sort of fitting that he saw his days as a forty-niner end during the 1990 season. That was also the season in which his production took a steep decline.

After being one of the focal points of 49ers offenses for seven straight years in the 1980s, a knee injury, a rookie running back named Dexter Carter, and a 49ers offense that was more concerned with passing the ball spelled the beginning of the end for Craig in San Francisco.

To me, the best chapters in this book were sixteen and seventeen. In those two chapters he laid it down how he felt about his last season in San Francisco, and then he discussed how he felt disrespected and tossed aside by 49ers management because of that infamous fumble in the 1990 NFC Championship game versus the New York Giants.

Meanwhile, another of Craig's aims in the book was to give you a limited amount of information on his private life which included his wife and kids, his budding acting career at the time, his modeling career, and etc. Some public figures don't want anyone knowing too much about their private life, they just want you to know about their entertainment career.

Pros of Strictly Business: The book gave you a good amount of information on Craig's playing career for the Niners in the latter part of the 1980s. Plus, Craig did a good job in giving you the reader his honest feelings on how he felt he was treated by his 49er head coach (George Seifert), his position coach (Al Lavan), the team owner (Eddie Debartolo Jr.), and others in team management after his fumble in the 1990 NFC Championship game.

Cons of Strictly Business: It would have been nice if Craig would have put in a chapter or two about his playing careers at Central High School (Iowa) and the University of Nebraska. There was barely a mention about two those stages of his football career.

In conclusion, it was the 1990 season in which Craig's frustrations with 49ers management reached its peak. And chapter seventeen was his chance to vent his frustrations with 49ers management. As mentioned before, Strictly Business was more than an autobiography on Roger Craig, the book also served as a therapy session for him, especially the last 24 pages of the book.

text:
I purchased this book at a used book sale awhile book. As a yoga teacher, I know it is important to focus on strengthening and stabilizing the entire joint rather than the often-heard idea of "hip opening." Author Charlotte Bell provides clear information and includes helpful illustrations. There are tips and postured offered pertaining to various types of hip dysfunction.

I had two reasons for giving this book 4 instead of 5 stars. The first is that there is an entire chapter on hip replacement surgery that includes information on finding a surgeon, questions to ask, recovery, etc.; for me, this information did not apply, and thus it felt out of place in this book. Secondly, there is minimal information on general sequencing for the hips, particularly how to develop a practice sequence focused on strengthening and preventing problems (rather than addressing issues after they arise). Still, I'm glad I purchased this book, as it has excellent information and will be a useful reference.

title: An amazingly horrifying middle grade horror!!!!
text:
“Did you know everyone is born with the capacity to be brave? The key is to prepare yourself before the challenging situation.”

I went up a hill, the hill was muddy, stomped my toe and made it bloody, should I wash it?

Justin is dealing with the recent loss of his mother when his best friend, Zee, returns from a long and terrifying disappearance. Only, Zee doesn’t return as he left. He’s changed. When Justin and his friends partake in a game of hide and seek that sets Zee off the deep end and unleashes a monster like never seen before, Justin understands why.

This was an extremely fun middle grade book! I love the concept of taking a childhood memory we’ve surely all experienced and flipping it on its head. I would have never thought a game of hide and seek that felt so mundane and normal could turn into something so horrifying. 😱

Because this book is middle grade, it’s written for the age group so don’t expect anything intricate. The characters are great, the evil ones so evil, the good ones so good, and the creepy ones so … *shudders*. Honestly, for a kids book, this is pretty darn scary! I don’t think I could’ve read this in elementary school. 😂

If you’ve got kids or are looking to dive into some fun, nostalgic, middle grade horror, this one’s for you! But the question is, are you ready to face your childhood fears? ☠️🪰

text:
This truly is a must-buy for any educator. This book provides so many useful tools and suggestions that we can implement immediately (even suggestions you can implement tomorrow!!). Sometimes learning about new concepts and theories in education can feel isolated, without much information about how to practice what we’re attempting to learn about. The structure of this book not only makes it an approachable and enjoyable read, but also makes it an excellent tool that I can easily reference back to.

I’ve always wanted my approach as a school psychologist to come from a place of strengths and encouragement, but felt lost with how to do so in a practical way. With the help of Byron and Kelsie’s reframes, I feel confident in my abilities to practice a strengths-based approach every day with all students, instead of just aspiring to do so. This book has the potential to significantly change our country’s education system in the best way possible, as long as we (as educators) are willing to read and take action!

title: Not bad, but irritating anachronisms
text: Part of the pleasure of reading historical novels is that their point of view is so different from the contemporary one; this novel slipped and slid all over the place. Even down to turns of phrase: "Shoot the messenger" (gunpowder didn't reach England until the 14th century, and I doubt you'd kill a messenger with an arrow), "put out a shingle": in the first place, hardly anyone could read, the middle class wasn't really established, so commerce was entirely different, and shingle meant stone (or an affliction, if that's what they called it then); no one built with them or made signs. Taking notes on slate with chalk was impractical (slate is heavy to carry around, chalk smears and small letters are difficult to write), etc. etc. The author has a sort of Flinstones CSI thing going on which falls flat. The main character's medical practices suspiciously reflect germ theory (we had to wait for the 19th century for that one), Jews weren't speaking Yiddish because it was a new language and anyhow it wasn't called that, people didn't sent notes to each other because there was little paper; they used messengers. I could go on for years. I just find this lazy. But if you don't find this annoying, and are patient with excessive exposition, the book is diverting enough. Mystery plot is a little creaky, too.

title: Fast-Paced Novel of International Intrigue
text:
The year is 2001 and Michael Wolfe, retired marine sharpshooter, is working in black ops for the Israelis in Haifa. His wife, Sara, plans to travel alone by bus to visit her parents. At the same time, Mohammad Al-Qaedi, an Iranian terrorist of some note, is planning a suicide bomb attack. Unfortunately for all involved, he picks the same bus that Sara has just boarded to commit this atrocity. Michael watches in horror as the bus explodes, his last glimpse of his wife being her face in the window, etched in terror.

Thus begins a decades long game of cat and mouse between Michael and the wily terrorist. Enter a former colleague of Michael’s who also has a history with Al-Qaedi and you have a multi-faceted saga spanning years. The action moves from the Middle East to the hinterlands of Missouri, to the stately town of London, and back again. Twists and turns abound as Michael and the terrorist cross paths, narrowly missing each other time and time again.

A Matter of Payback is the third novel in author, J.C. Fields’ Michael Wolfe Saga, but can be easily read as a standalone. It is a taut, tense thriller full of international intrigue and political machinations. Peopled by complex, fascinating characters, the novel moves at a fast pace and this reader had a hard time putting it down. Highly recommended for lovers of international intrigue, books about terrorism, and political thrillers.

title: Good Reading
text:
Change is hard for everyone sometimes.

I adored the warm and loving relationship between Henry and Liza. As well as being siblings, they were best friends who loved spending time together exploring the outdoors and making up imaginative games. They had a strong emotional bond, and it showed. Siblings having a wonderful time together is something I always love to find in picture books as it doesn’t seem to be as common as addressing sibling rivalry and other normal developmental stages of childhood that can bring conflict.

With that being said, there is something to be said for learning to enjoy time apart, too. I appreciated how gently the narrator approached the idea that Henry and Liza would both benefit from developing a few separate interests and friend groups. It was such a friendly way to encourage these characters to step out of their comfort zones while also acknowledging how lucky they were to get along so well.

The ending made me smile. Henry definitely didn’t appreciate being left at home while his sister started kindergarten, so it was interesting to see how his frustration and disappointment encouraged him to fill his time with new activities until she came back home again in the afternoon. Every emotion is valuable, even the difficult ones! Gentle stories are a great place to explore feelings that a kid might be reluctant to talk about, and there were plenty of opportunities here to do just that. While I can’t say much more about the ending without giving away spoilers, it was everything I was hoping it would be.

Henry at Home was perfect.

title: more mediocrity from Eric Vall
text:
Eric Vall writes two categories of books/series: those that start out pretty good and he drives them into the ground with a never ending plot structure, and those that start out mediocre and he drives them underground with a never ending plot structure. Sadly, this book falls into the later category.

The premise starts off with a little promise, but that is shattered before you reach 25% of the book. The MC is a hapless lone IT help desk guy (manager) working at a dead end job with no raises for 2 years (really?) who goes to the under renovation 12th floor of his work building, finds an unlabeled door that leads up to a mysterious (mysterious because the building is only 12 stories) 13th floor, where he finds a locked door. Good thing he brought his lock picks and sample lock, so he can unlock that door, right? And viola, a secret door to another world is found. From there, it gets even more unbelievable.

From fighting off creatures with a hard back book, using his spray deodorant as a weapon, the absolute cheese of the beings in power in this other world, and then bringing a cat girl back through the portal (who goes with the flow, accepting technology way too easily) and taking her out to a beach on her second day here, the story enters into farcical territory quickly. Throw in the over explanations of lots of useless info as page filler, and this book bored me into putting it down.

Men who died protecting our freedom and not all of them are Americans.  The battle that claimed the life of Chappy should never have happened and the author explains the behind the scenes details of the command structure and the jealousies of higher ranking officers who intervened creating a killing field that claimed the lives of good men.  The authors tell a really compelling true account of the war in Afghanistan, the battle that claimed Chappy and other great men, the deadly and formidable Al Qaeda and Taliban soldiers who were assisted by Russian soldiers, and the fiasco commanders who knew nothing but thought they could do better.  This is a great book.  It’s worth every second of your time.  John Chapman now lives in my mind and in my heart I am grateful to him, the Afghani soldiers, and the special forces men who gave their life for me.  Every American should read this book!

title: Developing a Strong Foundation for all Learning
text: I am an elementary school special education teacher who read this book to learn more about executive function.  Executive function deficits are common when working with students on my caseload and I wanted to know how I can better serve them.  I chose to read SLOW DOWN! Children are Learning! in order to understand what is going on behind the scenes that causes students to have difficulty managing multiple step instructions, prioritizing tasks, organizing materials, and accessing their curriculum.  Mengeu hits the nail on the head when discussing a significant shift in education in the last several years as we have put such great emphasis on test scores.  As teachers, we put so much pressure on ourselves to adhere to the standards in order to help our students perform well on state assessments; however, we are often dealing with young children who lack relational skills, organization skills, and communication skills. How can we continue to push on when so many children are filled with anxiety. I enjoyed learning more about the role of working memory, inhibitory control, and flexible thinking.  I would highly recommend this book for all educators, especially those working with elementary school children.

text:
Lali A Love’s newest book, The Keys to Eternity, starts off with an interesting discussion of world view. The characters learn that humans often view others through an antagonistic lens, where everyone is in constant competition for limited resources. A teacher counters this perception with the idea that we are all interconnected. As such, people must break free of the winner/loser paradigm that frames their perceptions of the world. This message is poignant now. I’m worried my country is sliding into fascism. People seem to relish in their hatred. Love’s book is fiction, but the message bears significance in our everyday lives.

With that out of the way, let’s turn to the fun events in the book. Jo continues to explore her powers, and Nisha becomes embroiled in a dangerous situation. title: Do Look Now and Look Again
text:
This is a book to read slowly savoring the photos and discovering, straight no chaser, who Walker Evans was as a human being.

Michael Lesy’s deep love for his mentor Walker Evans and all he represents suffuses the photos and the lyrical prose narrative that make up his new book. It is worth taking our time looking and looking and looking again at these selected camera shots until the people in them are seen for who they are and what life was doing or will do to them, captured here, forever and ever.

Lesy for fifty years (since his groundbreaking *Wisconsin Death Trip*) has helped us explore what it means to live and to die. Here Lesy brings Walker Evans to us in his human totality together with the human beings who played roles his life drama in act two (the 1920's and 30's) and late in act five (the 1970's). Lesy and his wife Liz come on stage in act five.

Spoiler alert: Evans' life was a tragedy like our own lives, but a tragedy fully lived and generous in what it still gets us to feel and understand.

Lesy, as always, gives us ways of thinking and feeling about what our American lives look like, on high and low rungs of the socioeconomic ladder. Here we discover anew what Evans' creative genius with a camera demands of us.

title: This gave me ALL the feels!
text:
If I could rate this more than 5, I would. Abby Jimenez writes such amazing books, I would read what she wrote on a napkin at this point.

“Don’t let them decide the life you’re going to live. You only get one.”

“Grace costs you nothing.”

I cried like a baby at the end of this book, full on tears. Not sad tears, more of happy and “Omg is this really over?” tears. This book hit me differently because I could relate to Alexis in so many ways, as she was going through so many things I currently am and have been, so it truly hit home.

There are so many things going on in this book that are so important. It’s NOT just a love story. It’s about finding yourself, and your way in this crazy life and doing what YOU want to do. It’s all about change, which explains why the dragonflies were appearing very often….Dragonflies resemble change is coming.

“Nobody can save you until you’re ready to save yourself.”

Daniels adoration and determination regarding Alexis was beautiful. He had my heart swooning and I could feel the chemistry coming off the pages. It was a little frustrating with Alexis being so stand-offish because of their different worlds, but it made sense in the end when it was all tied together. It was also frustrating about the age gap being mentioned SO much but I totally understood it; been there before. But alas, age is just a number and love is love.

“How he completed the final piece in my mosaic.”

“I think my soul recognizes hers the second I laid eyes on her. Our bodies knew it the very first sight.”

“Love follows you. It goes where you go. It doesn’t know about social divides or distance of common sense. It doesn’t even stop when the person you love does. It does what it wants.”

And omg the town of Wakan? I wish I could be there! It was so precious and I loved how the community came together and treated one another like family.

“Because sometimes family isn’t what you’re born into. Sometimes family is found.”

Alexis had the MOST character development I have seen from a character in a long time. She came from this extravagant lifestyle, a totally different world than Daniel. And Daniel, he changed her perspective in so many ways and I loved seeing that change in her.

Also, Bri rocks! Can’t wait for her story next!

T/W: emotional & verbal abuse by a partner and parent, domestic violence, death of a child briefly mentioned.

The book information says this was 3 of 3, hoping this is not true, as the ending has an abrupt, unfinished, unresolved feeling.
I very much do like this nautical, historical action series.
We lost characters without knowing what happened to them, & unfortunately, it did happen on the sea in this era. However, I hope there is a 4th in the series to follow, where we recover or learn something of the Amelie, & it’s crew.
Nick Turnhouse continues to be hindered or sabotaged behind the scenes, by those who wish to see his career curtailed. title: Not just a retread of Swordheart
text:
I came to this one straight from Swordheart , which I'd enjoyed, but I did my usual check of the negative reviews to see who didn't like it and why. The main complaint seemed to be that it wasn't an adventure fantasy, but a romance, and since I quite like a romance from time to time (and had enjoyed the one in Swordheart) that was more a selling point for me than otherwise.

The couple in Paladin's Grace and the couple in Swordheart felt, for a while, like they were exactly the same couple under different names, but differences developed. "Paladin of a recently dead god" is different from "magically trapped in a sword for centuries", and "widow of a vague man who didn't really understand sex" is different from "ex-wife of a toxic, gaslighting narcissist," but the differences go beyond those. Paladin Stephen is angsty in a different way from the magical sword fellow, Sarkis, and expert perfumer Grace is competent in different ways from the pragmatic housekeeper Halla. There are enough similarities that, if you liked one book, the chances that you'll like the other are high, but enough differences that you don't feel like you've just read the same book twice.

Not the least of the differences is the B plot that provides both complications and momentum to the main romance plot in each book. Swordheart involves a great deal of travelling and encountering various people who want to steal from Halla, whereas Stephen and Grace spend all their time in the same city, trying to solve a couple of mysteries, in one of which Grace is the authorities' prime suspect.

I will mention a few things that irritated me slightly, but were a long way from being fatal. The use of biblical names in a setting where the religion is explicitly not Christianity or Judaism is a pet peeve of mine, but I'm becoming more ready to forgive it. The author is not particularly good with possessive plurals, occasionally hyphenates when she shouldn't, uses "lay" for "lie" a few times (arguably a dialect difference rather than an error, but generally considered an error), and misuses a couple of other words, but other than that the editing is generally good. Both books also commit POV switches within a scene (one each). This book has a little bit of a deus ex machina, too, to get the characters out of a hole that the author has dug so deep that they need the rope ladder thrown down to them.

Aside from that, this is a strong romance between competent, pragmatic older characters (in their 30s) who wear their pragmatism as a cloak over strong feelings of personal inadequacy, driven along at a good pace by a pair of mysteries. Along the way, we get deep into the characters' heads, and I liked what I found there.

Recommended.

title: A journey back into simpler times.
text:
I grew up in South Holyoke & am just a few years younger than the author. This book jarred my memory of the childhood I experienced in simpler times. We had no cell phones but 3way party lines were in most homes, the ragman calling for rags & would appear in our alleys with his flat bed pulled by a horse is a sight not ever seen today. Small markets & varied shops were all in walking distance selling produce, blue jeans, paperclips & unfortunately were all in time shuttered & replaced by one stop shopping malls. We didn't lock our doors, we knew all of our neighbors by name & unlike today comradery with them was the norm.

For anyone who grew up in South Holyoke in the 50's & early 60's this is a wonderful book to bring you back to those times.

text: Pack of Lies is everything I wanted it to be and more! I've been obsessed with the Big Bad Wolf series (starring Cooper Dayton and Oliver Park) and my expectations for Pack of Lies were high, and they were 100% met and exceeded! The characters - Julien and Eli - jumped right into my heart and made me smile, laugh, and tugged at my heartstrings. I really love that we get both POVs - Julien the grieving, unaware human stumbling into a retreat for werewolves; Eli the lovable enigma of a werewolf who is confident on the outside but riddled with insecurities on the inside. Together they make a great team as they set about sleuthing in a setting that is peak mystery goodness - a mostly empty ski lodge in the winter with a small cast of dubious characters. The dual mysteries - unearthing the truths Julien's brother uncovered and looking for the mysterious mountain cryptid - kept me guessing right up until the end. Heart-pounding action, sizzling sexual tension, wrenching revelations, banter for days, and excellent character development kept me reading long after midnight! title: Fast-paced Thriller About a Family Vacation Gone Very Wrong
text:
The Island by Adrian McKinty is a fast-paced thriller about a family vacation that goes VERY wrong. It's one of the books I read last week while on vacation, and I'm very grateful our trip had nothing in common with this plot!

When Tom Baxter, a recently-widowed 40-ish orthopedic surgeon, is invited to be a medical conference keynote speaker in Australia, he brings his new young wife, his 14-year-old daughter, and his 12-year-old son along for a family vacation. The relationships are new and would benefit from some bonding experiences.

All goes relatively well until their itinerary brings them to Melbourne, and a chance encounter leads the Baxters to a remote island populated by members of a single family. Then a terrible accident launches a horrific chain of events, forcing the Baxters to run, hide, and fight for their lives.

I was on the edge of my seat and read this only during the day to avoid nightmares. The action was nearly constant and (for me) was intense and "believable." There's characters you'll love to hate, and humans and dogs meet violent ends.

Hulu has the rights to develop The Island as a limited series. I hope it gets created ... I'll be watching some parts through a mask of my fingers! Thank you to Little, Brown and Company for a review copy.

title: Better Than Lunch with Warren Buffett
text:
Few people ever get the opportunity to sit down and learn from ANY of the world's top investors. But this book provides detailed access to DOZENS of them who are a Who's Who of global investment superstars. A must-read in my opinion, for everyone - from novices to financial professionals.

It's long-overdue, future-forward, and solution-oriented. Nearly 400 pages of in-depth conversations reveal how, why, and where anyone can put their capital to work to generate attractive and competitive financial market returns - while also having a powerful positive impact in the world.

Most investment books I've studied (hundreds of them) focus on a single author - and too often they are just writing to promote themselves. But R. Scott Arnell did the opposite. He generously shares his rare access to world class investors who are the thought leaders, pioneers, and success stories of Sustainable & Responsible and ESG investing - across multiple asset classes.

Where other books I've read focus on one main approach, this one presents a diversity of investment strategies. The investors in this book don't all agree on how or where to invest, which makes it more interesting and valuable. But they do all agree that anyone today who isn't investing for sustainability is leaving money on the table - and missing out on a chance to make the planet a better place to live, for generations to come.

title: “This feels like us…when we both know it can’t be.”
text:
Sin Bin is the fourth book in the Carolina Comets series and it gave me all the feels. I had been anxiously waiting for Emilia and Smith’s book and it did not disappoint. These two were perfection.

“Because I can’t forget you, Emilia. No matter how hard I try…I can’t.”

Emilia and Smith spent a weekend together two and half years ago before they discovered that they both worked for the Carolina Comets. When they came face-to-face again, they decided to pretend like their weekend never existed, but neither could really forget. When they have to work together, will they be able to ignore the flame that’s always burning beneath the surface of every interaction?

“Being with her feels like coming home. It feels right.”

Oh, how I loved these two. Each encounter is fraught with tension and intense longing for each other. So much so that their chemistry is palpable and their push and pull relationship sizzles. They understand one another so completely even after years apart. Both are trying to juggle their career desires with what their heart wants and this forces them to make difficult choices about their futures.

Full of explosive chemistry, snarky banter, and so much heart, Sin Bin was an absolutely addictive read. Emilia and Smith will break your heart a little but you know they are destined for one another and their journey is heartwarming. I love all of these hockey guys and I’m so excited to see what’s in store for Miller.

title: sexy, angsty AF, suspenseful, action-packed, thrilling, slow build romantic suspense
text:
...A man with demons that run deep and dark...

The only woman who can bring him to his knees...

I received a copy of Lucifer's Sin from the author for an honest review.

Lisa Renee Jones' Lucifer’s Sin, Walker Security: Lucifer's Trilogy 1, is a standalone series within her Tall, Dark, and Deadly and Walker Security universe. After finishing Adrian’s trilogy, I couldn’t wait to read Lucifer’s. I was not disappointed. Lucifer's Sin is a sexy, angsty AF, suspenseful, action-packed, thrilling read that just barely scratches the surface of the mysterious and dangerous Lucifer, the amazing woman who owns his heart, and the mystery behind the night that tore them apart. Jones’ active, descriptive writing style draws you right into the action, keeping your total interest as the pages quickly fly by. The connections between her characters are the best. Ana’s and Luke’s relationship is complex, rife with anger, bitterness, frustration, and beneath all that longing, desire, and love. Despite their time apart, the emotional and sexual connections and attraction they share are deep and powerful, just like their personalities, which clash whenever they are together. Jones excellently develops Ana, Luke, and their relationship, though I expect deeper development and evolution in books 2–3. The relationships and interactions between the Walker Security men are also well developed and amusing.

One of Walker Security’s newest members, Lucifer’s still a bit of a mystery to his fellow team. A man with a dangerous past, he loves fast cars, fast women and lives his life on the edge, flirting with death. Walker Security saved him from the hell he’d allowed his life to become, pulling him back from the edge and his death wish—mostly. He’s haunted by demons and secrets, the most personal of whom owns his heart, owns him, still, even after her betrayal that made him the man he is today. When she reappears in his life, everything they both believed or thought they knew about the night that tore them apart, changing their lives fundamentally, is thrown into question and nothing is as it appears. They were both forced to make choices that they can’t take back now but regret how they hurt the other. The past comes back to haunt them, both putting their lives in danger.

I love Ana because she doesn’t let Luke or other men push her around. Ana’s a total badass chick. Rightfully so, as she is more than your average trained FBI agent. She’s perfect for Luke because, like him, she has demons and secrets that she has yet to make peace with either. Luke is so twisted up about Ana, hurt and angry, over her betrayal. It drives everything he is and does. But he’s all about keeping her safe. I’m looking forward to seeing more of what’s going on with him and her. I love when two people who are intensely drawn to each other but must resist it for reasons are thrown into close quarters and must rely on each other to survive in dangerous situations. On-the-run books are my favorites! So, I thoroughly enjoyed this one. But it leaves us with so many more questions than answers.

I highly recommend Lucifer's Sin for ANGSTY, sexy, slow build romantic suspense, and second-chance romances fans who don’t mind cliffhangers.

title: Intelligent, Informative, Engaging, and Easy to Read!
text:
Broadly speaking, Faithfully Different could be categorized as an apologetics work which specifically deals with issues of culture and worldview. The primary focus of the book is secularism and its impact on Christianity, with Crain’s primary target audience identified by as Bible believing, historically orthodox Christians. Or as she specifically notes, those who believe the Bible is God’s word, the Bible’s inspiration means God wrote it through people to say precisely what he wants it to say, and the Bible is the only sufficient source for authoritative information about salvation, faith, and godliness.
Throughout the book, Crain deals with many issues Christians contend with today such as scientism, philosophical naturalism, normative ethics and objective truth, public deconversion culture, worldview inconsistency, secular virtue signaling, secular co-opting and redefining of Jesus, social justice, critical theories, cancel culture, secular relativism, and more. With all of these topics touched on, Crain clarifies the main issue she’s addressing is that it is no longer the cultural norm in America to hold a biblical worldview; secularism is the new dominant cultural view, and it puts large pressures and challenges on historically biblical Christianity. This being the problem addressed, she states her main purpose in the book as helping Christians move past the general feeling something is wrong in the world today, helping them identify the specific things that are wrong, and enabling them to gain clarity on how to respond.

title: You will fall in love with Santa Biker!
text:
Santa Biker (Royal Bastards MC: Tonopah, NV #13) by Nikki Landis is another outstanding story about these dirty talking bad alpha bikers with a paranormal twist who play hard and love hard featuring Diablo SSA and Cleaner of the RBMC and Gina the woman with a past of her own who will change Diablo's life forever. Santa Biker is an age-gap story that is full of intrigue, violence, danger, pain and loss as well as an insta-love between Diablo and Gina. These two have been thrown together as Gina is friends with Bodie's ol'lady, now Diablo is about to take a chance and make his move , but he can tell Gina is troubled. Can he make her open up to him as he and his Reaper want her, Diablo's gift is that he can see the past and present when he touches blood. When he learns who her ex is, and the abuse her and her son had to endure, all he wants to do is take this man out in a violent manner. Now that she is being threatened he and his Reaper will do all he can to help her and her two children who he has formed an instant bond but Gina is refusing to stay at the crossroads as she will not be made to feel like a victim again. Diablo agrees but he tells her he will be moving in with her to protect her and her children. As they take their relationship slow at first, the sensual connection is building until these two finally take things to the next level with his Reaper's urging their coming together is raw, sexy and full of steamy moments.

With all of the twists and turns in this story, we get the backstory of Diablo's pain as he is still reeling from his past with the lost of his ol'lady years ago and Thunder who was kidnapped as Diablo loves him as a if he was his son, will he ever find him again? With the help from another MC who is connected to Thunder we learn what transpires between them as they both have a paranormal connection and the sacrifice that was made. As Diablo and Gina move on with their relationship Diablo finally opens up about his past which brings Gina to tears as all she wants to do is help this man who has captured her heart. Soon their happiness will be put to the test when violence is headed towards Gina. When Gina returns home she finds her Christmas decorations as well as her children's gifts destroyed, before she can call Diablo she is attacked by her ex and his friend. Diablo unable to get Gina on the phone he and his Reaper knows she is in danger. Vowing to not lose another woman he loves again, with the help from his brothers they rush to her home to find the house in disarray and now they will do what they do best to the intruders as their Reapers come out to play. Another dramatic rescue, as Diablo's Reaper will take care of Gina's ex in a violent ending when he reaps his soul. Once Diablo and Gina reunite , Diablo claims her as his ol'lady as he helps her heal from her ordeal, they both vow how much they love each other, especially when Gina tells Diablo she isn't afraid of his dark side which elates his Reaper. With Christmas here, Diablo makes sure that Gina's children have a Christmas full of love and happiness as he transforms into Santa Biker which brings Gina to her knees as she can't get enough of this man. Diablo finally has everything he thought he would never have again, love and a family and a Christmas surprise with the return of Thunder the son he has always loved. Nikki, you have once again given us a well-written heart-wrenching storyline with Santa Biker just in time for Christmas. If you love your bikers who talk dirty, are loveable, dark and violent with a Reaper twist then the Royal Bastards MC: Tonopah, NV is a must read. I recommend you read all of the books in this captivating series as well as Praying For Thunder by India R Davis.

title: Best new character in years
text: I found this novel completely by chance and the premise was different enough to peak my interest, I'm so grateful that I did. Dez is not your usual spec op soldier, we actually don't get much background at all from the bowlegged operator, and it makes such an amazing difference from the books I usually read. We don't hear about the years of experience and training that Dez obviously has, all we get is a brief look into the last mission he was a part of and we find he is so well qualified and able that he doesn't feel the need to brag. Dez Limerick is what's known as a gatekeeper, he opens doors and keeps them open, or closed, depending on the mission. He's exceptional at this job but he is ready to retire and spend his time traveling and playing guitar. He happens into a kidnapping of a young woman at his hotel and thwarts it rather easily, they weren't expecting anyone with his skill set, which leads him into looking into the theft of over a billion dollars. Dez sets out to uncover who is behind the theft which soon becomes a battle against right wing soldiers and a group of racists who are threatening the meltdown of a nuclear reactor. What I appreciate most is that Dez isn't the superhuman soldier that is in most thriller novels these days, hell, he isn't even the best fighter as he runs into a Green Beret captain who's combat skills are better by far. Dez is a breath of fresh air, he reminds me of Robert B Parker's Spenser, in that he wades into a mess and uses his fighting skills among other talents to get to the heart of the matter and figure out who the bad guys are and how to stop them. The parallels between the two made this an enjoyable read and I'm looking forward to reading more adventures with Dez, and hopefully learning more about his mysterious past. But even if we learn nothing more about him, his exploits are enough to keep me happy for many years to come. I will be looking forward to seeing each new book of this (fingers crossed) series.

title: Who are the Real Bad Guys?
text:
This review was first published on Kurt's Frontier.

Synopsis:

From being a half-breed son of a dragon named Lord Darkwing and a tavern wench, Morden’s fortunes change when an orc presents him with a book: Evil’s own Dark Lord’s Handbook. Now Morden is on the path to world domination. He’s raising his army and heading for the last dark lord’s fortress. The handbook will provide him with simple, easy-to-follow instructions on how to do it right.

However, other forces have noticed his rise and are moving to counter him. They’ve found a hero named Edwin, to whom they give a magic sword. Incidentally, the sword drives Edwin insane. Lord Darkwing has also taken an interest in what’s happening. The merchant and banking class meet to figure out who they want the winning side to be. Morden is left to wonder if he is the real bad guy.

Review:

The Dark Lord’s Handbook is another book of subverted fantasy tropes. Being a dark lord is not easy. Dominating and bending the world to your will is not as straightforward as it sounds. Many would-be dark lords have failed rather spectacularly, so Evil decides to step in and provide guidance for the next would-be dark lord in simple, easy-to-follow instructions: The Dark Lords Handbook. Morden, the latest owner of the handbook, is prepared to give it the old college try.

Paul Dale pokes fun at the epic fantasy genre, with some social commentary snuck in for good measure. The result is dry-witted entertainment fun. You may find yourself expecting one of the orcs to ask, “Are we really the baddies?”

text:
A few reviewers have already said this book is not an easy one to read (or review) and they’re not exaggerating. The author has bravely taken her own horrific lived experience of her kidnapping and rape to fuel this story of trauma leaving readers with a novella of strength, survival, and retribution. If you’re in a good spot to handle the content, it’s a powerful read worth your reading time.

Josey is a pretty teen who has a bright future ahead of her when, one terrible day, everything is derailed by two vile men and a gun. But before all of that happens, we get to know Josey. She’s flirty and free and enjoying her life. The story opens at a carnival where Josey gets lost in a mirrored not-so-fun house and has a disturbing encounter with a creeper. Already shaken, she visits a tarot reader whose reading is unsettling, to say the least. This sets up everything that is to come and also envelops you in Josey’s surroundings as well as the inner workings of her mind. The sounds, the smells, and the experiences put you quite firmly in her world and fill you with a relentless feeling of anxiety and dread that will cling to you long after you turn the final page.

I had to read this story in small doses because it is a lot to take in but in no way do I regret reading it. The writing is quite beautiful and the weaving in of the tarot is such a compelling and thoughtful part of the story. The cover, a haunting artistic rendering of the (dreaded) Tower card, tells you a bit about what you’re in for here in a way that ties in with elements from the story inside. It’s all so well put together. Three Days In the Pink Tower is an exploration of trauma that looks intimately at the disgusting face of evil and allows the writer to take back her power. It’s an important book that I hope many will take the time to read.
