title: Brilliant comic novels
text: Lodge's campus trilogy in one book, and I found myself hooked until the end, which is 600 pages or so.  The last o the three is less comic than...something else, not sure what to call it.  Some of the world in these novels, especially the first two, is familiar to me, since I got my PhD in Berkeley, the thinly disguised university prominent in the first two novels.  It was also fascinating to read about just how pampered and self-absorbed academic in elite institutions were in the 70s in the U.S.  The third novel is like a cold shower, as the Thatcher cuts pretty much end the dream in England.  Anyway, I laughed out loud during the first two novels and had to sober up in the third.  Still, these are not realistic novels.  People hop into bed with alarming regularity and Dickensian coincidences abound.  As a plus, you get tutorials in deconstruction, structuralism, post-structuralism and Thatcherite economics.  I was sorry when the trilogy ended.

title: Beautiful
text:
“You live through certain things before you understand them. You can’t always take the analytical position.”

This is my second book from Sally Rooney and I might just read all her books because her writing is so unique. I love how the author is able to aim at topics that test my perspective and allow me to get lost in the way the author visualizes the world.

This conflicted story is told from Francis's POV. Francis and Bobbi are both college students and poets performing at an open mic event. Though they once dated, they remained as best friends and one night Melissa compliments their performance following up to a second hang out which is how Melissa and her husband Nick become a part of Francis' life. It all becomes challenging when Francis develops emotions toward Nick.

Navigating all emotions that were slowly rising when both couples began to accept that monogamy may not apply to them was quite interesting, to say the least. Sally Rooney places the right emphasis on what our culture has taught us into believing and breaks down every layer of why we approach relationships the way we do. Poor decisions is the driving factor, causing a ripple effect of events, and most certainly Franci's persistence in not wanting to be seen as vulnerable her desperate need to reach out and speak up on her chronic illness. Every character is flawed in their own way but I appreciated how other topics like endometriosis was introduced and well displayed.

title: AN HONEST AND OBJECTIVE PERSPECTIVE ON CHANNELING
text:
Author Arthur Hastings wrote in the Preface to this 1991 book, “What is currently called channeling has existed since the beginning of recorded human history. The process is one in which information, ideas, creative works, and personal guidance come to our minds from a source outside our own selves. The individual’s mind seems to act as a receiver for another communicator. This book uses the term ‘channeling’ because it is current, but the process has been called prophecy, oracle, revelation, spirit communication, possession, and the inspiration of the muses. The Biblical tradition in Judaism and Christianity says that the prophets received and spoke the words of God. Today, there are many individuals who speak words that are said to some from disembodied teachers on other levels of reality. The process, though not necessarily the content, appears to be the same.”

He acknowledges, “The popular use of the term, and what most practitioners claim, is that channeling is the transmission through a human being of messages from a discarnate being using telepathy or bodily possession. Of course, this definition assumes the source is a separate, discarnate entity. The existence of discarnate beings in channeling remains to be proved. The fact that automatic writing claims to be from a spirit guide or a channeled personality who gives a name and address on the seventh etheric plane is not sufficient reason to accept the source as an outside entity. We can only say that the source CLAIMS to be a separate being or is EXPERIENCED by the person in that way; however, another part of the mind may be forming a secondary personality, as with people who have multiple personalities, or there may be a dramatization of another aspect of the self. One of the purposes of this book will be to explore the evidence for the possibilities of outside being in channeling.” (Pg. 4)

He recounts, “With the emergence of Seth as a channeled personality, Jane Roberts and her husband, Robert Butts, became interested in Seth’s psychic abilities. In 1965, they met G.H. Estabrooks, a professor at Colgate University and a long-time researcher in hypnosis and spiritualism. Estabrooks suggested some clairvoyance tests in which Seth would attempt to perceive targets set up in Estabrooks’ office. They performed seventy-five of these tests, sending Seth’s responses twice weekly, but never hearing from Estabrooks about any results. According to Roberts, Estabrooks indicated that he did not know how to evaluate the responses against the odds of guessing, and he did not have enough evidence to convince hard-nosed scientists. To my knowledge, Estabrooks did not publish or present any results of these tests, positive or negative, before his death. This is unfortunate because there are ways of evaluating this kind of ESP response, even if the odds are not precisely calculable.” (Pg. 41)

He observes, “The books dictated by Seth continue to be popular and influential. His ideas articulate assumptions now held by many people interested in personal change and New Age thinking. Jane’s work marks the dividing point between classical mediums, who called up spirits of the dead, and contemporary channeling, with its teachers, sages, and guides. Though there were other discarnate teachers before Seth, none communicated to the public so effectively. His presence created acceptance for the role of the channeled teacher that many others now play.” (Pg. 78)

He explains, “The scope of the A.A.B. [Alice A. Bailey] writings is vast and majestic, with a vision of complex connections and levels, of inner places and energies. The material is not easy reading because the language uses concept and words that have no certain referents. Sometimes ideas are called by one name and sometimes another. The writing seems technical, but nevertheless vague in terms of consistency and precision. It is like reading a technical treatise in a field in which you are ignorant of the meanings of the basic elements: the sentences are grammatical but you are not sure what they mean.” (Pg. 87-88)

He notes that “Helen Schucman was a reluctant, ambivalent scribe for ‘A Course In Miracles.’ She heard a mental voice dictating the material, transcribed it in her own form of shorthand, and read it aloud to her colleague Bill Thetford who typed the manuscript… Helen continued to have mixed feelings about the Course and her role. On the one hand, she was pleased that it was valued by so many people; on the other hand, she seemed to reject its application for herself. ‘I know it’s true,’ she once said, ‘but I don’t believe it.’” (Pg. 98, 100)

He points out, “Throughout this book, it should be evident that many channeled messages are lacking in content, and it is only the emotional tone and the assertion of coming from disembodied space beings, or whatever, that give them appeal, usually to persons who have no learned to be emotionally or intellectually critical.” (Pg. 154)

He summarizes, “C.G. Jung investigated many mediumship cases that we would call channeling… He was open to the possibility of discarnate spirits, but to him it was likely that the entities could be constructed by, and from within, the unconscious… He noted that… complexes can behave like spirits. He said in a letter that the hypothesis of spirits gave better explanations in the long run, though he was skeptical of individual cases. These theories assert that the unconscious mind is the origin of channeled entities and communications… the theories have many gaps, and the unknown of channeling is explained by anther unknown---the unconscious mind.” (Pg. 174-175)

He continues, “Some cases of channeling fit this model very easily… Even exceptional cases of channeling can be viewed form this model… Edgar Cayce is a confirming example, since he himself said in his trance state that the health readings came from his subconscious mind. I have been told by a group of channels in the Los Angeles area whose trans personalities said they were from the unconscious minds of the channels. Seth, channeled by Jane Roberts, did not claim to be an outside entity. He said at various times that he was an energy essence personality, an advanced form of her, Jane of the future, and that he and Jane were part of the same overall entity. His discussions of God and expansion of consciousness paralleled her own interests and suggests that he was from her own self. With the case of Ramtha, various observers have suggested that the entity comes from J.Z. Knight’s own mind, if indeed it is not deliberately acted out.” (Pg. 175)

He cautions, “Even with a channeled being whose messages appear to have some correct psychic information, there is no guarantee that other information is correct. Channels and entities apparently have no way to tell if the information is accurate psi, analytical interpretation, or wishful thinking. Total discrimination is not possible even with the most experienced human psychics---those with training and integrity--- and it is even less likely with untrained discarnate beings. When the channeled messages consist of metaphysics, past-life information, and other assertions that cannot be confirmed, there is no way to know their validity.” (Pg. 200)

He concludes, “A consistent theme in channeling… is the value of these higher qualities: justice, wisdom, righteousness, humility, compassion, service, knowledge, self-respect, understanding, and love. People and civilizations are judged by such qualities. Whether the tongues of channeling are from the minds of men and women or from the angels, their messages often remind us of those values. We should take these messages seriously, so that the knowledge that comes to us from channeling, or any source, will be used in wisdom and love for the benefit of people and the world.” (Pg. 204)

This is a fine, objective, and reasonably sympathetic work, that will be of great interest to anyone studying channeling.

title: This mismatched duo keeps the pages turning
text: An unlikely pair who get off to a very rough start, Dante and Jazz find themselves thrown together to solve a series of murders that just might be linked. Along the way, their sleuthing keeps the pages turning fast while they learn mutual respect and build a foundation for friendship. Not only is Craft’s writing crisp and funny, but if you’ve ever been to Palm Springs, you’ll agree that he knows this setting like the back of his hand. The weather, the mountains, the stylish architecture, the “howling leaf blowers” — all there. Just as important, Craft nicely depicts the seamless integration of gay and straight culture that is such a hallmark of the California desert’s resort towns.

title: This was beary good
text:
I really enjoyed this book, Gorri brings us a book filled with holiday cheer….lots of romance and good old fashioned fighting for one’s heart. Wade was definitely a rolling stone but definitely hit the brakes when he stumbled upon his fated mate. Charity was just all around sweet. Gorri isn’t afraid to mention things in her books many authors shy away from. Things like family values, prayers and love of community and giving back. I love this about Gorri and her writing shows how big her heart is when she expresses herself in her books. You can always tell how someone is based upon their thoughts and let’s face it, books are a gateway into many an author’s psyche right? At least that’s my viewpoint. Being so close to Christmas this book made me smile, especially during this depressing time of the year for me because even though it’s a book I know there are people like Charity out there and I know that family values are still alive today in America… even though it can truly be hard to find in some cases when you flip on tv and look at the one sided tale the media loves to spin. This novella was short and sweet and I enjoyed myself immensely. Also, I will 100% take the name playbear and use that at some point in time 😂. This grumpy bear 🐻 gave this book 5 Christmas 🎄🎄🎄🎄🎄 🦊 and a vixen for good luck. 😋. Happy holidays and happy New Year.

I received this ARC from the publisher for my honest and unbiased review.

title: Have you figured it out?
text: The Empress of Salt and Fortune is a beautifully written and immersive fantasy novella that follows the story of Rin, a young servant who is unexpectedly elevated to the position of empress. Set in a fictional empire inspired by ancient China and Vietnam, the novella explores themes of identity, power, and family through its richly developed characters and compelling plot. Nghi Vo's writing style blends elements of folklore and mythology with a contemporary voice, creating a unique and captivating reading experience. Overall, The Empress of Salt and Fortune is a must-read for fans of fantasy and historical fiction

title: The perfect thriller. Highly recommend this one!
text:
Holy five star read! If you are a thriller fan you do not want to let this one pass you by. It’s absolutely fantastic edge-of-your-seat perfection.
Tricia and Ethan are newlyweds who are searching for their dream home. They find a house that used to belong to a renowned psychiatrist who disappeared without a trace three or four years earlier, Dr. Adrienne Hale. When a violent winter storm traps them at the estate, they find that they have to spend the night.
Tricia decides to seek out a book that she can read to keep her mind entertained while she and Ethan wait out the storm. Tricia pulls on one book and discovers that there is a secret room. In that room she finds the audio recorded transcripts of all of the Dr.’s patients. Tricia starts listening to them and she learns all about some terrible events that occurred that lead to Dr. Hale’s disappearance.
Tricia keeps listening to the tapes, one after the other, late into the night. Each and every one gives a terrifying and shocking piece of the puzzle. As the puzzle pieces fall into place Dr. Hale’s web of deceit begins to unravel.
This book is absolutely fantastic. I have the audiobook version and let me tell you that it really puts you directly into the story. The narrator is fantastic and as the story unfolds she lends voice to each character and situation flawlessly.
This book has brilliant characters, fantastic writing, and a twist you will never see coming. Excellent book!

title: 3 cities--but 1,001 tales
text: Bettany Hughes, in this marvelous book, paints a lush panorama of life in Istanbul from the iron age to the age of Erdogan.  She tells us both what happened and what it felt like: sounds, sights, smells, tastes and touch.  And, while all roads may have led to Rome, all waterways led to Istanbul, making it a city of superlatives and sometimes also of extremes—courage, urban development, upward mobility and freedom…but also cruelty, catastrophe, inequality and slavery.  The role of women in the history of this remarkable city are highlighted as well. Lively, engaging and comprehensive, this book is a great introduction to the many faces of Istanbul as well as those within and how they affected the world.  Highly recommended.

title: Valentine's Day adorable book
text:
This heartwarming book will become a Valentine favourite I'm sure. Max, an adorable little bear cub, takes a peek into the heart-shaped candy box that is a gift for his mama for Valentine's Day. Oh the chocolate treasures that it houses look and smell delicious! All those sweets are very tempting and Max decides to taste just one. Oh my, how does one decide which one to chose when they all look so mouth-watering and yummy? Max makes his choice and the one chocolate turns into one more and one more and the little cub realizes that he has gobbled them all. The beautiful box is now empty. Oh my, what has he done? What about poor MAMA!

When he sadly reports his behaviour to Papa bear his beloved dad finds the perfect solution to his dilemma. Young kids will appreciate the papa/son relationship and how the problem is solved as they work together to make that happen.

This sweet holiday story teaches kids about honesty, sharing, love, and kindness. This book would be a perfect family read aloud and also would be an excellent addition to a classroom and school library. I highly recommend it.

I was very disappointed to see this.

title: A moving tale of justice, mystery and a powerful visionary future for Black people.
text: I had no idea what I was going to expect stepping into this novel and first meeting Andrel, the authentic and moving soul who is at the center of this book. Following his journal entries, meeting all the beloved family and friends in his orbit, and the initial itinerary of their trip together did not prepare me for the powerful waves of history, emotional anguish, and gripping futurism all encapsulated in this tale. Harriott's way of writing about the generational trauma carried in the Black community made the excruciating heaviness of the weight that has been carried more visceral to me than anything I have read, and made the search for true justice so deeply felt and understood. I loved reading this work that was  written from the depths of someone's heart and contained scenes that were painterly in their description and expression... so much so that I felt this would make an amazing film or tv series; this is a work that feels like it sprung forth from someones imagination in a deeply authentic and completely unpretentious way, and the message is so much greater than what the pages can even hold. I look forward to reading more of Harriott's work!

title: I enjoyed all three of the stories that make up Sparring Partners!
text:
John Grisham is one of those writers who readers can rely on to tell an excellent story. In SPARRING PARTNERS you actually get three shorter stories, in one book, rather than his more common single-themed novels. I enjoyed all three of the stories included in the book.

The first story is part of his ongoing series about the cases of small town lawyer, Jake and the town's, by now, familiar cast of characters. In the current case one of the town's plentiful lawyers has left town amidst rumors he stole money from a client using the funds to disappear. He's been gone three years when he makes contact with Jake. He wants Jake to test the waters and look into the legal implications of him returning from Costa Rica. Another great story from Grisham.

In the second story, Grisham uses it to raise his ongoing, and widely known, objection to the use of the death penalty. Some people don't care for an author using their novels as a platform for stating their controversial or politicized beliefs. That is any authors right, IMO, and if anyone has earned it, this prolific author has. Plus, I firmly believe in his message. If you don't like to read it or disagree with the message, and are bothered by it, you are fee to skip the middle story, or the entire book. I liked it and I admire Grisham's unwavering support for outlawing the death penalty.

The third, and last story is where the title SPARRING PARTNERS comes from. Two brothers, who hate each other, have been forced to work together as managing partners of the law firm founded by their imprisoned and debarred father. He has kept them working together with an ironclad cotract that will financially ruin them if the leave the firm. Sick of their fathers controlling ways, even from a prison cell, they scheme to find a way to keep him in prison and steal his fortune. This is a very disfunctional family, AND that was before their father murdered their mother, a decision the brothers fully supported.

All three of these stories are classic Grisham style. They keep you interested and flipping pages from beginning to end.

title: Repeatedly escaping the avalanche ...
text: Good fiction writing consists of well defined characters seeking to resolve some conflict. Will they succeed or fail? We read the story to find out. This waste of time has characters drawn from cheap romance novels who resolve disconnected and poorly outlined conflicts in three to five pages with the help of some convenient magical intervention. A total unknown arrives early in the story and is soon acclaimed king by groups of nobles who had previously held each other as rivals for the crown. Why did they take him as their king? He does a few inexplicable things, none of which are challenged or disputed or cause anyone fear. Why are there none, not one, of the nobles who resented the choice? Well, they just do, that's all. It goes on like that for far too many pages. There is no overarching story line, no suspense, no feeling, ever, that the protagonist might not get out of this situation. The writing feels as if the author is inexperienced and completely unsure how to complete this classroom assignment in story writing, so they just kept writing. These books are really, really bad.

title: “The eyes of the world are upon you.” (4.5 stars)
text:
I have only read two Alex Kershaw books to date, but he is quickly becoming one of my favorite people writing about WW II. I have more of his work already on my “to read” pile.

THE FISRT WAVE is about D-Day, and most of the text focuses mainly on June 5th and 6th, 1944. The text flits between all aspects of the invasion-sea, air-and the 5 beaches where troops made landfall. As a result of this format it focuses on British, American and Canadian forces, and specifically highlights individuals who fall into all of the aforementioned categories.
I picked up this text on the 78th anniversary of the events it depicts, and it seemed appropriate.

One of the great strengths of THE FIRST WAVE are the numerous moments of humanity that unexpectedly move the reader as you take this journey: General Eisenhower watching every plane carrying the 101st Airborne take off as the invasion starts, soldiers in a Horsa glider singing bar hall songs as they near France, a Canadian chaplain walking among the death and carnage of Juno Beach giving last rites to the dying, the jaws of defeat being forced shut by small pockets of men fighting inland at Omaha Beach, a kilted solider playing the bagpipes as British commandos land at Sword Beach…
I could go on.

Some quotes:
• “It was 12:15 A.M., June 6, 1944. The most important day of the twentieth century. The first Americans had arrived in France.”
• “Against the longest odds, in the worst imaginable circumstances, their courage and initiative had made a critical difference when it mattered most.
• “…that pride and a sense of responsibility were what really allowed men to carry on, to function, to not give up.”
• “In grief there is not always good sense.”
• “I can remember trying to pray- to thank God for bringing me back alive- but instead, I put my head in my hands and wept.”

I appreciate this book because it gives the personal account of D-Day, not the overarching historical overview. And as a result I see the people, not the “history”. Thus it is much more impactful.

Some other standout moments in the text include a soldier’s description of artillery shelling. It is simultaneously terrifying and beautiful. A stunning piece of writing. Also powerful are the reflections of officer Ace Parker as the war ends. It is sobering, and decimates the reader. His honest account of a soldier’s war ending is a highlight of the text, for many reasons.

The Epilogue, “In Memoriam”, is deeply moving. The generation this book depicts was my grandfather’s generation, and now they are gone. As I look around I have to ask, “When comes such another?”

THE FIRST WAVE is a first rate book. It is a book of stories about men who did an incredible thing. Read it!

title: Don't bother unless its forced on you by law school
text:
This book is horrible. I feel sorry for you if you are assigned this textbook like I was. Its a badly written book. Intellectual property is difficult enough already. Key to helping students understand the concepts is to use examples, especially in the sections dealing with patents. If the authors did not feel like using examples, then at least be decent enough to explain things to take the abstraction out. That's my first problem.
My second issue is that the authors do not provide a clear context at all. I find myself having to guess what the contextual situation in which the legal doctrines are applied.
My last issue is that the authors seem to choose erudition over understandability. This problem wouldn't be so bad if the first two issues were not present.
If you are assigned this textbook, find another reference book to help you, because this book will just drive you insane. If you are not in law school, and simply want to learn about IP, this is the worst book you can buy.

title: Another wonderful story from Geraldine Brooks!
text:
What a gorgeous reimagining of a fascinating bit of American history! Geraldine Brooks dramatically weaves together the story of a painting that came to light in modern-day DC, tracing the artwork all the way back to its origin 150 years earlier at the brink of the Civil War. The reader comes to know the gorgeous bay Darley (later renamed Lexington), the prize stallion who is the subject of the painting, through the eyes and heart of his trainer, a soft-spoken young man named Jarrett who happens to be a slave. Through the tragic twists and turns of the story, both horse and boy are sold to the highest bidder whenever it is convenient for their "owners." The story turns on the gorgeous relationship between Lexington and Jarrett, which reads like a poignant love story. They both endure because they have each other to count on. That's the heart of the story, but there's more to it.

There's also a present-day romance fraught with racial tension, mirroring the violent reality of slavery that permeates the earlier storyline. The author reminds us that we have not progressed nearly far enough in how we think about and treat our fellow man.

Amid the brutality of the story, Brooks weaves a lovely thread of artistry and understanding between horse and man - from the intuitive and compassionate trainer, Jarrett, to the artist who captured the soul of the horse on canvas, to the scientist who later articulates the skeleton and discovers the horse's secret. This book had me in tears more than once. The subject matter makes this a tough read at times, but it's well worth the read.

text:
Timothy Snyder is a multilingual historian at Yale with a vast background in Eastern European and Russian history. Since he reads and speaks languages from the area, including Russian and Ukrainian, he can (and does) read the original sources and contemporary papers to know what's being said to the inhabitants of those areas. The history of where the current national boundaries came from, of the politics and the myths of nationalism that roil the area today, is both fascinating and vastly more complex than any simple assertion that "Ukraine is really Russian." As authoritarians often do, Putin has distorted fact and history to provide a fig leaf for his naked aggression. His playbook is also visible in Trump's Big Lie.
This book is a richly detailed, well sourced account of essential background for understanding where the roots of geopolitical currents reside. Highly recommended.

title: Life in hiding

I didn't realize how much I had forgotten from when I last read this many moons ago. From the typical struggles of a newly-minted teenager in hiding to her gradual spiritual awakening as time goes on. She discusses sexuality as well, so this version might not be for the youngest of readers. To put yourself in her and her fellow Annex people in their shoes as they deal with fear, loneliness, restlessness and cabin fever on sometimes meager rations puts things in a whole new perspective for me. This is a book that is recommended reading material for both adolescent and older readers alike.

It's tragic that most of those in hiding in the Annex didn't survive the horrors of the Holocaust, not too mention the thousands of others who perished as well. Anne Frank left a legacy that reminds all of us to never ever forget all of those people who were needlessly murdered under the evil Nazi regime, and to never let such atrocities happen ever again.

title: 3.25/5 magic candy
text:
Rating: 3.25/5

Format: e-book & audiobook. I’d like to thank the author and Del Rey Books for sending me an e-arc of this book to review!

To sum up:
In this story, we get alternating chapters from twins from a magical and immortal family, trying to do what's best for their family and their realm. This family has celestial responsibilities, their actions move the Stars across the sky and the seasons change.

Review:
This story has a rich world, beautiful magic, a complicated set of siblings, and interesting political intrigue. Overall, I thought this story had a lot of potential but there was a lot that wasn't really explained about the world and why it worked the way it did. The reader has to just "accept" a lot about this world without it quite being shown to us. It's clear the author will likely elaborate a lot on this world in future books, but for me, it wasn't quite enough justification for me to get invested in this world. I also wasn't super invested in the love story which was a little disappointing. Part of it may have been the pacing, I think the "courting" phase of the relationship was a little too condensed so it felt rushed to me.

Overall, this book wasn't bad, but it left a bit too much to be desired for me. I think the descriptions and sibling relationships were well written though so I want to read what Power writes next!

title: Grumpy sunshine workplace romcom!
text:
Love at First Spite was such a hilarious and sweet book! It has a revenge plot, a grumpy architect, lots of flirtation, a workplace romance and solid female friendships.

Dani Porter finds out her fiancé is cheating on her with their realtor. She impulsively decides to buy the lot next to the house he bought for the two of them to live in, and build a vacation rental. This Spite House would be just to annoy her ex-fiancé. Dani has sworn off men after this debacle with her fiancé and decides to focus on revenge.

While Dani is an amazing interior designer, she needs an architect to help design the house. Enter Wyatt, a grumpy yet handsome architect in her office who is willing to help draw up the plans in exchange for some design work for his Nana. Dani doesn’t let Wyatt know her ex-fiancé lives across the street. Wyatt is still getting over a serious relationship who dumped him when his health was going through some issues. He’s very sensitive when it comes to love as a result of this. As they get to know each other more, something begins to blossom with them both.

This story was absolutely adorable. The spite house reminded me of Larry David’s spite store and all the things they add to the house just to annoy her ex-fiancé made me laugh. They added gnomes, wind chimes, a fire pit, and a flag of a rival university just to really push his buttons.

Dani has a good friend Mia and Mia’s bf’s older auntie Iris who also provide some comic relief. Iris even has a room to spare where Dani moves in. The two women act as confidantes and partners in crime to Dani throughout the book.

If you love enemies to lovers, grumpy sunshine, or workplace dating, this book is for you. I genuinely laughed out loud at some of Dani’s antics. Love at First Spite is on sale now!

title: It's Getting There
text:
Let me start by saying that I like this series, and I’ll be following it and buying the next novel. However… This book did get a lower score than the first, and was a less enjoyable read- at least in my opinion. One of the first things that jarred my experience was the difference in the stylistic choices of the novel. The first novel had a cute, bright cover and a simplistic formatting. This novel- the cover was so dark and grim it was hard to note much about it, beyond the neon text. It also was entirely different looking from the first book. I can see why the change was made, but it didn’t feel cohesive the way a story should. As for the formatting of the interior- I think it was better formatted. I liked the design at the start of each chapter, and I noticed less grammatical error, meaning it was better edited. However, one thing that really annoyed me was the apostrophes. There are these awful, huge apostrophes that always look unaligned with where they should be, and just were truly frustrating as a reader. I kept hoping I would get used to it, but by the end of the book, I still despised that aspect of the text.
However, overall, I liked the format better. And that’s unimportant in comparison to the writing. I actually felt like the writing in this novel improved on the writing from the first. It flowed easier, was more descriptive, and undeniably more entertaining to read. I felt like it made a decent leap in skill.
Despite the better skill of writing, I disliked the story a little bit more. It’s a continuation of Lily chasing Minho, of course, and that was to be expected. But I’m a fan of realism, and there were several points where I had to groan at what was happening. The classic tale of “average girl and hot, popular, rich guy have instant love story”. It’s a frightfully overdone concept, and there is a way to go about it to make it interesting, but I didn’t find that here. I was disappointed in Lucy’s instant way of falling in love, and in Minho’s, riding on a miraculous chemistry alone. The previous novel felt like a sudden start, like a chapter, and this novel feels very much the same: It’s rushed. There’s not enough growth, not enough moments to justify this dramatic, career-ending risk of a love story. It goes right from love at first sight, to the thick of the drama with Minho’s mother. I wish that it had a little more meat to it, a little more depth, and a whole lot more growth. I wish I knew Lucy more than just some silly American girl with a suffocating mother, who decides to come to Korea with her best friend. I want to know her dreams, her thoughts, her fears, what makes her tick. Similarly, with Minho- he is the stereotype of an idol, and I want to see more than that.
I may be hoping for too much from a romance novella. I’m a chronic series reader, averaging books of 500+ pages, so maybe I’ve been spoiled against such short doses of romance. But I will say that I hope there’s more to be found in the future books, and that things come together more cohesively.

title: Remarkable Fantasy Fiction
text:
I enjoyed a lot of fantasy fiction books as a young reader, starting with Lord of the Rings well before any movies were made, and reading Fred Saberhagen's Book of Swords series in middle school. But it's been awhile since I've read much fiction, and in the days of the smartphone we all have shorter attention spans, it seems. That said, The Conquest of Kiynan is brilliantly written and very digestible, with short, punchy chapters and a story that progressively builds steam to keep you engaged.

I'm incredibly impressed with Eric Caillibot's ability to craft a unique world with interesting tidbits of historical drama to add unique flavor to his characters and build a genuinely diverse world that feels well-rendered. But beyond that, he's able to write interesting dialogue that feels natural and authentic to the characters, maintain a cohesive narrative and drive the story forward in manageable chunks that don't dwell too long on any singular scene. There's enough detail there to build your imaginative sense of what's happening, without overwhelming the reader or diving too deep into a singular subject (looking at you, Herman Melville). Still, Eric's mastery of a diverse array of subjects really shines through as he describes his settings and characters, action and drama at a pace that keeps things interesting and fun.

The most amazing thing to me is that Eric is an aerospace engineer by trade, which isn't a field typically associated with creative writing... but his sheer passion for the art and the subject matter really shines through, and I'm so grateful to have picked up a copy of this book to get back into fictional reading again, after so many years away. It's a fun, engaging book, that leaves you invested in the characters and their fate, with a well-developed world that combines the weighty realism of how anything can happen (like early Game of Thrones seasons) with the fantastical elements of magic, but done in a plausible way that feels authentic and grounded. Highly recommended, especially in paperback.

title: The Challoner Bride
text:
**MINOR SPOILERS**
This book is a standalone. I bought several books written under the pseudonym Stephanie James at the same time because I enjoy the later books written as Jayne Ann Krentz. I have been disappointed in all of them and that was true with this book as well. I read the book decades after they were published. Sometimes I find it hard to believe that the author of these books is the same person who writes her more recent books. The women in the later books are strong and equal partners to their male counterparts.
I do not recommend this book at all and found it hard to read as I was annoyed with the chauvinism and other elements of the story.
As is typical with the author’s early books the male main character, Flynn, is described as a predator on the hunt. Flynn is trying to manipulate Angie, the female main character, from the moment he meets her. Later you find out his goal, which is easy to figure out from the get go, as he immediately talks about marrying for family traditions rather than love. In addition, Flynn’s attitude towards some of what Angie says is on the verge of derisive or mocking. Flynn lies and manipulates Angie and often disregards her opinion or how she is feeling. I am not sure what the appeal was to Angie but she falls in love with him..
When Angie tells the family story that connects her family (Torres) with the Challoner family, she relays that a family member a few generations back, Maria, was forced to marry to settle a land dispute. Maria takes a dagger to her wedding night but was disarmed. Flynn says “Any bride who shows up on her wedding night with a dagger in her nightgown needs a firm hand from the start.” The idea that the male is the boss in any relationship is typical of the author’s early books.
In addition, after they retrieve the dagger from a seller, someone sneaks into Angie’s room to steal it. Flynn wonders if she imagines it which is insulting.
Early on, Flynn kisses Angie and wants to do more. She says she thinks doesn’t think they should go any further and he says “I know…. Just let me see you for a moment. I want to know what the moonlight looks like on your skin.” And then he pushes her blouse down to her waist and touches her breasts. That is not ok. The author describes Flynn as being surprised that he is filled with the unexpected desire but that is no excuse for a loss of control and taking advantage of the situation. Angie later apologizes for leading him on. What? Dropped to 1 star. Later when they get to a hotel, they get connecting rooms. In the middle of the night, Flynn comes to Angie’s room naked and starts to get in bed with her. He says he will leave if she wants so there’s that, but it is incredibly presumptuous of him.
When Angie meets Flynn, she thinks he is a mercenary of some type. It is never explained why she thought that. It is true, and he was in the military. Perhaps Flynn manipulated her into thinking that but it did not make much sense. Why would you assume some random person you meet is a mercenary?
Flynn and Angie’s uncle, Julian, want her to get married to Flynn because of family traditions. I wonder if Angie was the one who thought so if the story would have gone the same way. But the author created a consistency between the woman who was forced to marry in the past and Angie who is pressured to do so in the present day.
The book is overly dramatic both in events and dialogue. The book has little relationship development.
The book switches between Angie and Flynn’s point of view.
I do not recommend this book.

title: The most essential business book for years
text:
Tony became a full-time employee at Apple at the same time I returned to Apple in 2001. I managed the Mac Hardware audio team, Tony... well, read the book.

He was one of the high points of working at Apple. Always enthusiastic, always insightful. He had a really awesome group of engineers around him, and he seemed to perform magic. Tony was always happy to give advice if you asked, and most of it was solid gold.

This book is a gold mine. Unlike most business books that string out a seven-point plan into hundreds of pages, or five bullet points into eighteen chapters, repeating over and over: This book turns hard experience into diamond sharp advice. You hear "learning mindset" a lot. This book is a masterclass in how to learn while doing: You can read about some of the failures Tony has experienced, and what he learned. More importantly you can see how those lessons were used to shape the epic successes. Not once, but over and over.

I miss Tony. I miss the enthusiasm, the incisive understanding, and interesting discussions. This book reminded me a lot of talking to him and watching him build some of the best tech products of the last couple decades. Really good read, really good advice. After reading this: What are you going to build?

title: It's fun & therapeutic as well.
text:
My child is, tragically, mentally ill, the bad kind of mental illness. She suffers so with schizophrenia, tortured by "voices" that belong to people/things that cannot be seen. They order her to commit crimes & assure her that "they" will kill her in her sleep.
We finally found a therapist who lives rather far away, but she has gotten used to seeing him on our computer screen. He is wonderful, a PhD & a genius & tenderly caring human being.
Together they have been trying to find the perfect distractions to draw her attention to something other than hurtful messages. They found several that work for awhile. One of the most effective has been coloring mandalas. She colored a wonderful elephant for me for Christmas, patterned in patches similar to those of adult-style coloring book outlines. I searched & searched for a collection of patterns of a little different theme, some pages that contained some personality & presentation attractive to a young woman with fashion curiosity.
I found it right there on amazon! THE FASHION COLORING BOOK! We are right now only a day after Christmas, & she loves it! I can't add enough exclamation points to convey the overwhelming delight in finding a gift that helps her to fend off stimuli that frighten her & threaten her, that make her sob & shriek toward the ceiling that she "can't take it any more."
I can't take it any more either. The FASHION COLORING BOOK gently moves her attention away from those evil, vile, torturous sounds & gives her--and me--some peace. (The sweet little cartoon fashion models are cute too,)
Thanks

text:

At first she she is lovely till she looks down at his hands, and then her entire demeanour changes, and becomes downright frosty! Of course everyone is perplexed, but most of all Richard. Each time the family gets together she stares daggers at him, and he has no idea why. When they all find out who Ashley is, Richard has to deal with the fallout with his family, some good, some bad.
Melanie writes this book with both Richard and Ashley's point of view. Each little nuance with their families or friends, gets your heart feeling sad, with the dynamics of past hurts, and possible lies.
If you haven't read the BAM or ABC books it's all right, you meet almost everyone in this blended family. I must admit, I could barely read the last few chapters due to my hugely leaking eyes.
I never knew I needed this book, till I began reading it. Thank you Melanie for this beautiful and moving chapter in Richard's life.

title: Good book. Lots of wisdom but you have to take the time to mine it.
text:
The level of experience reflected by this book comes across: a ton. So it is quite helpful and I recommend it to managers, tech leads, tech executives, etc.

A few notes:
* Many of the stated principles on the surface come across as obvious. They're not phrased in a provocative way. That may lead you to skip past them. Don't do that. There is usually a non-trivial observation or two in them. But you have to mine them.
* It's probably best to read slowly and gradually over time. I read one item a day and I think that worked well.
* I liked the anecdotes and wish there were more of them.
* I thought the references were great. Most books make little effort to cite their sources these days and this one cites many that I intend to explore.
* I like the fact that it made reference to some practices that aren't as popular anymore because they've been thrown out with the bathwater when Agile became trendy. You will benefit from some of these tools in some contexts.
* With so much experience and some connections back to tools and practices that aren't necessarily trendy today this book serves as one of the few that can help bridge the gap between generations of software engineers (similar in some ways to how Uncle Bob tries to -- but without the shaming).
* Most entries are a little longer than they could have been but have patience. There are non-trivial observations that are hard-won throughout and you'd be remiss to not give them consideration.

Read it.

title: Buy this book now! Like, right now Could not put it down!
text:
I had the opportunity to read the ARC of this. I read Heather's Date of Eyrinthia series earlier this year (which I thoroughly enjoyed) and so when I saw she was writing a new series, I definitely wanted to get my hands on it.

This book had me on the edge of my seat pretty much the entire time. I couldn't seem to put it down unless it was absolutely necessary. Absolute page turner! Full of intrigue, suspense, action, enemies to (not saying!), betrayal, elements of the supernatural, humor. .. I was laughing, biting my nails, blushing (at a handful of moments), in shock and honestly just felt a whole range of emotions while reading this. So many characters which such unique personalities. With the plot on hand, I kept finding myself questioning everyone's motives, who has what to gain from each of the multitude of events that take place (trying SO hard not to give any spoilers!). Who is lying, who is not, was what appeared to have taken place 'really' what happened, is so-in-so who they claim to be. Was able to connect with alot of the characters in different ways, you can get an understanding of why they "may" be a part of (not saying!). You don't have to agree, obviously, with anyone's motives, but I like being able to 'get' where they are coming from . When I thought I had an idea of who was responsible for (not saying!) , my suspicions we're completely thrown out the window with another twist in the story. My husband kept hearing me talk out loud off/on because, ALL the way to the last page (literally) there were surprises at every turn. Apparently, I exclaimed, "Are you serious?!", "Wait a second, (not saying) is/are who did that??", "Okay, I did not see that coming". "Ahhhhhhh....!" and "No!!.

Page turner.

Love, love, love this book. So thrilled it's going to be a trilogy because I *need* to know what happens. I love the detail of the world, society that Heather has created. She keeps you guessing, keeps you entertained,

Side note: She does include love/attraction/enemies to not in her books while keeping it clean. So, minimal spice for anyone that needs to know that. It's obviously not a main point of focus in her stories as, to me, she keeps all aspects evenly spread out through the pages. It's interwoven. It's an aspect of the story but *not the main point* of the story which I love. Normally, I read books that are midrange in the spice scale, but I know from FoE, her style when it comes to that kind of thing and I thoroughly enjoy the details she puts into the romantic relationships that exist in her stories. There can be minimal spice yet it will also make you blush and think, "damn , I wish I had someone want me/want to protect me/do those things for me/think of me/look at me/touch me" the way so-in-so does.

Heather, thank you SO much for writing this. I absolutely enjoyed this book and can't wait for the second one to come out. Two thumbs up and five stars.

title: Don't Overlook Any Clues
text:
** “As you say, Lestrade, this affair appears trivial, yet many of my greatest cases had inconsequential beginnings, and this one feels it has some promise to it.” **

Alex Woolf retells “The Six Napoleons,” an Arthur Conan Doyle Sherlock Holmes short story that highlights the power of deduction.

Lestrade of London’s Metropolitan Police asks Sherlock for his help in a rather unique case — a number of identical busts of Napoleon Bonaparte have been stolen and destroyed. As more and more of the busts are smashed, Holmes and Lestrade have to figure out why someone keeps destroying them — and what they have to do with a murder that occurred at one of the crime scenes.

“The Six Napoleons” reminds us to remember and file away clues while using the power of deduction to come to a solution.

Filled with delightful illustrations by Eve O’Brien, “The Six Napoleons” is told in a fun and easy way kids of all ages will understand. This series is a great way to introduce young readers to Doyle and the great Sherlock Holmes, but adults will also enjoy these short stories. The story slowly lays out the clues, allowing the reader to solve the mystery alongside the notorious detective.

Five stars out of five.

Arcturus Publishing provided this complimentary copy through NetGalley for my honest, unbiased review.

title: Requires some serious suspension of disbelief
text:
Rating: 3.5 stars

Mac and Cooper's relationship is super messed up and toxic right from the jump. Relationships founded based on an elaborate revenge plot will do that, I suppose.

Still, the chemistry between the two is really amazing. Mac is an entrepreneur who's part of the rich kids college crowd, and Cooper is a bad boy townie who hates the college "clones" with a passion. There's a little bit of an enemies to lovers vibe, but Mac doesn't realize she's the enemy... and then they become friends and the friends to lovers and mutual pining tropeyness abounds.

This also required some suspension of disbelief on my part, because I had trouble understanding how Mac is somehow a self-made millionaire based solely on her founding of two websites that basically sound like Reddit threads. O...kay? I also struggled a bit because so many of the characters were just downright unlikable - even Cooper and Mac at times. Mac's roommate Bonnie is the only character I was whole-heartedly in it for.

Still, both Cooper and Mackenzie some really great self-growth and come out the other side stronger individuals for it. And like I said, their chemistry is really amazing, with really fun banter especially when they're in a sort of frenemies stage of their relationship. This is a fun, flirty, steamy new adult college romance.

I'm not sure if this is part of a series - the title says it's "an Avalon Bay novel," so I'm hoping so because I'd REALLY like Bonnie's story!

title: Recommend reading this book if you are thinking about using microservices.
text:
This book is for architects and developers who are involved in designing microservices
and related architectures, who are implementing microservices design. This book is well-written, easy to read, and covers a wide range of up-to-date topics: architecture, microservices, event messaging, domain driven design, etc.
The philosophy of microservices is discussed, the various mindsets that need while adopting a microservices mindset, understanding the role of Domain Driven Design. Overview of data design is discussed, pitfalls of wrong data design are discussed, using a single database versus multiple, using sharding to scale the data problem.
This book is a great guidebook for how to deploy microservices in an organization that plans to move from monolithic implementation to distributed method of deployment. The users are architects and developers from the microservices space. This is an excellent book for anyone who is interested to learn about microservices design patterns, or who is planning to work on microservices on their new project, or who is looking to move their existing monolithic app into microservices architecture design.
I will highly recommend reading this book before you think about the technical design and implementation of microservices.

title: Wonderful Book!
text:
The world building of the spirit realm, gods, creatures, etc is so well written, full of specific descriptions you feel like you're there. Mina chooses to throw herself into the ocean to be the Sea god's bride in order to save her brother's love from that fate. When she arrives in the spirit realm she meets Shin an his two friends who attempt to take her soul (which she retrieves). The Sea God is asleep plagued by nightmares and in these nightmares and her own grandmother's stories she will find the answers she seeks–how to break the curse. For while the Sea God sleeps, storms rage and people die in war, too.

She has help from (whom she figures out later) is her descendants (great great grandmother and grandfather) along with girls she knew from her village who have passed (including the last Sea God's bride). She slowly figures out that the boy sleeping in the palace is the lost emperor from 100 years ago who was saved by the Sea God. The Sea God is actually Shin (whom her ribbon of soulmate fate ends up getting tied to). The Sea God gave his soul (a dragon) to the emperor to save his life but in doing so lost his memories (and his soul, thus becoming Shin). When she returns their memories to them with the help of a Goddess, she makes a wish on a dragon pearl to restore the emperor and the Sea God to their rightful places, returning her to Earth.

In doing so both boys lose their memories until they start having dreams and the Goddess of memory returns the memories to them. The Emperor asks Mina to marry him but her heart belongs to Shin and Shin finally returns to her asking for her to return to the Spirit Realm as his bride.

Mina is brave and clever and a great storyteller (just like her grandmother). Shin and his friends have depth and it is great to see them slowly learn to trust her. The Goddesses kind of suck, not gonna lie. At least on of them redeems herself.

title: Brilliantly funny and empowering!
text:
Elizabeth Zot has her work cut out for herself. A woman in the 1960’s, she understands facts, Chemistry, and that the fact that as a woman she will not be allowed into the scientific men’s club no matter how hard she tries. So, when she begins working at the Hastings Research Institute she is treated as a less than glorified secretary and gopher instead of the astute chemist she really is.

Calvin Evans is a brilliant prize-winning chemist who made the mistake of accidently assuming Elizabeth Zot was “just a secretary”. She immediately proves him wrong. As a result, they fall in love and become the fodder for all their gossipy co-workers who look at Elizabeth as just a gold digger who has a chance to marry well.

But Elizabeth and Calvin know better. They not only become partners in Chemistry, but in life as well. They are practical, organized and live a routine with their dog Six-Thirty who Elizabeth begins to teach words, which he seems to understand. They live in a happy test-tube bubble!

Until suddenly Elizabeth finds herself alone with a daughter no less, and her dog. After being fired from the Hastings Institute for being pregnant, Elizabeth realizes she must provide for her growing family. And through a series of what anyone else would call good luck, but to Elizabeth is embarrassing unluck, she finds herself the star of a… please don’t call it a cooking show, but…a cooking show called Supper at Six. So, Elizabeth does what she always does, and makes the cooking show about Chemistry, much to her producer’s chagrin.

But Elizabeth’s way of teaching how to cook is revolutionary to women, and needless to say misunderstood by men. When asked by a man why on earth she would want to wear pants rather than a skirt she responds with well why do you? As the show becomes more popular, she begins challenging the women who watch to become more independent and question their status quo, explaining they are able to do whatever they want in life. Needless to say, this does not go over well with some men and even some women!

But as we follow Elizabeth Zot’s unapologetic journey in life and the way she looks at everything so differently, especially for that time period, we are given a clear vision of where women were and where women should be and could be. An example her daughter exudes even in her young life.

Lessons in Chemistry is a wonderful, funny, heartwarming journey back to the past with wonderfully crafted characters, a beautifully told love story and many lessons to be learned about life.

title: Fascinating ghost story that bridges the past to the present
text:
New Orleans may be a city of voodoo and beauty, hurricanes and hauntings, but there is more to the story here. Rebecca Brown has to go stay with an aunt while her dad goes away on business, and she could not be less pleased. She doesn’t fit in at her snooty prep school, she lives in a creepy house, and she has no friends in this new place. That is, until she meets Lisette late one night in a graveyard. Unfortunately, Lisette is a ghost with a deep, dark secret that are connected to her own past.

We learn more about New Orleans, Mardi Gras krewes, and the family secrets that connect Rebecca to the city. We read about spine-tingling prophecies and ghosts that cause trouble. Rebecca is just not sure who she can trust anymore. She wants to be included with the parade; she wants to feel like an insider for just a little bit because her whole world is upside down. What happens next will keep you turning the pages of this compelling read. It is when the sky was black as ink and the stars diamond-sharp that Rebecca has to fight for her life.

Paula Morris has written a ghost story that bridges the past and the present day, and you’ll find yourself turning page after page to find out what happens.

title: Cicely dishes up its best
text:
THE NORTHERN EXPOSURE COOKBOOK was published about halfway through that series' run, in 1993. It is based on the conceit that village storekeeper Ruth-Ann Miller edited it as a fund-raiser for a future community center, and practically all the contributors of its over 80 recipes speak from the core characters' voices and personalities. Thus Joel Fleischman contributes Jewish favorites from his family and one "potluck" recipe only a dedicated non-cook could take seriously: strawberry Jello with banana slices pushed in. Maggie O'Connell offers mostly good-girl Midwestern fare like bran muffins (that, with twelve ingredients, is WAY too complex). Holling and Shelley are responsible for good ol' tavern food, like "Kick-Ass Chili," Lime Chiffon Pie, and the Hot Dog and Cheese casserole Shelly dishes up to prove to Holling she can groove on the Fifties, too.

Ruth-Ann herself offers recipes with a traditional cast, like her meat loaf and classic oatmeal cookies. But the snark factor and level of sophistication definitely rise with Adam, who offers us more challenging recipes like his German Apple Pancake, Eggs Florentine and Cumin Noodles, accompanied by a little sesame and a lot of sarcasm ("You note that I'm standing here within reaching distance of this cleaver?"). Town millionaire and self-designated community leader Maurice Minnifield is responsible for more traditional upscale fare, like "Greens with Balsamic Vinaigrette" and Poached Salmon. We tried Maurice's red cabbage-based coleslaw and found it bright, refreshing, and easy to assemble. Cicely's sole B-and-B is owned by two gay men, Ron and Erick, whose tastes in food if not in men are very similar to Maurice's, but who aren't heard from here. That's a pity.

As far as recipe content goes, this cookbook isn't too far different from a book with a title like RECIPES FROM OUR FELLOWSHIP HALL. But the humor takes it from a potential three stars to a full four.

title: Fascinating but wildly biased/blinkered portrayal of the times
text:
From the confused libertarian intro by a proclaimed progressive, Thomas Hartmann, to the sinister avoidance of facts by Sisson, we get this book. Its actually a fascinating book. Its etymology of the politics of ‘party’ and ‘faction’ is worth the price of admission. And Sisson is correct in underlining how important the divisiveness of faction is in preventing the “science of politics” from progressing past the stone age.

But wow. Hartmann in his intro (and Sisson thereafter) almost sounds like he’s wearing the tricolor cockade of the French Revolution. Which is shocking for someone who claims to be a progressive. He falls for every trope about the greatness of Jefferson and seems completely enamored with this complex historical figure. For example in his short introduction he spills much ink delineating Adams from Jefferson, writing about how humble Jefferson was, appearing at the door of the White House in plain clothes, while Adams liked to impress his wife with trumpets and fan fare. Yet he fails to mention how Jefferson built a greek pantheon of a home whereas Adams returned to his humble farm. He blasts Adams like most amateur scholars for the Sedition Act of 1798 (Adams was guilty) while somehow painting Jefferson as an innocent. But a simple study of the 1804 court case of Harry Croswell, a massive sedition case conducted while Jefferson was President, shows that our red-haired Virginian President was far from immune.

Further Hartmann mentions how hard the two men (Adams and Jefferson) fought each other to win the election of 1800, but history shows that it was Jefferson who was fighting alone. Jefferson fed the maws of the pamphleteers, often secretly, with cash donations and likely insider/secret information. Each year that passes we find out more about this. But the life story of the (murdered in 1803?) pamphleteer, James Thomson Callender, who was the first to reveal the private and damning letters he exchanged with Jefferson are really all one needs. Decades later Jefferson still claimed that he didn’t participate in such manners – but history shows him to be straight lying. TJ painted himself as the modern day Cincinnatus. And I suggest he’s right. I would bet that Cincinnatus was scheming behind the scenes just as hard as Jefferson did.

So what are we to make of this? We have Hartmann’s rather shocking claim that we should continue to honor Jefferson’s bloodthirsty approach to revolution. We should rewrite our Constitution every 35 years (at a time when we can’t pass a spending bill)! In order to accomplish such turnings of the soil, Jefferson backed Shays rebellion. Jefferson’s quotes on the French Revolution sound like they could have been written by Pol Pot. And we know how rare the 1700s were in the Framers’ ability to (just barely) pass any Constitution at all. Given what Sisson underlines about faction, how does Hartmann expect us to ratify these new Constitutions without further mayhem and bloodshed?

But here’s the central point. This book suggests that the fundamental conflict in the design of government is one between liberty and despotism (this is boldly declared on the inner flap of the book’s jacket and then underlined clearly at the end of chapter two). But that is wrong. The fundamental conflict is one between liberty and order. Greater liberty leads to less order and vise versa. Sure, greater order can often lead to despotism. But unlike despotism, order is not a bad thing. In fact it is often a glorious thing. And so when the Framers saw that we had freed ourselves from England, they packed up the bloodthirsty Jefferson and sent him to France and began to work on the Constitution. Notably the cantankerous and loud-mouthed Adams was also packed up, but likely due more to the fact that he couldn’t stop arguing. The Framers followed Adam’s ideas precisely, and Adam’s Massachusetts Constitution of 1780 not only precedes our federal Constitution, but it is also the oldest still-functioning Constitution on Earth.

So what did the Framers produce? Well…what we got was a document – the Constitution – which sought order as much, or more so, than liberty. The Framers created a “more perfect Union” which devised order between the member states, states that had previously been fleecing each other and threatening each other, more-so every day.

So, the Constitution is anti-democratic, in that it limits the power of the people. But it is also anti-monarchical as it limits the power of the executive. And wary of the dangers of Cromwell and runaway parliaments it seeks to limit the legislature as well. It is devised around checks and balances (notions that Adams screamed about endlessly) where some of the most important checks aren’t stated clearly. Note the lack of church involvement, the squirly ability for the military to fund and lead itself, the Secrecy of Article I, section 5 that keeps partisanship and lobbyists in check, etc. It is a republic, one that is very aware of the modern science of human nature. And no one was more cynical about human nature than Adams. Raisedd in a world of Calvinism, he trusted no one, and built government ideas that required no trust.

Further, the Framers sought rule of law (order) in order to maintain greater liberty than had previously been available. Contrast this (as the authors attempt to do, but fail) with the bloody anarchy of the French Revolution, and we find that their underpinnings of order had a valid basis. And one doesn’t have to spend much time reading Adams (did the authors read any?) to find that it was Adams who warned his fellow Framers of the dangers of revolutions and the resulting free-for-alls. Adams based his comments on his endless readings of the endless bloody democratic revolutions throughout history – surprisingly, there were many.

So…Adams was an ‘order’ guy, but unlike what Sisson and Hartmann suggest, Adams sought order as a way to preserve liberty. And yes, Adam’s record is severely stained by the Sedition acts and their execution under his watch, but Adams was not the one leading the charge there, and as a politician he might have had little choice but to go along. Both the Congress and his wife, Abigail, wanted far worse (she suggested capital punishment at least once). And as we know, Jefferson acted in precisely the same way when, oddly, the same pamphleteer, Callender, flipped sides and started to attack President Jefferson in precisely the way Callender had attacked Washington, Adams and Hamilton when they were in power.

To me Sisson is just a funky scholar, who, writing in 1974 when the book was originally published, missed a number of cool new turns of history. He deftly focuses on the problems of faction but he falls a bit too hopelessly in love with our wannabe Cincinnatus, Jefferson. After all, the real credit to the revolution of 1800 goes not to the party that comes into power, it goes to the gracefulness of the losers. Adams was the first ever deposed president to walk away from the job in peace. More needs to be made of that.

Hartmann however is guilty of populism. And he is bright enough to know this. He is selling lots of books by taking cheap shots at order in the name of liberty. Jefferson doesn’t deserve Hartmann’s fanboy praise. But sure, thank Jefferson for being the tireless defender of states rights (which in Jefferson’s case probably meant he got to keep his slaves and concubines). And Adams doesn’t deserve the tireless opprobrium that is unleashed here. He too sought liberty, but for him, liberty was purchased only after the state prevented folks from killing, fleecing, enslaving and raping each other. It is worth noting here that Adams was the only Framer who not only didn’t have, but adamantly refused, slaves. And unlike Jefferson, Adams wasn’t born with a silver spoon in his mouth or in his house.

Is this book worth reading? Hell yeah. I will surely reread sections of it a few more times. But...Is it honest and fair with the facts? No way. Hartmann is selling books to the rebellious progressives who are likely looking to wear their tricolor cockades. In his intro, Hartmann suggests that the Framers never considered the divisiveness of party, but just 40 pages later Sisson dedicated an entire chapter to how seriously the Framers understood and considered party. So one has to ask, did Hartmann ever read the book at all?

title: Another Brilliant Book by Liane Moriarty
text:
Stan and Joy Delaney have recently retired from running a prestigious tennis school. They have four adult children with very different and distinct personalities. Each of them could have become famous tennis stars, but they left the sport to pursue other things. One day, Joy disappears, and the only thing she left was a text message that is absolute gibberish. Her family is very concerned, but they are hesitant to call the police. After various clues and evidence start to pile up, Joy's disappearance is considered a murder, and the number one suspect is her husband.

Moriarty is an expert at dangling that carrot in front of the reader. She lets us smell it and get a little taste, and we continue to chase that carrot on a stick with eagerness and anticipation. I love it!

I was hooked and obsessed with the story from the very beginning. When I wasn't reading, I was thinking about the story and eager to return. I was so enthralled with the family and their individual lives.

I love the humor that Moriarty sprinkles in between the suspense. I was giggling out loud during certain parts. The family dynamic and the relationship between Joy and Stan is so relatable, and I love that Moriarty makes it so real and something we can laugh about.

I wish I could talk more about the story without giving anything away. The ending! Oh the ending! It was hilarious, heart warming, and angering all at once.

title: Essential Textbook for Anatomy & Physiology classes
text:
This was a required textbook for anatomy and physiology I and II classes. It was a great book with exercises for each chapter to assess what you had learned. These exercises were great tools for learning bones, veins, arteries, and organs within each body system. The other good thing in using the exercises is that you can find the answers through a Google search. Now, the results won't be the same exact version of the textbook your using but you can check that the content is right particularly for matching questions.
The illustrations are great and clear. A google search can find pictures of the illustrations for your own study guides. Usually each section explains the different organs within the body system in a table, however they sometimes are organized by location in the body or structure. So it takes some time to get used to how body organs and structures are organized in the book not how you think they should be. The textbook was easy to understand and was a great resource for making flash cards.

title: Rider-Waite with Crows!
text:
I have used tarot on and off for many years.
Recently I wanted to try to get more serious so I went to purchase some new decks but was apprehensive because well, many of them are slightly or overtly offensive.
Then I found these.
They are great!
Excellent quality cards, beautiful imagery.
Original and inventive but still true to the original meanings via Rider-Waite so therefore suitable for the beginner.
I like them so much!
They are basically Rider-Waite with crows, 😂, which is exactly what I wanted!
I am using these non-human cards for my Biddy Tarot course and I couldn’t be more pleased.
And the guidebook is good too.
It has slightly uplifting interpretations vs all the doom and gloom that can come from some other decks, yet is not so fluffy that it is diverging from original card meanings or sugaring over stuff.
I did originally buy the extra, big guidebook because I thought that meant the deck didn’t come with a guidebook, but it does.
I found the included guidebook plus my course more than sufficient to refresh on meanings so I returned the extra guidebook, (it was almost $40!) Just fyi..
What I love most is the artwork.
There is lots of detail which is really great for those who like to go off of that.
Also, I just love seeing all those crows in very human situations!
Especially the Lovers card and two of cups!
But novelty aside, it is just a really good deck, and it is my go-to tarot now and will most likely be ongoing too.

title: This book is a fever dream in the best possible way
text:
Y'all, Awad is moving into must-read territory for me.

Miranda Fitch's once promising acting career is now full of debilitating chronic pain, critical students, a failed marriage, and is a shell of its former glory. No one seems to believe her pain including an arsenal of doctors, therapists, her co-workers, her ex-husband, and best friends. She becomes completely focused on staging Shakespeare's All's Well That Ends Well, but things quickly begin to fall apart.

Later she meets three mysterious men at a local bar who hand her a special glowing drink and she wakes up feeling downright vivacious. Her students are obedient, she has energy for days, and the dean is on her side. What could go wrong?

Oooh, this one is good and twisted. I love a good descent into madness, but this one is more like an ASCENT into madness which makes for a spectacular read.

This book reads like a fever dream and I’m here for it. At points I could viscerally feel Miranda’s chronic pain, which is a testament to Awad’s writing.

If you enjoyed Bunny, if you lived for A Year of Rest and Relaxation, if you’re obsessed with Eileen, or you devoured Animal I think you’ll like this weird little read too.

title: Great new YA that questions stereotypes
text:
Teagan is hoping to win her first national pageant to earn enough scholarship money to pay for all four years of college. But when she arrives at the hotel in Orlando, she finds that her favorite TV show, a Sherlock Holmes adaptation, has its fandom convention at the same hotel. She struggles with keeping her two worlds separate.

Meanwhile, Kaylee hopes to use the GreatCon as an opportunity to try asking people to use their pronouns and to kiss a girl. They are up for a writing award for an original adaptation, the first work they have let others read that wasn't fanfic.

Their romance is fast, as it all takes place in a single weekend. It feels like the pacing matched that constraint well without feeling too much like instalove. The two bond over fandom and also about questions of identity.

I really enjoyed the way this book played with stereotypes, both in terms of gender stereotypes and also in terms of pageant girls and fandom nerds. The title really captures the idea of being true to oneself, and not having to fit in premade boxes. And I loved how feminism was worked in.

Thank you to Wednesday Books and NetGalley for the advanced reader copy. These opinions are my own.

title: Contains Essential Info About Jimi's Likely Murder and Corruption In Music Biz
text: Whether you're a Jimi Hendrix fan or you want to know how the music industry completely victimizes great musicians and rock bands, this book is an essential read. It is not a true autobiography though - Noel's girlfriend wrote it, from his diary entries and legal papers from lawsuits against music industry types. To me - a singer-songwriter - it is a shocking revelation and very discouraging. Noel's opinion on Jimi's suspicious death is also a shocker - and I began to make a list of other probable murders in the music industry afterward and it's quite a long list, making me wonder what's going on here. Noel explains the reason for it. The end of the book does get bogged down in lawsuit errata and Carol Appleby's explanation of it is rather confusing - although, to give her her due, I'm sure the lawsuits became so complicated, given Michael Jeffery's (Jimi's crooked manager's) chicanery, that it might be impossible to write about in a clear fashion. Could have done without the nitty gritty legal stuff. Sad, sad, sad, though - from Noel's point of view and JIMI'S. And very sobering. Jimi's killer - and the record industry itself - destroyed so many lives it really demands a Congressional investigation, you would think, of the music industry and its vicious, thieving, murderous ways. It's the inside information in this book that make it an essential read, and it's a quick read, so check it out. One thing, though - the copy I got had very fuzzy photos, almost as it this was a bootlegged copy. Dunno. But that was disappointing. Nonetheless, I didn't buy it for the photos.
