title: Commune, the cheap broken knockoff version
text:
Commune 1-4 is one of my favorite series -- I've been through it multiple times and enjoyed every minute. Commune 5 though, this is a travesty. I have about 2 hours left on the audiobook and I've started using the fast forward button A LOT because it is so incredibly boring.

The characters are paper cutouts of chest thumping thugs, toughs, and broDudes. Conflicts between the characters are always resolved by posturing with each other when they aren't resolved by fistfights followed up with back thumping makeup hugs. The females are all broDudes too. I couldn't care less about a single one of the characters and hopefully by the end of the book, they are all dead so the literary world never has to be burdened with their fictional existence again.

Then there is the non-story -- the book itself turns out to be an endless sequence of battle scenes mostly in the format of the most unrealistic Hollywood action movies -- some dude gets shot 50 times by high velocity rifle rounds at short range and still manages to crawl through tear gas, stand up, and push a grenade through a hole with his dying breath -- that type of baloney. I just roll my eyes and hit the button to skip forward 30 seconds several times.

Aside from a few of the soldiers, everyone else is treated as pure NPCs. Some sidelong references are made regarding the people who grow food, generate electricity, and make it possible for soldiers to exist, but if the main characters are paper thin, the rest of the society are barely mentionable ghosts who never complain and happily slave away apparently. These NPCs are ostensibly the focus of the bad guys and the good guys' entire reason to exist is to protect them, but we have merely a few minutes broad description of who they are. Remember Commune 3 and all the detail that went into opposing camp -- monetary system, food distribution, types of work people did. You get none of that here. It's like watching a reality TV show of tattoo artists being pseudo-philisophical. "You feel me bro?"

This book is a total drag. I mean, really astoundingly awful. It ranks among the worst books I've ever read. I'm actually angry because Commune 1-4 were so excellent. You know how you can totally feel the despair when Billy dies in book 1? Well Book 5 will have you cheering when characters bite it because you know you'll never have to hear from them again. That's how vast the difference is between 1-4 and whatever the heck this is.

title: Maggie O'Dell and Ryder Creed Face Off with Evil in FALLEN CREED
text:
In the seventh installment of the addictive Ryder Creed K-9 mystery series (after Hidden Creed), Alex Kava delivers a mesmerizing, dark tale of mayhem that spans the state of Nebraska.

This time out, Ryder drives from the Florida panhandle to Nebraska along with his partner Grace, a Jack Russell terrier, to assist on an investigation with Tommy Pakula, a special investigator of the Nebraska Human Trafficking Task Force.

In another county of Nebraska, Anne Brown, a rural postal worker, stumbles across a dismembered body in a black plastic bag. But this is just the first on a trail of bodies strategically left behind by a killer searching for the one that got away. Soon, Ryder and Grace travel to the site where the body was found to offer their assistance.

When inclement weather rolls in, Ryder finds the hideaway of a missing young woman named Libby Holmes. But he can’t escape the targeted knife skills of Ariel, a dangerous woman who has no qualms about stabbing him. With a knife wound, as well as two unstable women who may or may not be associated with the killer at large, Ryder uses every feasible means possible to save himself.

Miles away, Maggie O’Dell, Tommy, and a number of Ryder’s other friends race against the clock to locate him before the killer does. All the while, Maggie’s feelings for Ryder permeate her thoughts and actions until she sees him in the flesh.

Kava writes about their tenuous relationship in such a heartfelt, endearing way, readers will be eager to see how the two of them move forward despite being miles apart. In a novel that is as spellbinding as it is clever, Kava once again shares her vision with us with unparalleled skill, proving once again why she is one of my all-time favorite writers.

From the first chapter to the last, Fallen Creed is a pulse-pounding page turner fraught with intense emotion and characters we can’t help but care about. Readers will not be able to put down this harrowing thriller. This is Kava at her very best!

title: A spy returned, a life resumed behind The Wall.
text:
I received an advance copy of “ The Berlin Exchange “ from Net Galley in return for an honest review. Thanks to Net Galley, the publisher, and the author.
“ The Berlin Exchange” is a revising to the dark, early days of the Cold War. Berlin is divided by The Wall , mutual suspicion and ideology. The opening scene is of the exchange of Martin Heller, American, a physicist who worked on the ManhattanProject at Los Alamos. While there, he delivered classified information to the Soviets, acting out of feeling that the secrets should be shared with our ally because it would make th3 world safer. Now, ten years later, he is released from prison into East Germany, where his German wife ( also a spy, but who was not implicated at the time, lives with their son and new husband..
Martin is openly welcomed by the DDR authorities, offered a research job at a major research University and a nice apartment with amenities . He soon learns that all comes with a price: he must spy on his co-scientists. Martin quickly becomes disillusioned about life in the people’s republic. That is the thread of the plot.
Mr Kanon is an experienced writer of the spy novel genre. He delivers an captivating story, tightly plotted that builds to a dangerous climax. Using the changes in primary character Martin Heller’s attitude as he learns to live in the DDR the reader gains sympathy ,for him as a man conflicted by idealism and reality. Heller, his wife Simone, and his son Peter, whom Heller saw last as a baby in his mother’ s arms are all well done.
“ Exchange in Berlin” is a good spy story. It depends not so much on the tricks of the spy trade and the personalities of the characters. It is a diverting and entertaining novel, and well worth reading.,

title: Clever whodunit
text:
Nine Lives by Peter Swanson is a cleverly written mystery by a current master of plot-driven, fast-paced suspense. The premise is straightforward—nine, seemingly unrelated, people in different areas of the US are sent the same list of nine names, which includes their own! Once the authorities realize that, one by one, those named on the list are being killed, the plot is stoked by their race against time to locate and protect those on the list, and catch the serial killer.
Swanson unabashedly references his inspiration by Agatha Christie’s famous “And Then There Were None,” and his lead detective, Sam, a Christie fan, even rereads said novel, hoping to gain insight into the murders and possible motives. The writing is clean, succinct, and perfect for the short, action-packed chapters. The story unfurls from multiple POV, giving the reader insight into the victims’ lives and motivations, but none are greater than the sum of the parts in this intricate mystery. As those on the list become fewer, the plot grows richer and ends with a clever twist.
Peter Swanson is adept at the murder mystery-thriller genre. I always look forward to finding the “crumbs” of clues he drops along the way, and to his nods and references to famous mystery writers of previous times. Eight Perfect Murders is a good example, and now Nine Lives shines again with his clever storytelling and homage to masterful mystery writers. I recommend this book to classic mystery lovers and fans of well-plotted suspense!

title: Awesome course - worth getting Audible for!
text:
I can't believe this course doesn't have a ton of 5-star reviews! It's probably my favorite Great Courses lecture series ever, and I've listened to a lot.

There are 2 mysteries in each lecture: The first is the subject. You get a lot of clues about who the person is, but the name is not revealed until maybe 2/3 into the lecture. I know another reviewer here didn't like that, but I thought it was a fun way to approach the material. The historical figures are all well-known enough that I think most people with a general knowledge of history and culture would be able to figure them out before the name is revealed.

The other mystery is the disease/condition itself. Some of the historical figures lived recently enough that we can be certain today about their medical history based on their medical records and other available information. But some of the other subjects lived far enough in the past that there's still a lot of speculation, and it's very interesting to hear the various theories about what conditions/diseases they had and the evidence for each theory. It demonstrates how diseases are often complex and don't always tick all the boxes of the expected symptoms and presentation.

I learned a lot about the medical issues discussed, of course, but I also learned about the people in a way that changes how I see them. When you read a biography of a person on, say, Wikipedia, and you read a single line like "They died of liver cancer at the age of 66" (or whatever it may be), it's just a little factoid. These lectures instead show how the subject's condition/disease impacted their life, sometimes for years - experiencing the first symptoms, trying to find answers, suffering more as the condition progresses, seeking treatment, and, in many cases, ultimately dying from it - in a way that's very humanizing.

Finally, I really like the lecturer. He's engaging and explains things very well. After these courses I listened to another lecture series, Pediatrics Grand Rounds, that he also did, and that was also really well done.

Bottom line, this lecture series and the 2nd volume are 100% worth getting Audible for, if you don't have a subscription already. You can get the free trial and listen to a lecture or two. You'll quickly see if you like the format and the content.

title: Just when it starts to get going...it's over.
text:
Not long ago, I grabbed a stack of graphic novels and TPBs from the library because what I was looking for wasn't in, and Hex Wives was a part of that bunch. I liked the art on the cover, and the premise sounded interesting. It wasn't long, so it wasn't much of a loss if I ended up not liking it. Hex Wives starts strong, then kind of gets stuck for 80% of the book, then wraps up with some style, but because there were no more issues after this, it leaves A LOT of unanswered questions and seems like a waste.

The story follows a coven of witches, who, through the centuries, are hunted and killed over and over again (though we never find out if they did anything wrong), and the people who do the hunting have finally come up with a way to put an end to them. It's surprisingly crafty- create a kind of controlled environment to contain the witches, so they can't...do whatever it is they were doing to the public for so many years. Each of the witches has married a man that's part of the group trying to end their reign of witchcraft, but one of them soon discovers that there's more to her and the other ladies, and that they've been lied to about what's going on. Yeah, this can't end well.

I started out liking the characters and what was going on. The first issue gives some backstory on how when the witches die, they're reborn some time later and just keep coming back, eventually finding each other and their power grows when they're a group. But like I said, we're never given any info on why the witches are hunted. I'm assuming it's part of the religious thing during the Salem witch trials and all that, but not once do they say if a witch used a baby for ingredients or anything horrible like that. A few details about the witches' life are thrown around here and there, like the importance of their cauldron, and a strange sculpture kept in one's home that seems like it's important. By the end of the book, you don't find out any more about these items than the witches do. That's probably the biggest con for me- the lack of much really happening, and most of the story just being the women slowly realizing they have powers and their husbands are scum. There's s decent message about smashing the patriarchy here, but it feels like they could've done more. Even the climax was over in like 4-6 pages. There was a romance between two of the ladies shown early on in their past lives, and we never come back to it or know if it's an ongoing thing through their many lives.

The art style isn't anything special. It's pretty standard, with a few nice touches on some characters. I liked how Nadiya's hair was drawn, and Rebeckah had a cool design. The husbands are nearly indistinguishable from one another, though that's probably part of what they were going for. Sometimes the artwork gets VERY lazy though, to the point where character proportions don't make any sense. One panel had a guy sitting on a couch and his legs were drawn so strangely that it seemed like it was just pant legs dangling off the couch, like he didn't have anything below the waist. Another had Rebeckah's legs turning into small stumps with no shape, whereas the other ladies' looked normal. It's weird how it feels rushed at times. When things get violent, it's not cranked up, and I appreciated that. No excess blood that makes you wonder how a body contained so much. There's also a cool scene involving a cat that actually impressed me with how strange it was.

Some people have mentioned that Rebeckah's dialogue is forced, cringey, and stereotypical. I kind of agree. It's weird that she's the only character using modern slang, when they're all trapped in this fake 1950s Leave It To Beaver-era community and there's no sign of anything from the past 30-40 years, save for a random tablet or smart phone thrown in very quickly. She also has this moment near the end that stood out like a sore thumb, where she accuses her husband of having a fetish for black women so he could say a certain word (she herself doesn't even say it). He's barely in the book at all, and then out of nowhere she starts throwing this at him and it's really weird.

Hex Wives isn't terrible, and if it had bothered explaining a little more, or more had happened instead of just the focus on the witches realizing they're witches, I might've liked it more. There are some good ideas, like the witches using their blood to activate their magic, but this is the kind of thing I'm not going to remember much of in a few months. I recommend going through it at a book store or library, or if there's a big sale. I'd give it a 2.5 if I could, but I don't feel right giving it a 3.

text:
"The Cowboy's Journey Home" is a romance. Yates left home to join the military because he felt guilty but didn't want anyone else to be burdened with the truth. He returned after being discharged due to a bad injury, but he didn't want to talk about that because he didn't want to worry anyone. Anyway, much of the story was about him not answering the questions of why he left so abruptly and how badly he was injured, but he was still able to rebuild his relationships to some degree. He spent time with his old girlfriend, Laurel, whose family was feuding with his for generations. They spent time together as they helped a single-parent family through the Big Brothers/Sisters program. Laurel and Yates supported each other, helping each other with some problems they faced. Yates finally confessed and found forgiveness and healing.

Laurel bravely stood against the feud and forgave Yates (as Christ would want) even though she was hurt and angry at how he ended things. The dog was ex-military, an explosives detection dog. title: I’m obsessed!
text:
This book is very much vampire world meets Hunger Games, but with lots of twists and deadly monsters.
A human born into a world of vampires, Oraya was adopted by the Vampire King. She was raised to fear everything around her. With the encouragement of her adoptive father, she enters into a tournament that will either kill her or allow her to become one of the most powerful creatures in the world. She will finally be able to stand up for her own people. Is her motive enough to keep her alive and fighting until the end? What happens when the allies she meets cause her to second guess everything she has ever known?
It took me a bit to get into this book, but once things got interesting, I was hooked! I was, and am, obsessed with this book! I am counting down the months until book 2 comes out.
It seems, to me, that the author knew where her story was going and wanted to get there right away. There is not a lot of introduction before Oraya is in the tournament and all hell is breaking loose. I really wanted more in the beginning. The author gives you bits and pieces of Oraya’s past throughout the book, but what I was missing was that character connection before she entered the tournament. It took me a while to connect with Oraya, but that connection did eventually come.
In the story, Oraya is both loved and abused by her adoptive father. I love how the author wrote this relationship because it felt so real. The lines blurred between fatherly love and abuse in a way that is relatable. This was an example of exceptional writing, in my opinion.
I would give this book 5/5 🌶️🌶️🌶️🌶️🌶️. Although they are few, the spicy scenes are 🔥. The banter between the main characters is witty. I laughter out loud a few times. I also ugly cried during certain parts (read it to find out why). This is a book I will end up reading over and over again. It is definitely a new favorite.

title: Loved Joan!
text:
Joan is Okay is currently my favorite read of the year. I enjoyed this reading experience so much and highly recommend that readers who love a quirky and intelligent main character, as well as a first generation American perspective, pick up this book asap.

Joan is a 36-year-old ICU attending physician living in New York City. She is Chinese American and the story weaves in her experience as the daughter of immigrants and reminded me of Beautiful Country and the experience of families separated by immigrating in phases and the pressure to fulfill the American Dream.

Joan is Okay is a story of individuality, grief, home, and family. Joan is an incredibly smart main character, and, as a reader, I was rooting for her to continue to unapologetically be herself even if that self didn’t fit into the mold others expect of a woman in her thirties.

The first half of the book was delightful. I kept smiling at Joan’s clever observations of everything from her coworkers to her robot vacuum.

Halfway through the book, the setting shifts from 2019 to 2020, and I felt a sense of doom knowing that Joan is an ICU doctor in New York City, as well as of Chinese descent with family living in both the US and China. I was worried that the second half would be tragic, but it was not too heart-wrenching. However, we get a meaningful glimpse the impact of travel bans and fears of discrimination from Joan’s family’s point of view and a brief glimpse into Joan’s worklife during spring of 2020.

As a heads up, the writing style lacks quotation marks. While this sometimes bothers me in other books, I thought it worked well for Joan. The reader is seeing and hearing life the way Joan experiences it.

In short, I loved this book. I adore Joan, and I would love to read a sequel!

Thank you to Random House and NetGalley for the eARC of Joan is Okay in exchange for an honest review.

title: Did Not Live Up to the Hype
text:
The cover of this book is stunning. The description/synopsis is amazing. I was so excited to read this book. But it just did not live up to my expectations. At all.
The first part of the book seemed to be about a young girl trying to fight the strictures of her society in early 1800s Scotland and pursue a career in the medical field. It was very atmospheric, describing resurrection men moving about misty and gloomy cemeteries in the dark of night and the grimy realities of surgery and medical practices at the time. But then it changed directions and kind of got lost in the vague details of Hazel's family and her mother's aim to ensure Hazel marries her cousin ASAP. The story lost focus and some things that had no bearing on the story were described in excruciating detail, while other things where skimmed over in such a way that ended up just making me confused. When, almost halfway through the book--after meeting for about the 3rd time and actually having a real conversation for the first time--Hazel and Jack fall into insta-love, the pacing of the story got even more jerky and disjointed. And I wasn't sure if this was supposed to be a YA romance, a creepy mystery about grave robbing and nefarious "doctors," a coming-of-age story, or what... I found myself skimming over large portions, not really caring to come back to the story when I put the book down, and not at all interested in what became of two rather boring characters in Jack and Hazel. (And all of this on top of glaring anachronism, inaccurate historical detail, and continuity issues.)
I really wanted to like this book, and was excited to read it. But that excitement soon dwindled. I would not recommend this book.

title: I love Ashley but I don’t love this book…
text:
I’ll start by saying that I’ve been a huge fan of Crime Junkie from the very beginning. I recommend it to everyone. When I heard Ashley wrote a book, it was an immediate add-to-cart situation for me. That being said…I’m pretty disappointed.

I’ve gone back and forth with wondering if I’m being too harsh with this review because I expected a lot more from Ashley (which I did), or if I’m disappointed because this was a truly mediocre book. It may be a mix of both, unfortunately.

That being said, here are my qualms with All Good People Here:

* There is too much “telling” and not enough showing with describing the setting. There were far too many details that were unnecessary.

* I’ve been a Crime Junkie stan since 2017, but I’ve been a grammar junkie for way longer. There were multiple instances of poor sentence structure which really threw me off while reading. For example, “Krissy pulled on the heel of her other shoe then hurried over to slip a hand into Billy’s.” This sentence makes it sound like Krissy is slipping a hand into Billy’s shoe, which honestly had me in a giggle fit for 10 minutes just picturing it.

* The plot reads like something we’ve all read before—very been-there-done-that. It seems like Ashley is borrowing from a lot of different stories, both fiction and true-crime. I see a lot of JonBenet Ramsey’s story in there, and definite traces of Gillian Flynn’s Sharp Objects. Since Ashley Flowers is a true-crime podcaster, it’s understandable that she’d have these stories circulating in her mind while writing her own story. However, I just wish her story had been more original.

After saying all of that, my biggest issue with the whole book was the AWFUL ending. I had read other reviews and I thought people were being too hard on her, but that ending was truly terrible. I was planning on giving the book 4 stars until the ending. I’m disappointed and I really expected more from Ashley.

Finally, I’m definitely looking forward to reading more from Ashley in the future, but I really hope she works on honing her writing skills.

title: A story of disillusion and love — and a remarkable bear
text: “Genius is the recovery of childhood at will.” These words Czeslaw, the narrator of Bernard Hafeli’s novel “Bear Season,” attributes to Rimbaud near the end of his story. If you change “childhood” to “innocence” in that claim, then Mr. Hafeli demonstrates a kind of genius in this affecting coming-of-age account. In it, young Czeslaw discovers a growing respect for his family despite or even because of their failings. It’s Hafeli’s respect for the dignity of his characters — their dreams, their delusions, their vulnerability, their basic decency — that allows him to fashion a narrative that straddles the line between innocence and experience with a vision both clear-eyed and tender. A story for all seasons.

title: One of those books you’re grateful to have read
text:
This is an exceptional read. Told as a story, but explains the operation of the U. S. Federal Reserve from around 2000 through 2021. What is revealed is that through the dysfunction of our legislative process, our fiscal response has shut down to respond to our country’s economic health present and future. As a result, the monetary function of the Fed has been the only tool in which to respond to market emergencies, especially the market crash of 2008. The Fed’s quantitative easing policy never really faded once the asset markets and banks grew conditioned to the environment it created. Over the years, as debt markets expanded nontraditionally, and asset inflation grew leading toward debt crash, the Fed stepped with the most far reaching rescue plan in its history. In looking at the Fed’s actions, it became apparent that the beneficiaries were the banks, the market, large corporations, hedge funds, large investors, the people in top income brackets. None trickled down to employees, to the middle class, etc. The Fed’s policies were disruptive and kicked the problems to the next month, year, decade. The long-term was ignored. And with the Republican and McConnell Senate, legislation was frozen.

This is a clearly written book. I took my time. This was my first focused book on the Fed and I am grateful I read this one first. It was easy to study and think about the concepts and events and understand Leonard’s story.

title: Genius!  How to even describe this amazing pair of books??!!?
text:
Fortune: Red and Fortune: Gray -- WOW!

A.J. Scudiere wrote a set of interlocking books about the same adventure (misadventure? depends on which book...) saturated with multiple interlocking mysteries which work together but very greatly depending on which viewpoint you take. The same major incident from two different viewpoints, one viewpoint in each book. And you'll get a different adventure depending on which book you read first. It's so good that I wish I could forget the entire thing and read the books again in the opposite order than the one I chose -- I'd have experienced the same overall adventure, but entirely differently. I probably need to read the first one again, maybe both, just to understand how A.J. put it together and really understand these characters and events... it's like a great movie (not a good movie, a GREAT movie) that you want to watch again and again to get more and more of the depth and nuances.

I'm aware of another two books where Orson Scott Card wrote a second book about Ender's Game, but from the viewpoint of Bean. When I read the book from Bean's viewpoint I thought that was genius, and it was -- two great books about the same circumstances, but different stories due to the different character viewpoint and experiences. I have to wonder whether this inspired A.J. to write this pair of Fortune books. But A.J., with her amazing imagination and craft, has taken this concept to an entirely different level.

A.J. clearly designed the story from the start with two interlocking books in mind. You have to read both books to get a full picture, but she leaves you thinking about it long afterward, how the mystery fits together, how the threads of fate are actually working, how the levels of surprise twists, nefarious choices and retribution work... she'll have you wondering what's a horrible act and what is an ethically correct choice, even though it's dangerous. All because she gets you to love and respect specific characters, and the depth of character... but then, watch out! Who is really a helpful character and who's behind the scenes doing harmful things? Just when you think a character is trustworthy... the twists and surprises A.J. has layered into the story, even after you think you've figured out portions... this level of mystery could only have been accomplished with her approach of two separate stories about the same circumstances. And truly, only A.J. Scudiere could invent and pull off such an approach of genius. Kudos to you A.J. Scudiere!

title: Autobiographical novel
text:
In this autobiographical fiction we follow an unnamed character, born in Brooklyn, coming of age with her brother in a household where communication has always been a problem. Her parents are deaf and never taught her sign language. Communication between family members was chaotic, almost impossible. The discrepancies between her parents start even on how they both met, and when they finally decide to divorce, she leaves with her mother and brother to a village in southern Italy.

The book is about the feeling of being a total stranger among family members, a stranger in the country where she grew old, a stranger in the country she was born. It is about the weird feeling of not belonging anywhere and the ache for being part of the world and to belong somewhere. The protagonist wishes to find her place in the world, wandering between the United States where she always came back for vacation to be with other family members, Italy where she grew up with her mother and brother, and England where she lived for many years.

The title of the book in its original language, “La Straniera “, as well as its translation in Portuguese, “A Estrangeira”, fits and describes more the character of this story. “La Straniera” or “A Estrangeira”captures perfectly the feeling of being a foreigner, an outsider. It took me a while to get into this book but when I did I was mesmerized about the dysfunctional childhood the protagonist had and how “normal” does not exist (which by the way I totally agree with) in this family. I love family dramas, so I loved this novel and definitely recommend it.

title: Models
text:
I read this eleven years ago (12-Oct-2022). I read Krugman for professional reasons. I am not an economist, or a banker, or anyone who has a professional need to understand the currents of money running through the world. (That is to say, no more than everyone else.)

However, I do build models. By that I mean mathematical models -- simplified representations of real things that are precise enough to allow mathematical representation and make predictions. Krugman's singular talent as an economist is his ability to produce tiny little models that allow one to understand economic reality with gem-like clarity. He also writes with a similar clarity about modeling.

Most people misunderstand the nature and purpose of models. It is not the job of a model to be accurate, or to be right. It is not a defect of a model that it simplifies reality. In fact, simplifying reality is the PURPOSE of a model. That's why we call them "models". The goal of a modeler is to find the simplest (mis)representation of a real problem that catches the essence of what's going on.

Here Kelly is hired to look into a case of a granddaughter going into hiding. Kelly goes undercover in a homeless shelter. She finds rampant drug dealing and other shady activities. No sooner does she discover these illegal activities, she is fired. Not long after a young woman goes missing. Kelley decides to investigate regardless, and with the help of her half-sister, Hannah, goes to a homeless tent city, undercover.

This is a quick read that keeps the reader engaged. It is fast paced and at 218 pages perfect for an afternoon mystery read. You will love Kelly's dog, Floyd, and her daughter (who is deaf), Mitz.

title: Another great fairytale retelling from Anneka Walker
text:
Book Review: The Dreaming Beauty

Do you enjoy a good fairytale retailing? Author Anica is doing a wonderful job with this new series of hers. Retellings can be tough. You want the connections there, but also desire to give it fresh air and originality. This book definitely achieved that goal for me. With a refreshing cast of characters and a rumored haunted cottage thrown into the mix, this gave the story a well rounded focus that still kept you guessing on what was going to happen next.

“There is nothing better when you’re lonely than a magical adventure that transports you to another world.”

Tansy White’s past is shrouded in mystery. Raised by her three delightfully precocious and wonderful aunts, Tansy has been given the freedom away from the constructs of society to become the uniquely wonderful individual she has grown into. In an effort to protect her, they whisk her away to Rose Cottage on her birthday. It is at this cottage that the mystery will slowly unfold as Tansy’s dreams and her realities gradually intertwine to set forth a string of events that help her find where she truly came from.

It is at this cottage that the family meets Marcus, the quiet and intellectual brother of the neighboring Duke. Marcus has his own troubles as he fights nightmares that he cannot find the source of. He is immediately intrigued by Tansy and the mysteries around her. His friendship with not only her, but her aunts was where the heart of this story truly lies.

I enjoyed this book with a it’s mysterious twists and magical elements. It is a delightful reimagining of Sleeping Beauty with its own unique story and plot.

title: Decent reads until the final book.
text:
Towards the end of the final book Chalkier effectively writes; "And then a big space battle happens."

Ho-hum. No officers on deck, no crew fighting for their lives, no boarding actions, no description of the battle whatsoever. But, that's kind of in line with much of the series. What you have here is a spy-ops novel that explores the possibilities of using psychiatry on operatives to gather intel about the opposition.

Er, honestly the best part about the series are the original book covers, but even then the prose doesn't deliver on the action. The first book, "Lilith" deals with a world where the inhabitants have to concentrate in order to keep inorganic matter from falling apart. I'm sure that's supposed to represent some kind of social allegory in a behavrioal science vein, but it's pretty tiresome.

The second book deals with a kind of high-tech water world with some huge sea creatures that come across as comic book caricatures. You really don't get very good descriptive prose anywhere here, and the final scenes of this book are essentially "Okay, you're not spies / badguys ... and we're all ..."

The third book deals with a kind of "magic" manipulation by utilizing the same virus that infects all four Diamond worlds, but it reads pretty plainly, and there's a pretty disgusting scene in the intro part of the part of the book that has no bearing on the rest of the book, much less the rest of the story.

And the final book touches on some sexual exploration, but ultimately deals with a kind of mutation that allows the denizens to survive extreme cold, or so I recall. And that's when the main protagonist comes roaring to make things right. After an intro scene of a robot infiltrator who causes havoc back at Security HQ.

Does it work? Is it worth buying? Eh, a lot of science fiction is, unfortunately, at least in the 60s and 70s, and even the 1980s, written by people who aren't very good writers. They're competent enough to get their stuff in front of an editor, and to get someone to print their book for publishing, but it's pretty dry stuff mostly, or so experimental in exposition that you wonder what the heck you're reading.

And, unfortunately, unlike the hype about the genre, scifi actually DOES NOT comment on society or politics, but shows psychiatric rehab strategies, or people who are deemed to have "abnormal psychology" and are, in the doctors' combined opinions, "in need of therapy", or some super-secret agent with some psychiatric training to take them out. So, all those samurai manga or novels, all those stories about Roman Nobles and Generals taking their own lives, or someone on the battlefield sacrificing themselves to save their troop, remember, according to the doctors, all they needed were some anti-depressants and some therapy.

That's kind of how this book reads. It's supposed to be James Bond in Space, or on a set of four worlds using different psychiatric strategies to get to an objective in a James Bond or undercover cop kind of way. But ultimately books and the series they comprise are simply not that exciting nor compelling. I mean I read them as a high schooler, found them interesting for what they were, but I've read better.

It's not really a bad series as such, it's just that there're better authors out there. Chalker's always been a bit mediocre, but if you're looking for something different, then this series will kill a week or two, maybe more depending on your tolerance.

title: A Novel of China and Beyond
text:
I admit that I struggled a bit in reading Dancing in the River by George Lee. It reads almost like a memoir, but it is called a novel. That leads me to think that much of the story is autobiographical with fictional elements. In the story, Little Bright learns to fear anything Western. He is growing up when Mao’s Cultural Revolution keeps people fearful because neighbors report on neighbors. His family is targeted.
I found Little Bright’s love of language inspiring. The story is sprinkled with admirable sentences and sayings. When he returns home after being away, Little Bright waxes poetic about his return. One of the lines I found poignant follows here: “When the veils of night began to shroud the sky, I saw the same familiar stars dispersed and sparkling overhead.”
Another line that struck me occurs late in the story: “I would never forget this day when I broke myself into pieces.” These lines at the very end of the story sum up the poetry found throughout the story: “My vision brightened at last. As my inward eye opened and dove into the sparkling blue water, I saw my own mind dancing in the river.”
Certainly, for book clubs, Dancing in the River provides much for discussion: Mao’s Cultural Revolution, people’s reactions to that revolution, escape from the tyranny, and Little Bright’s own development.

title: A new form of Southern Gothic - tragic yet beautiful
text:
Known for its history and beauty, Charleston, South Carolina, is one of my favorite places in the United States. My favorite Charlestonian of all time (besides my wife) is Denmark Vesey, who led a failed slave revolt in 1822. He left my church in Charleston (Second Presbyterian Church) to help found Mother Emmanuel AME Church – the same church that hosted a horrific Bible study in 2015 that ended when a white racist murdered nine people. Yet the race riots that he sought to provoke never happened; instead, the families, the church, and the city responded in love and forgiveness. All this captures Charleston in a nutshell: great history, scarred by human failures yet triumphant in virtue.

This book alternates back and forth between storylines – one modern, one older. In one vein, it tells the tragic story of the 1822 revolt, including the skilled but enslaved blacksmith Tom Russell, and these old-time affairs engage with one family’s modern ones in 2015. Faulkner’s oft-quoted line makes an appearance in this book as a theme – “The past is never dead. It’s not even past.” This novel dives deeply into issues of race, so deeply that I had to take a two-day break to process before finishing. Jordan-Lake reminds us that our histories, presents, and futures are all “tangled” – that is, intertwined with each other. Such human entanglement is true whether through DNA, historical interactions, or movements of the heart.

In this narrative, Kate is a Harvard PhD student in history who was recently placed on probation. Her mother recently died, and her father, long absent from her life, is also deceased. Kate came to Charleston to understand her mother’s hidden yet haunting past. She becomes entangled in a series of suspenseful dramas that eventually all come together. The uniting of themes almost strains credulity, but they sure make for a good story! Much Charleston history is shared – the “tangled” story of Draytons, Rutledges, Maingaults, and Pinckneys, family names that span the skin-color divide (both because of naming newly freed individuals as well as because of horrific rapes). The history is respectful to the gothic-ness of southern history in that it is truthful about painful issues but also appreciative of the cultural beauty subsequently created. Anyone looking to confirm simple stereotypes about southern racism, ignorance, or bigotry will be disappointed by this tale’s complexity.

Of course, this book spins good yarn that keeps the reader engaged in suspense until the end. There are detailed issues that the author did not write perfectly – for example, the area code of Charleston in the 1990s was 803, not 843 – but most readers will not catch those details because of the intriguing storyline. This tale presents a newer type of Southern Gothic, in the vein of Flannery O’Connor, Walker Percy, and William Faulkner. It plumbs the depths of the region’s Christian religion to show simultaneously the depths of its historical bondage and the heights of its forgiving hope. In an era when America is discovering how to talk constructively about race in light of fraught history, this book deserves to be on the reading lists for those interested in the conversation.

title: Everything I wanted, needed & more!
text:
Okay listen, if you think you are ready for the emotional rollercoaster that is this book, read it. But you have been warned. This book was everything I wanted it to be and more. Something this author does so amazingly is build and strengthen the relationships in such a beautiful way. The found family trope is executed so beautifully. You know her golden heart and will to fight for those she loves cannot be destroyed by the darkness that wishes to ruin her. Reylan is husband material. That is the best way to describe this Fae warrior that you believe could only be a myth. His love, support and utter belief in Faythe cannot be matched. Love cannot even explain what they feel for one another, the bond they have.

The world building was done beautifully, the last 15% of the book had me feeling all types of emotions. If I went over every single character I adored from this series, and what makes them so incredible, this review would probably be as long as this book. However, I'm going to shorten it down to the fact that I recommend this series wholeheartedly. Please give this series a chance, you will not regret it. Because this world and the characters within it make you feel as if you are there with them in this journey. You feel absolutely everything. And I guarantee you will fall in love with every single character you meet. Even the ones who are meant to be the "villains". Give this a shot! 💛

title: You must see BABYLON 5 to get this.
text:
This review is about the 3 books as a whole. I have not actually seen BABYLON 5. I just got interested in this as a Telepath story. Someone told me this was a standalone series, although set in the B5 universe.
The first book was kind of a muddle. Obviously the Senator is an evil manipulator. The author got a little too carried away with the violence and Spy stuff. I kind of got lost. Why do writers think readers want pages and pages of description about shooting, killing and blowing stuff up?
The second book was better. The story of young Bester was very good. I was pretty concerned about the fate of the Telepaths. I wanted so badly for them to get justice. In this, the author made me care very much.
As for Book III...I think about 40 years were skipped over. Bester has become a villain, but none of that is explored. For some reason he wants to go "normal" and take up with a normal woman. At this point I realized that I am not going to learn about the "Telepath wars"; I will have to watch 5 seasons of Babylon 5 to understand what's going on. And since it is only available on some obscure paid streaming service, that's not going to happen. So I quit reading.
In general I don't believe there was ever a resolution in B5 to the problem of Telepath justice. I wish my Telepathy had kicked in and told me not to read this series!

title: she's tricky tricky tricky
text:
Thank you Flatiron for so generously sending me an ARC of Acts of Violet, one of my favorite books so far this year. I am a fan of Margarita Montimore for her inventive, engaging narratives and fascinating characters. Oona (Oona out of Order) mesmerized me with her unique journey and self growth through and over and back in time; the development of sibling relationship between Sasha and Violet, their childhood, mixed with magic and mystery in Acts of Violet was thoughtful, filled with some well executed plot and character development moments, kept me engaged and uncertain (in good ways) about where Violet was and who she really was. I loved that this was told mostly from Sasha's perspective but blended with well placed podcast scenes, backstory letters and childhood scenes, and blended with broader magic and family/friend relationships.

This is a story that is more than magic tricks, it is the complexity of sister relationships, the strong gender dynamics in magic, the way we treat women who dare to be different and evocative... I read this in May and am still thinking and talking about it a month later. This is a book that is perfect for readers who are fans of this author already but I also hope the story wins new fans, finds space in contemporary and women's fiction book clubs, and that the characters and themes resonate with readers like me.

Misty M. Beller is a favorite author of mine and I am always excited to read her new releases. A Daughter’s Courage is book 3 in the Brides of Laurent series. I read Book 1 in the series and I was excited to read Book 3.

The time is 1817 in the Canadian Rockies. Charlotte Durand has set out on a journey to find a skilled worker to repair a treasured chalice that she accidently broke. She wasn't prepared for the Snowstorm that would hinder her journey. She thought it would take 2 days, but now she is cold and trapped alongside the Mountain Lake. Damien Levette, a local trapper, is worried for Charlotte when he finds her alongside the Lake. He wasn't anticipating having to help someone else during the Blizzard, but he knows he can't leave her alone. Will Damien and Charlotte survive the cold and the Snowstorm? Will Charlotte find someone to fix the Treasured Chalice?

WOW, this has to be the BEST book by Misty M. Beller that I have read. Charlotte is a very strong woman and very independent. She really loves her Village and her People. Damien is a strong man and has a heart for others. I really LOVED seeing them work together to survive the storm and cold. The friendship that grew over time was so special. This story is one of strength, perseverance, trust, forgiveness and faith, I was captivated by the story from the very first page and did not put it down until I finished! I HIGHLY recommend this book to anyone who enjoys Christian Historical Fiction! FANTASTIC BOOK!

title: Great story
text:
I discovered John Hart in my workplace - a jail. While logging property I noticed an inmate's copy of The Last Child. The title was intriguing so I read the description and knew I had to read it. I purchased it on kindle and that was it - I was hooked. I read slowly, savoring every word, going back and reviewing parts. Since I work full-time and run a household and a side business I mostly read a chapter or so at bedtime. During my time reading Last Child, I actually woke up at night thinking about that story. I was obsessed with it.

As of yesterday, I have finally completed all of Hart's books, this last one being King of Lies. He now has a special place on my "favorite authors" bookshelf, joining Charles Frazier, AG Riddle and Dean Koontz. As you can see from the picture I only have four copies of Hart's books right now but more are on their way from secondary market purchases.

About his stories: I love the fast pace, the mystery, the individuality of the characters, and most of all, the positive endings of hope and renewal. I appreciate so much that he stays out of woke-ism. He leans slightly left but in such a vague way that it is never offensive or insulting to the conservative reader.

I can't wait to see what his next one will be!

title: A New Favorite Shelley Shepard Gray Book!
text:
I have found my new favorite Shelley Shepard Gray book! And that is saying something, because there are quite a few of her titles that are high on my list. But there is just something extra special about Coming Home.

It is partially due to the fact that it is a second chance at love story. I have found that I truly enjoy a well written novel where two people who once loved each other get that chance they thought was gone forever. And these two main characters, Chelsea and Anderson, definitely thought their time together would always remain a thing of the past.

Another reason I loved this story was the community where it was set. I felt like the characters in this town were real people. From the firefighters, to the senior citizens gathering at the community center, to Chelsea’s son, Jack, and Anderson’s parents, the author created a wonderful setting for this book and all future stories to come.

I could feel the connection between Anderson and Chelsea from the first moment they saw each other again. The straightforward way Anderson approached the topic of he and Chelsea getting to know each other again was refreshing. Yet, even still, Anderson and Chelsea struggled to let go of the difficult moments from their past, the “what ifs” that could have been, guilt, and even the fear of being hurt. But these two did a remarkable job of sharing their hearts in braveness with each other when it really mattered. I also thought the connection between Anderson and Jack was beautiful and spoke to the very honorable man Anderson had become.

I loved this book from start to finish and am anxiously awaiting the next novel in the series. Coming Home is a clean, contemporary romance title and the first book in the Woodland Park Firefighters Romance series.

I received a complimentary copy of this book. All opinions are my own.

title: A Modern Bedtime Classic
text:
How can you help your children see the Bible come alive through their imagination? In Good Night Tales, C. S. Fritz presents you with a family treasury of read-aloud stories.

The Grand Story of Redemption

Fritz’ background as an artist, pastor, and father are on full display in the form of this beautiful children’s book. Using gorgeous illustrations and captivating narratives, this book points to the Grand Story of redemption.

I was most interested to see how Fritz used simple tales of trolls, sheep, snails, and elves to present big truths and interesting ideas. They reminded me of the classic fairy tales we all know, but these are told better by taking us back to our faith.

A Modern Bedtime Classic

What I loved most was how the book is undergirded with the Bible. Each story was inspired by a passage of Scripture. While A Sheep’s Journey is based off of Psalm 23, my favorites were those that come directly from Jesus’ parables.

Discussion prompts are included for parents and children to go deeper. This book is a modern bedtime classic. It will help you connect with your children, bring truth to their minds, and lead their hearts to the King.

I received a media copy of Good Night Tales and this is my honest review.

Meditations With Cows is a delight on many levels. It gives us a knowledge and experience of cows that we might not have otherwise. We learn that cows are sensitive, caring, intelligent animals. We also learn a great deal about natural methods of farming and the benefits of buying from the non- corporate farms.

I bought it originally because I became interested in cows when I saw and heard videos that show how strongly cows respond to music when it's played near them. For example, in response to someone playing an accordion, a herd grazing in another area walked to stand around where this person was playing, and listened attentively. There are also other examples of cows going to where music is played and listening.

While this book doesn't comment on this, it offers a wealth of information about what the writer has learned from her experiences raising cows.
Well written, wonderfully informative, and
thoughtful.

title: Fast Track enabled me to ace the test
text:
Several years ago when I did the Technician and General tests in short order, I dabbled with various guides and, in the end, just did my best to understand the concepts and answers as best I could.

I knew that the Extra test was going to be a lot harder, so I thought I needed to get more deeply into the material. As an experiment I ordered both the Fast Track paperback and audio book, and used them together -- reading along with the book in front of me while listening to the audio. This may seem like overkill, but it definitely kept me on task and added more dimensions to the experience. After each chapter I took the practice test for that section on QRZ.com. After finishing the book, I shifted into taking practice tests over and over, keeping a list of problems I found difficult, and kept going until the list got shorter. I also booked an appointment for the final in-person test, which gave me a good deadline to stick to.

I have to say that when I took the final test, I probably got lucky -- after all, fewer than 10% of the question pool ends up on anyone's 50-question test. I think I must have gotten primarily easier ones, because I felt confident when I turned in the test sheet that I was sure of all the answers, and was happy to get none wrong.

So I'll say that the Burnettes' test prep definitely worked for me. Not everyone is the same -- I have friends who really like the ARRL books, but I find them a little dry. They seem like a great reference book for the material worth keeping, though.

When I bought the Fast Track book and audio, I also bought a copy of their "Fast Track to Mastering Extra Class Ham Radio Math." I have to be honest and say this didn't really help me. It seems geared for someone who's found math generally difficult. I've always done pretty well with math, so I found it too simple. It's really up to everyone to gauge their own level and how much they can get from it. I did like Burnette's explanations of the TI-30XS calculator -- I bought one, practiced on it and used it on the final test.

Good luck to anyone thinking about going for Extra!

title: An interesting point of view
text:
Having read Marie Benedict’s book “The Mystery of Mrs. Christie” I was interested to see how Nina De Gramont would handle the story from the viewpoint of the “Mistress”, Nan O’Dea. Point and counterpoint - not so much. This is mostly Nan O’Dea’s story with fairly shallow digging into the mystery of Agatha Christie’s disappearance in December, 1926. Which is not to say that this isn’t an interesting story, it just isn’t going to move any understanding of the actual disappearing act further along.

The writing is beautiful, soft and rich. De Gramont captures the time, period and mood perfectly. The story is well conceived if not what I was expecting. The depiction of Nan O’Dea is drawn allowing the reader to attach subjective praise or criticism and either would be valid. While the havoc Nan O’Dea wreaked upon the Christie relationship was despicable, sympathy for O’Dea’s situation was not unreasonable either. De Gramont leaves room for this dichotomy of emotions as to what is fair given the historical circumstances. And there is the rub - to make sense of this story you now have to set aside Agatha Christie as a main character and see her as a mere foil in the telling of Nan O’Dea’s tragic history and what she perceived as her necessary insertion into the Christie’s relationship.

I wonder … if the final few pages had been incorporated into the first few pages …would the telling be truer and alert the reader to be prepared for a good story but not the story we thought we had been promised. Thank you NetGalley and St. Martin’s Press for a copy.

title: Unknown History brought to the forefront
text:
The stories of medical discoveries that have changed the face of the medicine world throughout history are often not recognized by the general public. Rod Tanchanco talks about how that fact was the start of the inspiration to write this book.

The stories in this book talk about the ordinary people that helped change the face of medicine, intentionally or not. These are not the absolute full stories of these people and discoveries, but they are extremely well-written and put together. There is also an extensive list of resources and sources listed at the end of the book that can be used to further research what might interest the readers.

Even if you don't know a lot about medicine or the medical world - this is still a really interesting book to read. It humanizes some of the medical advancements and just what these advancements meant to the people that pioneered them and the people that needed them desperately.

I received this book free from Netgalley and Rod Tanchanco to review and this is my honest review.

title: Addicting collection
text: Talking to Ghosts At Parties is a delightful new collection of flash fiction. The stories were so entertaining and clever, causing me to read the book very quickly. Reading it was like munching on a bag of chips—each story on its own is pleasurable and you can’t stop reading after just one story.  Dark realities of corporate life is a theme in the book, exhibited in “In the Place Where All of Your Bandmates Go,” “Clamp Down” & “Infinite Growth.” However, these dark realities are approached with a witty sense of humor. White is able to take simple things like a toaster in “Toast” and also more complex ideas like Astronomy in “Eric the Astronomer” and weave them into poetic meditations.  Many of his stories use satire, providing commentary on social media in “The Lost Art of Letter Writing” in addition to observations on daily interactions such as in “Crisis Actor” and “Pop Music Is the Ideal Music to Run To.” The stories are bingeable, reading one of them won’t be enough to satiate a literary appetite. title: A View of Teacher-Training History from 80 Years Ago
text:
“A Century of Public Teacher Education: The Story of the State Teachers Colleges as They Evolved From the Normal Schools” by Charles Athiel Harper; Greenwood Press; © 1939, First Greenwood Reprinting 1970; 175 pages, hardcover.

This is a history of Western education and the rise of schools completely separate from Far Eastern cultures where education had a two millennia system, relying on scholar tutors to prepare the bright boy for government via meritocracy. In contrast, Western governments had long been dependent on the political power of the rich and lacked any intrinsic cultural valuing for education per se. Thus the six chapters here outline the various steps in American history by which the training of teachers came to be recognized, advancing in rigor as the need for a knowledgeable citizenry also increased, mainly due to science. The seven chapters are laid out in time periods. While it is inspiring to see the various giants of U.S. education make progress, it is important to realize that the concept of American exceptionalism was built from the beginning, and that this includes a major dose of anti-intellectualism that not only survives to today, but is probably a more critical factor than in early times.

Chapter 1 focuses on beginnings in Massachusetts. Among the pioneers are Thomas Hopkins Gallaudet who founded what is today the American School for the Deaf, James Carter, Charles Brooks, and the very energetic proponent of normal Schools, Horace Mann. Many of these pioneers drew their knowledge from travel in Europe where variations in schooling were expanding. Horace Mann was acutely aware of opposition from not only the ignorant, but also of “Certain religious groups, many teachers [amateurs], most private educational institutions, and some taxpayers.” Considering that today, K–12 education in most states takes up half of the states tax money, it is obvious that we have come a long way. At this time, teaching was hardly considered a profession.

Chapter 2 continues with the spread of normal schools through eastern U.S. from 1839 to 1860. The problem of getting good recruits to come to normal schools was difficult to solve. The best candidates we seen to “...possess [1] purity and strength of moral and religious character, [2] good health, [3] good manners, [4] lover of children, [5] a competent share of talent and information, [6] a native tact and talent for teaching and governing others, [7] a lover for the occupations of the schoolroom, [8] the common-school spirit, a martyr spirit, [9] some experience in teaching.” There were four “school terms” of study that along with practice teaching could occupy three years.

The extension of normal schools into Michigan, Illinois and then west of the Mississippi from 1850-1875 is in Chapter 3. Many colorful figures with strong character are described. In many cases, experienced administrators from eastern normal schools were recruited to go west to start new normal schools. Chapter 4 covers 1860-1900 with discussions of the nature and contributions of normal schools, mich of the change accompanying the changes in state colleges and universities at this time. There is also a growing emphasis on “lab school” associated with teacher’s colleges. [I taught at Indiana State University’s Lab School in 1973–75, but it was obvious that these were on their way out at that time.]
Normal schools transition to state teachers colleges from 1900-1926 in Chapter 5 and is heavily focused on the rise in high schools in the U.S. at this time. Chapter 6 concludes with discussion of 20th century teachers colleges as seen up to this publication in 1939.

With the explosion of Chinese education under Deng Xiaoping in the 1980s, China expanded with a large number of their schools still named Normal Universities or Teacher Colleges. I find that nearly none realize why the name “normal” is used, and I must explain the term’s origin from the French: “école normale.” The U.S. long ago ceased using “normal” in university names, but older U..S. teacher-trainers, and this book, likewise do not recognize this etymology.

title: The definitive work on a remarkable radical thinker
text: Kristin Waters brings overdue attention to Maria W. Stewart, the vanguard Black feminist political writer. An indentured servant who was orphaned at age five, widowed in her 20s, and cheated out of her enterprising husband's estate, Stewart defied racism, sexism, and poverty to become a leading light of early 19th-century "Black revolutionary liberalism." With painstaking research and eloquent prose, Waters shows how Stewart refashioned the ideas of the Enlightenment--by and large the province of well-to-do white men--to suit the abolitionist urgency of a poor Black woman in New England. This book will be a lasting tribute to the formative intellectual years of one of this country's most original and compelling thinkers.

She finally becomes a non-entity, until a random old lady (knowingly?) tosses some lima beans into her furniture. The author obviously needs some serious psychiatric help, and now so does my child.

title: Wickedly funny, but trigger warnings for anxiety
text:
Alexis Hall returns to his Winner Bakes All series for a second book. The setting is a new season of Bake Expectations, a fictional equivalent to The Great British Baking Show This is a stand alone novel but the show judges, director Jennifer (my favorite side character) and the comic relief appear in both books.

Paris Daillencourt is entered into the competition by his roommate Morag. Even though he has great baking skills he is always sure he will be the next person sent home. Fellow contestant Tariq Hassan, is cute, self confident, very gay, and very Muslim. They fall into a the beginnings of a relationship while filming. The focus of the book in not romance but on Paris and his debilitating anxiety. Tariq tries to understand Paris and his thinking, but Paris needs more than to be taken on as a project.

The fun parts of the story include roommates Morag and the four Daves. Bake Expectations casts mates, judges and crew add to the fun mix. The filthy language (over 200 f-bombs) and stream of consciousness rants are hilarious. But the reality is the main character has GAD, general anxiety disorder. And the more I read, the more overwhelming and anxiety inducing the character feels. Hall accurately portrays Paris from blanking out, continually catastrophizing, to having a panic attack. I never understood why his parents didn’t contact him, (which is probably the point since Paris doesn’t understand).

I started out laughing and really liking being back in the baking show world. But the further I went the harder it is to read. It gets repetitive as Paris spirals and I had to force myself not to skim read. I was glad where it ends up and it feels realistic to the characters and their situations. I’m giving it 3 stars with big trigger warnings for people who suffer from anxiety.

title: Another great mystery for V.I. Warshawski, this time in just 36 pages.
text:
Photo Finish is part of the V.I. Warshawski series. It is a very short story (called an eSpecial) published in 2011, between Dead Land and Overboard (so, book 19.5?). It is only available as an ebook. Warshawski (only her closest friends call her Vic) is a law school graduate, now self-employed private eye. She is one of the first female private detectives in Chicago (and in the world of crime fiction). She is smart, tough and (mostly) fearless. At this point in the series she is 50ish, single and living in her hometown of Chicago.

A handsome young man appears at Warshawski’s office claiming to be looking for his long lost father. He is short on details, somewhat vague with his answers and pays the retainer fee in cash. Warshawski is a bit suspicious but begins researching in her typical way, searching various birth records and data bases etc.
What she finds is a tragic story about the death of this young man’s mother.

At just 36 pages there’s not a lot of depth but it is still an enjoyable read. As always, it is fun to see Warshawski put 2 and 2 together. ⭐️⭐️⭐️⭐️

title: Absolutely. *Masterful!*
text: This is the finest example of writing that I have read in decades. I am in awe of this woman's unique ability to craft words into sentences that inspire awe with their beauty and also the depths of their meaning. I am now an enormous fan of Margaret Renkl's writing. I am currently reading her second book, Graceland at Last, Notes on Hope and Heartache From the American South. She is wise and astute. A sharp student of nature and the immense complexity and necessity of its connection with humanity. She writes deftly about why we should care and the urgent consequences to all matter of creation when we haven't and when we don't. Yet, Renkl is not a doomsday writer. She spins a soft web of words around the reader's heart. She cradles that  heart, holding it as it hurts for what is broken and wrong in our world. Meanwhile, she gently pulls the threads that glisten, showing us how, still, this is a beautiful life worth living, and, that, yes, there is redemption. I gave both her books as gifts this holiday. *Brava! Brava!*

title: A steamy romance where a soul is at stake!
text:
This is not your ordinary fantasy romance novel, this one takes steamy to a whole new level. The characters are amazingly depicted and it makes you feel like you can see how they would look in real life. The setting and experiences are beautifully depicted so the story comes alive in your mind as you read it.

We start out meeting Beelzebub who is a demon that we love to hate, as he has the gift of gluttony. We’ve all eaten one too many sweets or overindulged in something we desperately wanted. Beelzebub whispers in his marks ears to always want more, always have more so he can mark their souls and send them to hell when they pass without them knowing what they are getting into. That is until he meets Clara who can’t be swayed by his ministrations. This is where the fun starts and Beelzebub starts to change his outlook and his mannerisms which catches the eyes of others. Now Clara is caught in a battle for those wanting to claim her that tests each entity and their actions. Can Clara make it out unscathed or will her soul be caught up in a civil war in the bowels of hell?

If you like steamy romance novels with a fantasy twist on angels and demons then you should definitely read this book. I became lost in the pages and couldn’t stop reading once I started. I just had to know what happened next. This is a book full of characters you’ll love to hate and others you simply love!

title: Refreshing character study
text:
I’m just coming off reading books with similar character traits: The Rosie Project and Eleanor Oliphant is Completely Fine. This book allows the reader into the mind of a person with autism in ways the other two did not. It’s not up to me to determine if it’s 100% accurate, but having traits myself and having a friend with a child on the spectrum opened my eyes to how behavior manifests and why.

It’s a sad and uplifting story all at once. The parents are incredibly ill equipped to care for Christopher. They get a few things right, but other things dreadfully wrong. As a result Christopher figures out how to fend for himself. Situations arise where he could just lay on the floor rocking and screaming but he figures out how to handle them in his own way by using math and logic. I found this fascinating and eye opening as I’ve approached some things in life in a similar fashion.

The way the book is written may not be for everyone, but it resonated with me and seemed accurate for a 15 year old boy on the spectrum. Best so far of all the books I’ve read with characters on the spectrum.

title: Ingenious faux Victorian novel
text:
I haven't enjoyed a (fiction) book this much in a long time. Of course, I was partial to it from the beginning since I also enjoy Collins and other Victorian authors (with the exception of Dickens, who seems grossly overrated to me), as well as modern works inspired by those (such as Cox, The meaning of night, or Palliser, The Quincunx).
This book hits the Victorian style pitch perfect. It is also ingeniously constructed around events from Collins's and Dickens's lives, with some of their writings thrown in for good measure. It is at the same time a very funny book, being a gentle parody of the Victorian sensationalist novel, and an intriguing mystery.

I am surprised this masterpiece didn't do better in the amazon ratings. The main reason for this seems to be what other reviewers perceived as a too slow overall pace, but of course a leisurely pace is exactly what one should expect in a Victorian novel, real or recreated.

title: Great Series Conclusion!
text:
A Home for the Stars by Laura Kemp is book three in The Lantern Creek Series. In my opinion this is not a stand alone novel and you need to read the first two books in her series to enjoy the conclusion. You will be lost otherwise. I've read the first two books and it took me a while to figure it all out and put the pieces together. I admit I am not as young as I used to be and I've read a lot of books between the second book in the series and this one so my memory took a bit to kick in. I wound up loving this conclusion to the series.

I loved her characters and worried throughout the book that Justine was going to change the future and would not be with Dylan in the end. I'm not going to tell you how this all comes out in the wash. I will tell you the majority of the book takes place years ago. Justine is transported back in time and meets her ancestors. Now, I think that would be awesome. Don't you?

I fell in love with this series at page one of book one. I encourage you to read all three books. You're going to love this series. It is different but, it is subtle in the beginning. I think the best way to read them is one right after another. When I finished book one, I had a hard time moving on to another book. I wanted more of Justine's story. Now, you can start at the beginning and read your way through them and avoid any confusion at the end and satisfy your need to know more.

In short my Michigan gal has done it again! I was hopelessly in love at the end of A Home for the Stars. I dreamt about Justine and her family, travels and experiences all night last night! That my friends is the sign of a good book.

I received a complimentary copy of this book from the author. Opinions expressed in this review are completely my own.

title: Fun, enchanting, and a classic Lauren Blakely romcom
text:
Oh, Harlan, you wonderful swoony man, you are the stuff of romcom dreams! You're just what our girl Katie needs to shake her out of her funk and get the love and happily-ever-after that she deserves, even though it took YEARS for the two of you to find your way back to each other.

Katie and Harlan's meet cute is told in the ebook A Wild Card Night, which is included in the audiobook of A Wild Card Kiss. They meet at a wedding, the feel an amazing instant connection. They're perfect for each other. But their timing isn't right, and they go their separate ways, only to reunite the day of Katie's wedding gone awry.

From the minute they find each other again, Harlan knows that Katie is the one that got away, the one that he wants to make happy, the one that he just needs to be around. There are plenty of obstacles in their way, professionally and emotionally, but they are just so good together that why would you put a love like that on hold? You wouldn't! Lauren Blakely writes such a compelling, fun, and utterly enchanting romance that not only do the the lead characters fall in love with each other, but the reader falls in love with them, too. How could I not love the woman that shows up at the bowling alley alone after her failed wedding, and the man that is content to the be the friend she needs until he can be more?

The audio, narrated by Erin Mallon and Zachary Webber, is perfect for these two characters. Erin and Zachary are both able to bring so much humor and earnestness to their portrayals. They bring it all - emotion, heartbreak, longing, humor and sizzle. They are two of the finest voice actors narrating, and it's always a treat to listen to them.

title: Great book which answers questions people are asking
text:
This is one of the best and most engaging books I've read about issues of daily life and faith that I have read in quite some time. With years of experience as a scientist, author, and pastor, Nate Aaseng has pulled together reflections that most folks in the pews want to read, One of the challenges with the modern church is that we seem to continue to argue and debate issues that don't connect with daily life. We seem to answer questions that nobody is still asking. Yet in this volume Aaseng addresses 28 straightforward questions that most human beings seem to ask at some point along the faith journey. And, in doing so, he honors the fact that sometimes we as believers have doubts about faith along the way, and that God is okay with this.

This is not a collection of sermons, but each subject addressed could easily be converted into sermon material that any congregation would benefit from. The writing is very easy to read and follow, almost conversational. It is well reasoned and logical, but also is open to the unknown, the unanswerable, and a freedom to ask questions about the God who is larger than our understanding.

This is a wonderful gift to any Christian who has questions, doubts, or curiosities. And it is also a wonderful source of reassurance to those who may not have these questions burning in their hearts now, but remember the time that we did. With a true pastor's heart, author's pen, and scientist's mind mind, Aaseng has pulled together a wonderful source of encouragement and hope for any believer. I highly commend this book to anyone who seeks to follow Jesus Christ in the 21st century.
