title: Excellent story, somewhat misleading description
text:
River of the Gods is a fantastic, thoroughly researched tale, and there could be no better writer to tell it. Millard's writing is engaging, scholarly, and sensitive, and I found the book hard to put down. For all these reasons, I hesitate to give it anything but five stars.

But I am docking the book a point for one glaring problem: It is NOT the story of three explorers, as the jacket description and cover art imply it to be. It is still very much the story of Burton and Speke, the two Europeans whose tale has already been told in past accounts.

The third man pictured on the cover and described on the jacket, Sidi Mubarak Bombay, makes no appearance until deep into the book. He is then given a couple of pages of biography, after which he is mentioned only intermittently throughout the rest of the saga. His story is only briefly fleshed out in any more detail in a few pages of the epilogue.

This was quite disappointing to me. I specifically read this book because I was interested in a different, less Euro-centric Nile-discovery story--I was intrigued by the jacket description. The cover implied that this book would be that story, but as I read it, the mentions of Bombay always felt tantalizingly incomplete. He is also a very two-dimensional character and quite idealized, whereas Burton and Speke are described in all their complexity. They were certainly more flawed men than Bombay was--but surely he wasn't quite as perfect as he comes across?

There is clearly a great deal more to Bombay's life story than was included here. Millard briefly mentions his time spent enslaved in India, and even more briefly, his successful explorations of Africa after his Nile journeys. It's possible these elements of his life weren't detailed because this book centers on the hunt for the source of the Nile, but that doesn't fully explain the omission. We are given a long account of Burton's journey to Mecca prior to his Nile exploration, and additional, briefer accounts of Burton's various consulate postings, his ongoing conflict with Speke, his journey to the American West, and the evolution of his thinking about race after the Nile journey is complete. Nothing like that amount of detail is given about Bombay's life either before or after the expedition to the Nile.

I find this a bit baffling, because Millard clearly did make an effort to tell a fairer, less racist, and more inclusive story than past Nile-exploration accounts have been. She included Bombay in the first place, and she also unflinchingly described racist views held by Burton, Speke, and many of their contemporaries. Her language throughout the text was sensitive, for instance, using the term "enslaved person" rather than "slave."

My best guess is that Millard set out to write a book about Burton and Speke, and along the way discovered that Bombay deserved accolades in his own right. Maybe she discovered this too late, though, and needed to write Bombay's story and accolades in as afterthoughts because she had already designed a loose book structure around Burton and Spekes' stories.

The result, unfortunately, is that Sidi Mubarak Bombay's story is still largely untold. While this book does him more justice than past accounts, it does NOT treat his story with the kind of rigor and detail given to Burton and Speke. This book is very much about them.

All that said, it is still a story very well told.

title: Addresses varied disciplines, but audiobook format makes it tough to follow
text:
Academic writing has a reputation for being a bit dry and only interested in the dissemination of abstract information. Concreteness, style, and vivacity often fall to the wayside. As Sword points out, much of this dryness is due to social structures, not deliberate mastery of the craft. This book teaches how to bring a sense of style to academic writing without compromising its informational purposes.

By examining 1,000 academic papers in ten different fields, Sword compiles a list of examples of good and bad practices. The style of writing is often dependent on one’s field of study. This style, in turn, is enforced culturally by educators and institutionally by editors of journals. Fortunately, by Sword’s analysis, many journals allow and encourage a lucid style. Why then does such a dry style persist among so many writers? People have been told, over and over again, that “this is just how it is.” Or they have been discouraged from taking risks by one or two people on dissertation or tenure committees.

Sword hopes to free us writers from those shadowy shackles by showing little ways to make communication more effective. There’s no inherent rule that academic writing has to be dry, and overly abstract writing is simply ineffective and bad, not helpful. Not every writer will feel freedom to try every suggested tool, but every reader should be able to come away with some new approach to try out. The biggest obstacles cited are fear and anxiety. The ten very different fields examined demonstrate style can be found everywhere – if we only would have the verve to use it.

The biggest shortcoming of this book lies in its format. I listened to it as an audiobook and found myself wanting to consult the examples visually. Many tangential pericopes fill the text – usually a good feature – but these were hard to follow audibly. I suspect reading the print version would solve this problem squarely.

Obviously, this book seeks to address communicators across many fields who write for academic audiences. Those who write for popular journals or newspapers may find this book of limited use. By using abundant examples, Sword’s study seeks to be relevant to basic sciences like medicine as much as the social sciences or even the humanities. When not used to excess but still not eschewed, style facilitates communication and makes academic studies full of more intrinsic impact. Though immensely important, academic words can lose lingering power by becoming drier than they have to be, but Sword teaches how to resuscitate them back to life.

title: Exceptional!
text:
What an exceptional ending to the U.S. Marshals series, or is it? The story of U.S. Deputy Marshal Madison James and Jonas Quinn starts with the first book of the series titled, The Escape, followed by The Chase. Now, in The Catch, audiences will read the exciting revelation of who killed Madison’s husband Luke so many years ago. Audiences don’t have to read the first two books in the series to enjoy the novel though there are some exciting events that happen with the two main characters as the author puts enough background in this book to catch up anyone who has missed out.
The Catch is filled with twists and turns in the continuous action as Madison and Jonas provide protection to victims of a multitude of crimes, as well as try to locate a missing woman with the child she was watching. Throughout the book, it seems like Madison and Jonas never get time alone to discuss if their friendship is becoming more for either of them. On top of that, Madison is still working through her grief of losing her husband and finding his killer.
I enjoyed the various secondary characters like Piper who is bright and locates information for the two marshals sometimes before they even make a request. The other characters that have interesting, developing stories are Becca and Ava and their friendship of a sort. Trust seems to be an issue for both but wait till you read why these two women are very careful with who they give information to!
I enjoy reading Lisa Harris’ novels that blend faith, romance, and suspense into well-crafted tales. The only issue I ever had with the series is waiting a year between the release of each book. For avid readers such as I, it isn’t hard to forget the nuances of a story when so much time elapses between installments. However, I cannot wait to see what Lisa pens next for us to enjoy. So, grab the book and enjoy a time of adventurous romance!

title: Another Satisfying "Big" Book from Diana Gabaldon
text:
I had this newest "big" "Outlander" series book ordered for delivery as soon as it came out at Thanksgiving, 2021. Why have I just now read it? I read too many comments on a fan site, which didn't allow spoilers for the first six months, but the comments seemed to feel that Ms Gabaldon had written a lot of lovely scenes but there wasn't much action. It sounded like there was a bunch about William, who honestly isn't my favorite character.
However, I actually thoroughly enjoyed all 902 pages of it! I found a nice balance of lovely scenes to action scenes, and really enjoyed the through-line of Claire's new bee hives brought to her at the beginning of the book and which give the book its title. There's plenty of Jamie and Claire (never enough, though) w/ Jamie fighting in yet another battle in which he doesn't want to actually fight; lots of Roger and Bree; and I wasn't nearly as annoyed by William's plot line as I thought I would be, b/c William's plot line also featured Lord John Grey, my absolute favorite secondary character in Gabaldon's books. "Bees..." also sets us up w/ plenty of mystery to be solved in Big Book #10 - whenever that will be written - w/ danger coming from Roger and Bree's "present-day" (1980ish) plot line. I plan to re-read it again soon, to pick up nuances I missed from the first reading. 5 out of 5 stars, enthusiastically.

This book is a great story about a deadly pandemic sweeping the country and its effects on the residents of a youth correctional facility. There really wasn't any mistreatment or 'misgendering' portrayed by any adult in the facility; there was more mistreatment among/between the residents. I would have enjoyed the book more if not for the author trying to make a gender statement. The author's note afterward mentioned that she purposefully made all of the characters Caucasian to prevent race issues from obscuring the gender issues. She didn't need to worry about this because the characters could have been any race based on their names and reactions. Even so, the story is a good read.

title: Black Love Song
text:
Honoree Fanonne Jeffers has created a brilliant master piece in this sweeping historical fiction. It is a love song to everything Black culture and a epic in its scope. It reminded me of Marquez’s “100 Years of Solitude” but with the magical realism expressed in the emotional kaleidoscope of the Black and Native experience in America from time immemorial. You will not get through this fast. Resign yourself to be only a long spiritual journey through a family against the racially tinged struggle that is America.

If you venture to read “The Love Songs…” please please please first read “The Souls of Black Folk,” “The 1619 Project,” “Caste,” and any other books you can on the unabashed history of America. You cannot truly appreciate the fiction part of this historical fiction until the gritty history is baked into your DNA. Only then will you realize how brilliantly Jeffers has weaved in multiple narratives and threads into this one tome. Through her well thought out characters we get an all too personalized retelling of our collective history as it concerns every facet of life.

Those deep dives into various topics make every page a journey of historical reckoning, navigating academia and it’s rigors, love and loss, race relations, blood ties, and so much more. The bitter reality it is painted against makes the collective stories feel like our own in a laugh out loud, cry out when triggered, reflective in others kind of way. It is everyone’s story and Ailey’s at the same time. I sincerely believe W.E.B Du Bois would have been proud of Jeffers bringing his long cherished pieces into the present with what I think has to be her Magnum Opus.

title: Complex with a Shocking Conclusion
text:
What’s it about (in a nutshell):
Two Nights in Lisbon by Chris Pavone is a thriller about the disappearance of Ariel Price’s husband and everything that follows, including different investigations and a complicatedly twisted plot for justice.

Initial Expectations (before beginning the book):
Looking at the book cover, I think of old James Bond movies because it has a 70s look. But the blurb is a whole different kind of description. It talks about a husband disappearing from the hotel the couple stayed at while in Lisbon on business – which would be more of a domestic thriller. Two Nights in Lisbon is quite a lengthy book for the genre, so it seems like it may be a complicated tale.

Actual Reading Experience:
I love the writing style the author used in telling this thriller. It’s in third-person narration but switches perspectives in small scenes within each chapter. You learn about Ariel’s past and present, how she works to save her missing husband through her eyes, and the investigation through a reporter, the local police, and the CIA, who are all three doing independent research and discovery. The way the story is written helped take a pretty lengthy tome and make it read relatively quickly.

The story tackles a few social injustices, predominantly how women are not listened to, especially when they try to alert people about sexual assault and rape. The story also talks about media, power differentials, and politics. There are a few soapbox moments, but I only mildly took note of them as they had the capability of pulling me a bit out of the story.

I loved the twists and turns the story took. It was quite dizzying at times as the story changed quickly, and the plot doubled back on itself. I was very right about it being a complicated tale. There are so many layers, and fortunately, all my questions found answers by the end, which satisfied me. I only wish the story had been a bit more streamlined, as I didn’t believe the length felt justified. I thought that large parts reiterated what had been told, and character histories rambled slightly.

Characters:
Ariel is the main character and the only one I got to know. She’s a bit elusive, very private, and has many anxieties/fears. Yet, she is strong and independent, never tolerating injustices or feeling happy to sweep things under the rug. She preferred to stand up for herself and others.

To Read or Not to Read:
Two Nights in Lisbon will bring you to a world full of thrills and twists and give you an international thriller encompassing many social issues and investigative bodies.

title: Historical flashbacks done to perfection
text:
I don't often read historical fiction because it's often repetitive or slow-paced. This book was such an inventive way of presenting a historical love story, alongside a modern one. I think it's the best example of using flashbacks that I've ever read. She juxtaposes a colonial woman's love story with a modern career woman's love story in a way that brings out the nuance in both of their situations. The side characters are also reasonably well developed, so that we understand some of their motivations or see growth in those characters too. Oh, and it has some spooky mansion vibes too!

This is my first book by Susanna Kearsley, but I will definitely be reading more.

***SPOILERS***
***The rest of this post is how SLAVERY WAS REPRESENTED IN AN HONEST WAY, but please read if it would make you more comfortable before picking up the book.***

This book does discuss slavery, but the way it's done didn't make me uncomfortable like some other historical fiction. This an intellectually honest white person's view on a black person's potential experiences in colonial America. There are several reasons for that.

1. None of the main characters support slavery, but that's contrasted with two side characters being manipulative in their treatment of other people. The author wisely represented that to enslave another human being reveals a broken moral character and greed for dominance in general. Those two side characters are cruel and calculating towards several people of their own race too, which I think is highly plausible.
2. The main character's family tries to prevent mistreatment of Violet at the hands of the two side characters, even though it causes financial hardship for them at one point. However, Violet is still a slave, and her viewpoint is represented well. She is NOT portrayed as overly grateful for "saving" her from their uncle, which is fair because she still doesn't have free will to go or to do whatever she wants. However, Violet does set boundaries and then reminds family members about her boundaries and/or the truth about her position as outsider.
3. Another side character is introduced who is a black man, and the revelation of his background and he and Violet's story together is intriguing.
4. The characters from the modern storyline discover that Violet existed and fight to have her story included at the local museum, and it realistically (but admittedly perhaps mildly) shows the pushback that could occur on starting that initiative. (They're successful, btw.)

text: This 700+ pages book is aimed at general public (and not at professional historians, c.f. the 1-star review which missed this point).  It provides a very readable summary of the entire history of Poland (in Part I), and then proceeds to cover the entire life of Joseph Pilsudski - as the Insurrectionist, the War Hero and the Head of State.  Book's author is, by his own admission, not a "professional historian" but may be because of that he wrote a book that is very accessible to a general reader, who is likely not familiar with the history of modern Poland in particular, and much of Central and Eastern Europe more broadly.  And yet, this history (in the XIXth and XXth century, if not before) had many "lessons learned" useful not only to understand Pilsudski's life and accomplishments, but (tragically and unexpectedly) to put the latest developments in Ukraine in their historical context.  Thus I recommend this book not only to those who want to learn more about Pilsudski and the resurrection of Poland, but also to everyone who wants to expand their understanding of Russia and its behavior, which (in its imperial ambitions and unbounded cruelty) is unchanged for several centuries.

title: A Suspenseful Coming-of-Age Mystery
text:
Our Little World transports the reader back to 1985, when almost-seventh-grader Bee Kocsis is enjoying a carefree summer, until her neighbor’s little sister goes missing from the nearby lake. What was thought to be a safe community is upended by the failure to find the girl, and people start to stick to themselves and grow suspicious. Even within her home, Bee is finding the relationship with her sister to become strained in the wake of their neighbor’s disappearance.

This is a strong, gripping coming-of-age story that follows Bee as she navigates the sudden change in her community and the ensuing confusion brought on by adolescence. Bee is dealing with complicated family dynamics and learning that things aren’t always as she expects.

While this read did leave me with nostalgia for the ease of life in the 80s, it did hammer home that a story such as this could happen anywhere. Our Little World is a great choice if you’re in the mood for a suspenseful mystery.

text:
An amazing collection of deeply philosophical stories that also entertain.

"The Future is Female! Volume Two." contains 23 stories by such renowned authors as Ursula K. Le Guin, James Tiptree, JR, Connie Willis, and others.

Each story is well written with a definite message. They are all creative and worthy to read. They tend to be dark, ranging from tantalizingly confusing dystopian to reassuringly comfortable dystopian to entertainingly and/or humorously dystopian to oddly disturbingly dystopian to thought-provoking dystopian to sadly understandable dystopian to terrifyingly real dystopian to psychologically depressingly dystopian to abjectly horrifying end-of-the-world in a really really bad way dystopian.

In all honestly, a few stories did not deserve my overly general "dystopian" label. For example, the story of an alien assigned to represent his species as an ambassador at the United Planet was more humorous and entertaining than dystopian. Though one has to feel sorry for the poor alien since things did not exactly work out according to his plan. Another story was downright amusing in the conclusion that time travel to the past can not be easily used to solve dystopian problems. And one of the stories that felt dystopian had an absolutely happy ending, but I can't go in any detail since that would be a spoiler...

I absolutely recommend this book to the discerning thinking reader, and look forward to Volume Three of this series.

I thank the editor, authors, and publisher for kindly sharing a temporary electronic review copy of this work. Thank you!

title: Storyville Prostitutes
text:
Storyville was a legalized red light district in New Orleans that functioned beginning in 1897 until it was closed in 1917 under pressure from the military. In 1912, an obscure commercial photographer, E.J. Bellocq (1873 -- 1949) made a series of photographs of prostitutes working in Storyville. The photos were little-known until they were shown at an exhibition of the Museum of Modern Art in 1970. MOMA published a book of the photographs in 1970 that went out-of-print and was subsequently expanded in 1996 into this book, "Bellocq: Photographs from Storyville, The Red-Light District of New Orleans" which also appears to be now out-of-print. The book includes 52 of Bellocq's photographs as compared with the 34 of the MOMA volume and includes as well an introduction by Susan Sontag and interviews about Bellocq and his photos.

Bellocq seems to have taken these photos simply for himself but their origin remains unknown. The highly evocative photographs have come to symbolize Storyville. Bellocq's carefully posed photos show some of the women in full dress while others are nude. The photos manage to be both revealing of the character of their subjects and also enigmatic. They also allow a glimpse at the interiors of Storyville brothels, which have long been destroyed.

I recently revisited this book of Storyville prostitutes after many years. There is something fascinating about this place and its women. Bellocq's photos get inside his subjects and allow viewers to reflect upon the women and their lives.

Bellocq's photographs have a distant echo in the famous photographer Susan Meiselas' book "Carnival Strippers" which documents the women working in girlie shows in small New England carnivals in the early 1970s. These carnivals, like the Storyville brothels, are no more. As did Bellocq, Meiselas was able to win the trust of her subjects and to provide insight through her photography into their lives. Meiselas' book has been re-issued in several editions, most recently in "Carnival Strippers-- Revisited" (2022) which I have reviewed here on Amazon. Bellocq's and Meiselas' photographs capture something of the mysterious nature of human sexuality when it is commodified, but never lost.

Robin Friedman

title: Story is a bit more fantastical than others, but still fantastically gripping
text:
Let's face it, Box lets his usual anti-federal-government feelings run away from him on this one. I'm sure it plays well in rural western states where most of the land is owned by the American people, but still a fun read.

Extrapolating from (and oversimplifying) the Pickett vs EPA case in Idaho, Box concocts a story of a federal bureaucrat drunk with power. Of all the bad-guy tropes in the Pickett novels - ne'er-do-well locals (or Southerners), corrupt county officials, greedy developers, power-crazed plutocrats, environmental (or anti-government) evangelists, rogue Special Forces spooks - the craven bureaucrat is his favorite. Some of the "all I care about is retiring with my pension" nonsense about bureaucrats is exaggerated beyond the grain of truth to almost lose any credulity.

Almost, but not quite. Even if the setup completely strains reasonable belief, maybe it's the over-the-top ridiculousness that makes this runaway freight train of a novel one of my favorites. Just set aside a few hours and enjoy more twists and turns than a log ride on the Twelve Sleep River through Savage Run canyon laden with wildfire smoke.

A Better Part of Valor is the 3rd book in the series, but can stand alone very well. This book is a strong, seamless continuation of the series. I loved reuniting with my favorite characters, especially Val, Beth, and Gil. There are also several new and captivating characters we get to know.
I’m not traditionally a fan of police procedurals, but the Val Dawes series definitely had me hooked. The plot of this book is clever af, with twists and complexities that kept me guessing the whole time. The attention to detail is fantastic, and each character comes to life. Corbin’s character developments continue to impress me, and this book (like the others) leaves me wanting to know what’s next for everyone. My favorite relationship is the fond mentor/friendship/(maybe more??) between Gil and Val. It’s great to see her opening up to him and gaining a comfort she’s never allowed herself to feel, especially with men. And how can you not love Gil? He’s just the best. The ending was equal parts thrilling, terrifying, and immensely satisfying. The shifting POV in the third act ratchets up the suspense and adds a great glimpse of a truly evil mind into the narration. Another great read from Corbin!

title: Required Reading For Every Thinking Person
text:
Many of the critical reviews are about Kennedy accusing Bill Gates and Fauci conspiring to make money off the vaccines. Anyone that thinks Bill Gates and Anthony Fauci aren't motivated by money.......how did Bill become the richest man in the world, and how did Fauci become the highest paid bureaucrat in our government? When there's billions of dollars involved, it's safe to make the assumption that the people handling it are going to get some for themselves. A congressperson might not be rich when he enters office, but you can bet they'll be a multi-millionaire by the time their term is over.

It's obvious the vaccine push has been for profit - children didn't need the vaccine, and they were at no risk from Covid. Yet, the vaccine was forced on them, and, sure enough, the sick and dead numbers started mounting up almost immediately. The big pharmaceutical corporations exist to make money, and they couldn't lose in this situation -- no liability (how did that ever get through Congress, unless it was bought and paid for?). All they had to do was discredit other treatments, and they were home free.

It's amazed me throughout the past two years how much of the public has accepted Fauci's pronunciations without question, and even demonized those who didn't agree. Talk about sheep being led to the slaughter.

title: An Incredible Audiobook
text:
America is supposedly a beautiful country, full of opportunity for everyone. This is a memoir about the author’s journey of moving from China to the United States as a young kid, and growing up undocmented in America. And she quickly discovers that America is not exactly the beautiful country she’d envisioned.

She describes her family’s struggles to make a life here, to survive here. And we see how the fear that comes from being undocumented will stay with her for a long, long time. The author had a difficult childhood. They are poor and she and her mom work in a sweatshop to make money. She is constantly malnourished because there is not enough money to feed her properly. It was heartbreaking to read about how she doesn’t want to burden her parents with her hunger.

A few times she mentions her love for reading and how books kept her company when she didn’t have anyone else. She also writes about poor treatment from some of her teachers- how they underestimate her and how she succeeds despite them.

I listened to this book on audio (I love listening to a memoir when it’s narrated by the author) and I thought the audiobook was great. I felt she did a really good job of writing from a child’s perspective, which is not an easy thing to do. This was a beautiful memoir of the author’s experience of growing up as an immigrant in America and a stark reminder of the fact that America does not treat all of its people equally.

title: A New Yorker in Finland
text: For someone who has lived most of her life in big cities (Tokyo & New York), Naomi Moriyama discovers living in Finland's Karelia area is like nothing she's ever experienced. She describes being in the Finnish forest as "a reality that has fed (her) body and soul". She lived among Finnish women, not as a tourist but as a temporary resident, so she was able to make personal connections not available to someone who is just visiting the country. Also having her young son and husband along, allowed her to experience Finland's educational system, which is far superior to the U.S.  Her research and references on Finland's history and society were more in depth than I expected. But what I perceive as her naivety about forest living and gathering edibles, is why I gave the book four out of five stars. Since I experienced "forest bathing" as a child, I took much of what Naomi said about the forest as a given, and felt her "mystical" experiences in the woods seemed a little over blown. I also never saw the woods as a source of food. There is very little to eat there for humans. Mushrooms are not that nourishing and identifying them should be left to an experienced mycologist.  With that caveat in mind, I would recommend this book as a short course in Finnish sociology and gender roles.

text: It’s been six months since Freddier Munroe’s sister, Kaylee, committed suicide and he just can’t seem to move on with his life.  He blames himself for not being there for his sister on the night that she took her own life.  His parents decide to send Freddie to a therapist in the hopes that she will be able to help him cope..  The therapist recommends that Freddie spend time in Kaylee’s room and think about the times that they spent together. Freddie works up the courage to enter her room. title: A Moment that lasts 30 min
text:
Ben Aaronovitch has written many story-like things that he calls "Moments" as part of his Rivers of London series. These are charming and informative vignettes that mostly present one character at a moment in time. I call them story-like because, unlike what we usually call stories, they do not really have plots. I think they're great.

He also wrote this one story, A Rare Book of Cunning Device for Cityread London 2017. It is available only as an audiobook, or at least that was the only form I found. (Edit 22-Apr-2022: this story is also included in the story collection Tales from the Folly.) As it happened, I needed (for the first time in two years -- Covid strikes again!) to take a longish drive (four hours), so I was in the market for audiobooks. This one was too brief to satisfy, but served to whet the appetite for another Aaronovitch audiobook.

It felt very like one of Aaronovitch's Moments although it takes Kobna Holdbrook-Smith (the voice of Peter Grant) 30 min to read it. The main characters are Peter, Postmartin, and a new one, Elsie “Hatbox” Winstanley, a librarian in the British Library. Peter has been called in to investigate some strange happenings in the British Library. The three of them eventually identify the source of the disturbance. However, its origin and eventual disposition are left mostly up in the air.

This lack of a real finished plot is what made it feel to me like one of Aaronovitch's Moments. It was fun, but I would have liked something a little more finished in return for half an hour of my time.

title: A straightforward storytelling adventure...
text:
James's "exile" is a nice surprise and an enjoyable read. Unlike many fantasy/science fiction books, with a lot of florish and embellishments, Solomon's Exile is a clean and well-written, straightforward tale. I was surprised because it is not the prose style I usually read; this book is about the narrative and the story as it unfolds. I felt like I was right in the story watching it as a unseen observer, not distracted by unnecessary "garnishment"-which is all too often overdone in many fantasy stories.
Mr. Maxstadt does a fine job in being economical and direct in his writing; I mean this as a high compliment. It is one of the hardest things to do well as a writer and not diminish from the work and story. His style was reminiscent to me of the science fiction and fantasy I enjoyed reading from the Authors of the 1950's and 60's.
Solomon's Exile is a good read, and should be appealing to all readers of different genres.

title: Fabulous Resource
text: I’ve had a real struggle to know how to cook for my husband, who had a massive heart attack several months ago. It’s really hard for a salt lover (me) to suddenly have to figure out how to adapt to using NO added salt. Because of the salt issue, eating out is a rarity now, and cooking the same few dishes over and over has gotten old and tiresome for both of us. This book has great info, but the information is plainly stated and to the point. The recipes include how many grams of salt are in each ingredient, since salt is naturally in meats, vegetables, etc., and it all adds up. That alone is valuable information. I finally understand why meals that I thought were low salt, actually had more salt in them than I realized. I could tell that my husband was getting too much salt because he weighs himself every day, and when it suddenly goes up overnight, it’s water retention, due to too much salt. I was so frustrated and anxious trying to figure out what I was doing wrong. There are no photos, which doesn’t bother me, since it has such a nice variety of recipes, and I’ve been cooking long enough that just reading the ingredients and instructions lets me know if it’s worth trying. Pretty pictures don’t always mean tasty food. I may have to adapt some of the recipes that call for sugar, since my husband is diabetic, but there are also many that would require no substitutions, even for diabetics. I feel hopeful and encouraged for the first time in a long time, that cooking low salt but enjoyable meals may actually be possible.

title: Stop Victimhood Questions and Replace the Productive Proactive Questions
text:
This is a must read I think for people in leadership roles but also for the people in any organization there are a lot of quick stories with the same take away. What can I do: to make this work better, to motivate my team, to add value to...etc. It is a mindset that I think everyone needs to try and get into if they are in a leadership role.

I recently left the company I had been working for the last twelve years and the awesome team I had cultivated there. Going into a new company and new culture was a little scary and I wasn't sure what to expect. In some ways the company culture is better and in some ways it was worse. There are always trade offs right, but starting with a new team I found there were a few people in it that played the blame game actively and while some statements made might be true they weren't productive to getting work done.

The Question Behind the Question (QBQ) is a great starter book to identify when you are asking an incorrect question as opposed to a productive question. For example some of the incorrect questions management asks are things like:

"Why doesn't the younger generation want to work?"
"When will we find good people?"
"Why aren't they motivated?"
"Who made the mistake?"
"When will they get ingaged?"

While those are questions they really fall into a victimhood stance of things happening to you. There is nothing proactive in those statements, nothing that you are doing to fix these issues. Some better questions would be:

"How can I be a more effective coach?"
"What can I do to better understand each person I manage?"
"How can I build a stronger team?"

I think this is a must have fast read for anyone in management. Some managers don't capitalize on the differences of their teams and instead trying to treat everyone the same and I have found that is a horrible way to operate. Instead it is better to identify what are the strengths and weaknesses of all the team members and help they play to their strengths while developing their weaknesses.

This is a short enough book that I assigned it to a few of the people on my team I'm trying to develop for future leaders but also used some of the examples in our weakly meetings to talk about and identify how to change mindsets and work together to do less finger pointing and more how can I help fix this issue. I'm fortunate in a lot of ways there are so many tools to already do that but there are always areas of improvement and times that victim thinking needs to be squashed and this book will help with some tools of how to change the script from victim questions into something that is proactive and productive.

title: An Interesting Take on an ABC Book
text:
This is not your traditional ABC book for younger kids, although it could still appeal to the younger ones who are beyond their years intellectually. With the attached learning activities and lesson plans, this book would be great for homeschoolers and classrooms alike.
Overall, I like this book, mainly because it’s so unique compared to other ABC books and because, with the advanced vocabulary, it’s suited to older kids for whom you wouldn’t normally think to buy an ABC book.
Unfortunately, the illustration style ruins it for me. Many of the pictures seem unclear and too busy, and as a result, they detract from the story rather than enhancing it. Also, for the letter D, I noticed it’s Lillian’s blue-sleeved arm “drenching the diamond duchesses” rather than Zoe’s bare arm, which is opposite of what the words say.

title: A loving paean to his craft
text:
If you’ve read Richard Morgan’s past works – if you haven’t, you should – you know that he’s passionate about poetry as an art form as well as his own instrument of expression. Morgan is a maestro; his creativity and ability to capture a range of emotions, experiences and life observations are a treat.

Now, in his latest book, Richard pays homage to poetry, the art form itself, in the manner at which he’s a master: in poetry! And true to form, it’s delightful reading. A loving look at the genesis of an idea, the artist who gives it life, and the craftsmanship that transforms it into poetry.

“Poems on Poems and Poets” is unique, a creative tour de force, filled with whimsy, thoughtfulness, and reverence for the poets of the world – the famous and the not-so-famous. He loves them all, and you’ll love this poetic tribute.
